structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: The preface introduces the convergence and recent advances of pattern recognition and machine learning, especially Bayesian methods, graphical models, approximate inference, and kernels, and explains the textbook's broad scope, intended audience, prerequisites, reference policy, and online resources. It describes chapter exercises, difficulty ratings, solution availability, and the practical companion volume with Matlab code. The remainder acknowledges institutional, editorial, technical, permissions, reviewing, and personal support received during the book's preparation, concluding with the author's signature and date.

structure.title: Mathematical notation
structure.summary: The text first establishes the book’s intuitive mathematical philosophy and defines its vector, matrix, interval, identity-matrix, functional, asymptotic, statistical, covariance, and data-matrix notation. It then presents the complete contents of a comprehensive pattern-recognition and machine-learning book, spanning foundational probability and decision theory; probability distributions; regression and classification; neural networks; kernel and sparse methods; graphical and mixture models; approximate inference and sampling; latent-variable and sequential-data models; model combination; exercises; and appendices on data sets, distributions, and matrix properties.

nodes.title: 1 Introduction
1.1. Example: Polynomial Curve Fitting
nodes.summary: The text introduces pattern recognition through polynomial regression on noisy samples of sin(2πx). It defines polynomial models and least-squares fitting, illustrates underfitting, good fit, overfitting, model selection, RMS training/test errors, the effects of coefficient growth and data-set size, and the relationship to maximum likelihood and Bayesian modeling. It then presents regularization, including ridge regression and neural-network weight decay, showing how λ controls coefficient shrinkage, effective complexity, and generalization, and discusses validation-set model selection. Finally, it begins probability theory as a framework for uncertainty and introduces random variables and limiting-frequency probability using a two-box fruit-selection example.

nodes.title: 1.2. Probability Theory
1.2.1 Probability densities
nodes.summary: The text explains Bayes’ theorem through a fruit-box example, emphasizing the distinction between prior and posterior probabilities and illustrating how evidence can outweigh prior beliefs. It defines independence through factorization of joint probabilities. It then introduces continuous probability densities, their normalization and interval probabilities, cumulative distribution functions, transformation under changes of variables via the Jacobian, multivariate and mixed discrete-continuous distributions, and the extension of the sum, product, and Bayes rules to densities. Finally, it defines expectations as probability-weighted sums or integrals and begins discussing their estimation from finite samples.

nodes.title: 1.2.2 Expectations and covariances
nodes.summary: The text explains probability densities and their normalization, extensions to discrete and mixed variables, and the applicability of probability rules such as marginalization and factorization. It then defines expectations for discrete, continuous, sampled, multivariable, and conditional settings, followed by variance and covariance formulas for scalar and vector random variables, including the fact that independent variables have zero covariance.

nodes.title: 1.2.3 Bayesian probabilities
nodes.summary: The text introduces Bayesian probability as a coherent framework for quantifying and updating uncertainty, contrasting it with frequentist probability based on repeatable frequencies. It motivates Bayesian inference through rationality axioms, presents Bayes’s theorem and the roles of priors, likelihoods, posteriors, and evidence, and applies these ideas to uncertain model parameters. It contrasts Bayesian inference with maximum likelihood, error functions, bootstrap-based frequentist uncertainty, and discusses the advantages, criticisms, and computational development of Bayesian methods, including Monte Carlo and deterministic approximations. The section then begins an introduction to the Gaussian distribution, defining its density, parameters, standard deviation, and precision, and includes biographical notes on Thomas Bayes and Pierre-Simon Laplace.

nodes.title: 1.2.4 The Gaussian distribution
nodes.summary: The text introduces computational approaches to Bayesian inference, contrasting flexible but expensive Monte Carlo methods with scalable deterministic approximations. It then develops the univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, explaining their parameters, normalization, moments, variance, and mode. For i.i.d. Gaussian data, it defines the likelihood, motivates log-likelihood maximization, derives the maximum-likelihood sample mean and variance, and explains the variance estimator’s bias, its unbiased correction, and its connection to overfitting. Finally, it reframes polynomial curve fitting probabilistically by modeling targets as Gaussian around the polynomial prediction, while also presenting a brief biographical note on Laplace and related illustrative figures and exercises.

nodes.title: 1.2.5 Curve fitting re-visited
nodes.summary: The text explains maximum-likelihood bias in Gaussian variance estimation, its reduction with increasing sample size, and its connection to overfitting in complex models. It then reformulates polynomial curve fitting probabilistically by modeling targets with Gaussian noise, derives the likelihood and log likelihood, shows that maximum likelihood yields the usual sum-of-squares objective and an estimate of the noise precision, and expresses predictions as a Gaussian distribution. Finally, it introduces a Gaussian prior over polynomial coefficients, showing that MAP estimation produces the regularized sum-of-squares objective, while emphasizing that full Bayesian curve fitting requires integrating over all parameter values rather than making a point estimate.

nodes.title: 1.2.6 Bayesian curve fitting
nodes.summary: The text moves from maximum-likelihood polynomial regression to MAP estimation by adding a Gaussian prior over coefficients, showing that MAP is equivalent to regularized least squares. It then presents fully Bayesian curve fitting, in which predictions average over the Gaussian posterior of the coefficients, yielding an analytic Gaussian predictive distribution whose variance reflects both observation noise and parameter uncertainty. The associated formulas for the predictive mean, variance, posterior covariance, and polynomial basis are given, along with an illustration. Finally, it introduces model selection, explaining complexity control, overfitting, validation and test sets, and cross-validation as a way to use limited data efficiently.

This section develops probability theory as the foundation for reasoning under uncertainty in pattern recognition. It introduces random variables, joint, marginal, and conditional probabilities, derives the sum and product rules and Bayes’ theorem, and extends them to continuous, mixed, and multivariate probability densities, transformations, expectations, variances, and covariances. It explains Bayesian and frequentist interpretations, inference with priors and likelihoods, computational approaches, and the Gaussian distribution. These ideas are applied to maximum-likelihood, MAP, and fully Bayesian polynomial curve fitting, including noise and parameter uncertainty, bias and overfitting, regularization, predictive distributions, and model selection through validation and cross-validation, with historical notes and supporting illustrations and exercises.

nodes.title: 1.3. Model Selection
nodes.summary: The text introduces model selection after illustrating a Bayesian predictive distribution for degree-9 polynomial fitting. It explains how model complexity is controlled, why training performance is inadequate because of overfitting, and how validation and separate test sets can be used. It then presents S-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation for limited data, including their averaging procedure and computational drawbacks, especially with multiple hyperparameters. Information criteria are introduced as training-data-based alternatives, with AIC defined as ln p(D|wML) − M and BIC noted as a related criterion; their tendency to ignore parameter uncertainty and favor overly simple models motivates a fully Bayesian treatment. The text concludes by beginning the discussion of the curse of dimensionality.

nodes.title: 1.4. The Curse of Dimensionality
nodes.summary: The text discusses the limitations of cross-validation and information criteria for model selection, motivating Bayesian complexity control. It then explains the curse of dimensionality through grid-based classification, polynomial parameter growth, and the concentration of volume and Gaussian probability in thin high-dimensional shells. High-dimensional learning remains possible when data has lower effective dimensionality or local smoothness, illustrated by image manifolds. Finally, it introduces decision theory as the process of converting probabilistic inference about inputs and targets into optimal predictions or actions, using medical diagnosis as an example.

nodes.title: 1.5. Decision Theory
1.5.1 Minimizing the misclassification rate
nodes.summary: The text introduces Bayesian decision theory for classifying observations, using Bayes’ theorem to relate priors, likelihoods, joint probabilities, and posterior class probabilities. It defines decision regions and boundaries, proves that minimum misclassification is achieved by assigning each input to the class with the highest posterior probability, and extends this result to multiple classes. It then explains why classification objectives may need to account for unequal consequences of errors, introduces loss matrices and expected loss, gives a cancer-diagnosis example with highly asymmetric costs, and derives the general rule of choosing the decision with the smallest posterior expected loss.

nodes.title: 1.5.2 Minimizing the expected loss
nodes.summary: The text explains decision-making in classification when errors have unequal consequences. It introduces loss matrices and derives the rule of assigning each input to the class with minimum posterior expected loss, emphasizing the cancer-diagnosis example. It then presents the reject option for uncertain cases, controlled by a posterior-probability threshold and extendable to loss-based decisions, and begins distinguishing inference from decision.

nodes.title: 1.5.3 The reject option
nodes.summary: The text explains loss-based classification, in which an input is assigned to the class with minimum expected loss given the posterior probabilities. It then describes the reject option for uncertain cases: inputs whose maximum posterior probability does not exceed a threshold θ are withheld for alternative handling, with θ controlling the rejection rate and the criterion extendable to loss-sensitive decisions that include rejection costs. A figure illustrates the reject region, and the text begins distinguishing inference from decision in the overall classification process.

nodes.title: 1.5.4 Inference and decision
nodes.summary: The text develops decision theory for classification and regression. Classification decisions minimize expected loss, while a reject option defers uncertain cases using a posterior-probability threshold, with rejection adjustable for loss. It distinguishes generative models, which infer class-conditional densities and priors, discriminative posterior models, and direct discriminant functions, explaining their relative complexity, data requirements, access to input-density and novelty detection, and loss of posterior information in direct classification. Posterior probabilities enable changing risk criteria, optimizing rejection, correcting for class-prior changes caused by balanced training sets, and combining modular models. Combining independent X-ray and blood-test evidence produces a naive Bayes posterior proportional to the two model posteriors divided by the class prior, followed by normalization. Finally, for regression under general loss the expected loss is defined, and squared loss is shown to be minimized by predicting the conditional mean E[t|x].

nodes.title: 1.5.5 Loss functions for regression
nodes.summary: The text explains naive Bayes classification through conditional independence, posterior computation, class priors, normalization, and limitations of factorizing marginal distributions. It then develops regression decision theory, showing that squared-loss prediction is optimized by the conditional mean and decomposing error into reducible prediction error and irreducible conditional variance. It presents three levels of regression modeling, introduces Minkowski losses and their mean, median, and mode optima, and concludes by introducing information theory, where information measures surprise and has a logarithmic dependence on probability because independent information is additive.

This section introduces decision theory as the process of choosing optimal predictions or actions after probabilistic inference. It develops Bayesian classification under both equal and unequal error costs, using posterior probabilities, decision regions, loss matrices, expected loss, and a reject option. It distinguishes generative, discriminative, and direct classification approaches and explains how posterior probabilities enable prior adjustment, changing decision criteria, novelty detection, rejection, and evidence combination through naive Bayes. It then treats regression, deriving the conditional mean as the squared-loss optimum, decomposing prediction error, and generalizing to Minkowski losses and their mean, median, or mode optima. The section closes by introducing information theory and its logarithmic measure of surprise.

nodes.title: 1.6. Information Theory
Ludwig Boltzmann
nodes.summary: The passage develops continuous entropy from the discrete case, explaining the divergent discretization term and defining differential entropy. It derives, via constrained variational maximization, that the Gaussian is the maximum-entropy continuous distribution for fixed mean and variance, gives its entropy, and notes that differential entropy can be negative. It introduces conditional entropy and its chain rule, then defines asymmetric Kullback–Leibler divergence as the extra coding cost of an approximate distribution and states its nonnegativity and equality condition. The text begins the convex-function argument used to establish this result and includes biographical sidebars on Boltzmann and Shannon, along with references to exercises and appendices.

nodes.summary: The text contains Exercises 1.12–1.41 from an introductory treatment of probabilistic machine learning. It covers Gaussian moments and unbiased variance estimation; symmetric matrices and polynomial parameter counting; Gamma functions and high-dimensional sphere geometry; concentration phenomena for cubes and Gaussian distributions; Bayesian classification, loss functions, rejection, and regression under various losses; entropy, Jensen’s inequality, maximum entropy, transformations, conditional entropy, mutual information, and KL divergence; and computational or proof exercises involving binary-variable information measures and mean inequalities.

The section presents Claude Shannon’s role in founding information theory and develops entropy, conditional entropy, KL divergence, convexity, Jensen’s inequality, data compression, likelihood-based density estimation, and mutual information, including their key properties and interpretations. It also gathers exercises spanning probability, Gaussian distributions, covariance, estimation, regression, classification, transformations, high-dimensional geometry, concentration, entropy, and information measures.

The section introduces Shannon’s foundations of information theory and develops entropy, conditional entropy, KL divergence, convexity, Jensen’s inequality, data compression, likelihood-based density estimation, and mutual information, emphasizing their main properties and interpretations. It also includes exercises covering probability, Gaussian and covariance analysis, estimation, regression, classification, transformations, high-dimensional geometry, concentration, entropy, and information measures.

This section introduces information theory through information content, Shannon entropy, coding and compression, and the interpretation of entropy as disorder. It extends these ideas to continuous variables and differential entropy, derives the Gaussian maximum-entropy result, and develops conditional entropy, KL divergence, convexity-based inequalities, likelihood applications, and mutual information. It also includes historical biographies, references, and exercises spanning probability, statistics, machine learning, geometry, and information measures.

The section introduces pattern recognition and machine learning through handwritten-digit classification, explaining training and test data, targets, learning, generalization, preprocessing, feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, supervised and unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. It then develops polynomial curve fitting and the problems of underfitting, overfitting, regularization, model complexity, and generalization, followed by probability theory as a basis for uncertainty, Bayesian and frequentist inference, probability distributions, parameter estimation, predictive uncertainty, and model selection. Model-selection methods include validation, cross-validation, AIC, BIC, and Bayesian complexity control, with discussion of the curse of dimensionality and effective dimensionality. The section next presents decision theory for classification and regression, including losses, rejection, posterior-based decisions, generative and discriminative methods, naive Bayes, and optimal regression estimators. It concludes with information theory, covering information, entropy, coding, differential entropy, KL divergence, mutual information, and related inequalities, applications, historical material, references, and exercises.

nodes.title: 2 Probability Distributions
2.1. Binary Variables
2.1.1 The beta distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the mean and variance of the binomial distribution, introduces the beta distribution as a normalized conjugate prior for the Bernoulli/binomial parameter, and derives its moments and beta-form posterior. It interprets the hyperparameters as effective counts, explains sequential Bayesian updating and predictive inference, compares Bayesian and maximum-likelihood results in the large-data limit, and discusses posterior concentration and the average reduction of uncertainty through the law of total variance. It concludes by introducing multinomial variables and their 1-of-K representation, while listing several associated exercises.

This section develops probability models for binary outcomes, beginning with the Bernoulli distribution and its moments, likelihood, sufficient statistic, and maximum-likelihood estimate, then extends the analysis to the binomial distribution for counts of successes. It addresses maximum-likelihood overfitting and introduces the beta distribution as the conjugate Bayesian prior, deriving its moments, posterior updating, predictive distribution, interpretation as effective counts, large-sample agreement with maximum likelihood, posterior concentration, and uncertainty reduction. The section ends by introducing multinomial variables and their 1-of-K encoding and noting related exercises.

nodes.title: 2.2. Multinomial Variables
2.2.1 The Dirichlet distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the multinomial maximum-likelihood estimate and defines the multinomial distribution for category counts. It introduces the Dirichlet distribution as the multinomial’s conjugate prior, explains its simplex domain, normalization, visual behavior, and effective-count interpretation, and derives the Dirichlet posterior. It also relates the binomial-beta and multinomial-Dirichlet representations for two-state variables, includes a biographical note on Dirichlet, and begins the section on univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, noting their maximum-entropy and central-limit-theorem motivations.

The section generalizes Bernoulli variables to K-category multinomial variables through 1-of-K encoding, defines their probability model, moments, likelihood, sufficient category counts, and maximum-likelihood estimates, and introduces the multinomial count distribution. It then develops the Dirichlet conjugate prior, including its simplex support, normalization, interpretation as effective counts, and posterior, relating the two-category case to the beta-binomial model. It also includes a biographical note on Dirichlet and transitions to Gaussian distributions via maximum-entropy and central-limit-theorem motivations. The supplied preceding discussion additionally states the Bayesian mean and variance identities and the resulting average reduction in posterior uncertainty.

nodes.title: 2.3. The Gaussian Distribution
nodes.summary: The text transitions from Dirichlet and binary/multinomial representations to an introduction of the univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, giving their parameterized formulas and explaining their importance. It motivates the Gaussian through maximum entropy and the central limit theorem, illustrates convergence from uniform-variable means and the binomial distribution, and previews a technically detailed treatment of Gaussian geometry and matrix-based analytical properties. It also includes a biographical sidebar on Carl Friedrich Gauss and his major mathematical and scientific contributions.

This section introduces probability distributions as building blocks for pattern-recognition models and uses them to develop density estimation and Bayesian concepts under an independent, identically distributed data assumption. It covers Bernoulli, binomial, multinomial, beta, and Dirichlet distributions, including their moments, likelihoods, sufficient statistics, maximum-likelihood estimates, conjugate Bayesian updating, predictive behavior, effective-count interpretations, posterior uncertainty, and overfitting. It then motivates and introduces univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions through maximum entropy and the central limit theorem, illustrating their emergence from averages and binomial limits while previewing their geometric and matrix-based analysis. Biographical notes and exercises are also included.

nodes.title: Appendix C
Carl Friedrich Gauss
nodes.summary: The text introduces the Gaussian distribution through the central-limit behavior of sample means and the binomial distribution, then develops its geometry, matrix representation, normalization, and moments. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues transform the Gaussian into independent coordinates, showing that constant-density surfaces are ellipsoids and that μ and Σ are respectively the mean and covariance. It discusses positive definiteness, parameter growth, diagonal and isotropic covariance restrictions, and the Gaussian's inability to model multimodality, motivating latent-variable and structured Gaussian models such as mixtures, graphical models, image Markov fields, and linear dynamical systems. The passage concludes by setting up conditional Gaussian distributions through partitions of variables, means, covariance, and precision matrices, beginning the derivation of a conditional density.

nodes.title: 2.3.1 Conditional Gaussian distributions
nodes.summary: The text develops the conditional distribution of one subset of variables in a multivariate Gaussian given another. It defines block partitions of the variables, means, covariance, and precision matrices; derives the conditional mean and covariance by expanding the Gaussian quadratic form and completing the square; and then converts the results between precision and covariance representations using a block-matrix inverse and Schur complement. The resulting conditional distribution is Gaussian with mean linear in the conditioned variables and covariance independent of them, providing an example of a linear-Gaussian model.

nodes.title: 2.3.2 Marginal Gaussian distributions
nodes.summary: The text derives the marginal of a partitioned multivariate Gaussian by completing the square in the variables being integrated out. It shows that the marginal remains Gaussian with mean μ_a and covariance (Λ_aa − Λ_abΛ_bb^{-1}Λ_ba)^{-1}, which equals the covariance block Σ_aa. It contrasts the convenient use of covariance matrices for marginals with precision matrices for conditionals, summarizes the conditional and marginal Gaussian formulas, illustrates them with a two-variable figure, and begins the setup for Bayes' theorem involving a Gaussian prior and a linear-mean, constant-covariance Gaussian conditional.

nodes.title: 2.3.3 Bayes’ theorem for Gaussian variables
nodes.summary: The text illustrates marginal and conditional distributions of a multivariate Gaussian, then derives Bayes’ theorem for a linear Gaussian model. It obtains the joint precision, covariance, and mean, the marginal distribution of y, and the posterior conditional distribution of x given y, including the Gaussian convolution special case. It concludes with maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian, giving the log likelihood, sufficient statistics, and the sample-mean estimate of the mean.

nodes.title: 2.3.4 Maximum likelihood for the Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text derives marginal and conditional Gaussian distributions for a linear-Gaussian model, then develops maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian. It gives the log-likelihood and identifies the first- and second-order data sums as sufficient statistics, derives the sample-mean and sample-covariance estimators, and explains that the mean estimate is unbiased while the covariance maximum-likelihood estimate is biased by a factor of (N−1)/N. It presents the standard unbiased covariance correction and introduces sequential estimation, where data are processed one observation at a time for online or large-scale applications.

nodes.title: 2.3.5 Sequential estimation
nodes.summary: The text completes maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian by deriving the sample covariance, establishing that the ML mean is unbiased while the covariance is biased downward, and presenting the usual unbiased covariance correction. It then develops sequential estimation: the sample mean is updated recursively as each observation arrives, motivating the general Robbins–Monro root-finding algorithm, its convergence assumptions, and its application to sequential maximum-likelihood estimation through stochastic log-likelihood gradients. The Gaussian mean example shows that an appropriate step size reproduces the batch solution and that the approach generalizes to multiple dimensions. Finally, the text introduces Bayesian Gaussian inference, beginning with inference for a known-variance univariate Gaussian, its likelihood, and the use of a Gaussian prior for the unknown mean.

nodes.title: 2.3.6 Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text completes the Gaussian sequential-estimation discussion by showing that the score’s regression function is linear and that suitable step sizes recover the maximum-likelihood mean estimate, including the multivariate extension. It then develops Bayesian Gaussian inference: Gaussian conjugacy for an unknown mean with known variance, sequential updating, and the limiting relationship between Bayesian and maximum-likelihood estimates; gamma conjugacy for unknown precision with known mean, including posterior parameters, precision interpretation, and effective prior observations; and the normal-gamma conjugate prior when both mean and precision are unknown. The multivariate analogues are Gaussian, Wishart, inverse Wishart, and normal-Wishart priors. Figures illustrate the relevant distributions, and the section concludes by introducing Student’s t-distribution as the result of integrating a gamma-distributed Gaussian precision.

nodes.title: 2.3.7 Student’s t-distribution
nodes.summary: The text introduces the Wishart and normal-Wishart conjugate priors for multivariate Gaussian precision and mean, briefly notes the inverse Wishart alternative, and then derives Student’s t-distributions by integrating a Gaussian precision with a Gamma prior. It explains the t-distribution’s parameterization, Gaussian and Cauchy special cases, scale-mixture interpretation, heavy tails, robustness to outliers, regression relevance, and graphical demonstrations. The multivariate t-distribution is presented through a Gaussian-Gamma mixture, with its density, Mahalanobis-distance form, mean, covariance, and mode. Finally, the text begins the treatment of periodic variables, explaining why ordinary Gaussian modeling and arithmetic means are coordinate-dependent and introducing unit-vector representations on the circle as an invariant alternative.

nodes.title: 2.3.8 Periodic variables
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of the multivariate Student’s t-distribution and its moments, then develops methods for modeling periodic variables. It explains the failure of ordinary averages and Gaussians on circular data, defines a rotation-invariant vector-based mean, and derives the von Mises circular-normal distribution from a two-dimensional Gaussian. Its normalization, concentration interpretation, large-concentration Gaussian approximation, and maximum-likelihood estimators are presented. Alternative periodic modeling methods and mixtures of von Mises distributions for multimodal data are discussed. Finally, the text introduces Gaussian mixtures, using the bimodal Old Faithful data to demonstrate why they can outperform a single Gaussian.

nodes.title: 2.3.9 Mixtures of Gaussians
nodes.summary: The text moves from limitations of single Gaussians, illustrated by the bimodal Old Faithful data, to Gaussian mixture models and their probabilistic interpretation. It defines mixture components, mixing coefficients, normalization constraints, responsibilities, parameter estimation, and the use of numerical optimization or expectation maximization. It also reviews alternative periodic-distribution constructions and explains that von Mises mixtures support multimodality. Finally, it introduces the exponential family, gives its general normalized form and interpretation, and demonstrates that the Bernoulli distribution is an example with natural parameter ln(μ/(1−μ)).

nodes.title: 2.4. The Exponential Family
2.4.1 Maximum likelihood and sufficient statistics
nodes.summary: The text develops exponential-family distributions by deriving their moments from derivatives of the normalization function, then applies maximum likelihood to independent data. It shows that estimation depends only on summed sufficient statistics, gives Bernoulli and Gaussian examples, and explains consistency as the sample size grows. It notes that sufficiency also supports Bayesian inference, introduces the general conjugate-prior form and its posterior updates, and interprets the prior strength as pseudo-observations. Finally, it begins discussing noninformative priors and how prior exclusions persist in the posterior.

nodes.title: 2.4.2 Conjugate priors
nodes.summary: The text explains that exponential-family maximum-likelihood estimates depend on the data only through sufficient statistics, gives Bernoulli and Gaussian examples, and notes consistency as the sample size grows, with sufficiency also applying to Bayesian inference. It then defines conjugate priors, shows algebraically that they produce posteriors of the same form, and interprets the prior parameter as the number of pseudo-observations. Finally, it begins discussing noninformative priors and the preservation of zero-probability assignments in the posterior.

nodes.title: 2.4.3 Noninformative priors
nodes.summary: The text explains sufficient statistics and their asymptotic role in maximum-likelihood and Bayesian inference, then derives conjugate priors for exponential-family distributions and interprets their parameters as pseudo-observations. It discusses noninformative priors, including the issues of improper normalization and parameterization dependence, and derives uniform priors for location parameters and 1/σ priors for scale parameters, including the equivalent precision formulation. Finally, it motivates nonparametric density modeling over restrictive parametric forms and introduces normalized histogram density estimation.

This section introduces the exponential family, its normalization structure, natural parameters, and sufficient-statistic representation, and shows how Bernoulli, multinomial, and Gaussian distributions fit this form, including the sigmoid and softmax parameterizations. It develops the resulting moment and maximum-likelihood theory, emphasizing sufficient statistics, consistency, and applications to Bernoulli and Gaussian data. It then explains conjugate Bayesian priors and their pseudo-observation interpretation, examines noninformative priors and their parameterization and normalization issues, and concludes by motivating nonparametric density modeling and normalized histograms.

nodes.title: 2.5. Nonparametric Methods
2.5.1 Kernel density estimators
nodes.summary: The text develops nonparametric density estimation from local probability counts. A region around x contains K of N samples, yielding p(x) ≈ K/(NV) when the region is small enough for the density to be nearly constant yet large enough to contain sufficient data. Fixing volume produces kernel estimators, while fixing the number of points produces nearest-neighbour estimators, both of which are consistent under suitable conditions. It defines a box/Parzen kernel, derives the corresponding hypercube estimator, and then introduces the smoother Gaussian kernel estimator, whose bandwidth h controls the trade-off between noise and oversmoothing. Valid kernels must be nonnegative and normalized. Kernel estimators require no training beyond storing the data but have evaluation costs linear in dataset size. The section concludes by motivating nearest-neighbour methods, which adapt the region size to local data density rather than using one fixed bandwidth everywhere.

nodes.title: 2.5.2 Nearest-neighbour methods
nodes.summary: The text compares kernel and nearest-neighbour nonparametric density estimation. Kernel density estimators use a bandwidth h whose value balances noise against over-smoothing, allow any nonnegative unit-integral kernel, require only data storage during training, and have evaluation costs proportional to the data-set size. K-nearest-neighbour density estimation instead adapts the neighbourhood volume to contain a fixed number K of points, with K controlling smoothing, though the resulting estimate is not globally normalizable. The method extends to classification by applying local density estimates to each class and Bayes’ theorem, yielding posterior class probabilities proportional to the number of class representatives among the K nearest points; K = 1 is the nearest-neighbour rule. Figures illustrate bandwidth and K effects, decision boundaries, and oil-flow classifications. The text notes the asymptotic error bound of the nearest-neighbour classifier, computational improvements from tree searches, and the need for flexible models beyond the limitations of basic nonparametric and parametric approaches. It concludes with exercises on Bernoulli moments and entropy, the ±1 Bernoulli formulation, and normalization of the binomial distribution.

The section briefly completes the discussion of noninformative Gaussian scale priors, then introduces nonparametric density estimation as a flexible alternative to restrictive parametric forms. It develops histograms, explaining their normalization, bin-width effects, practical advantages, and limitations from discontinuities and the curse of dimensionality. These ideas motivate kernel density estimators, including box and Gaussian kernels, bandwidth smoothing, consistency, and computational properties, and nearest-neighbour estimators, which adapt neighbourhood size to local density. Nearest-neighbour density estimation is extended to Bayesian classification, with discussion of smoothing, decision boundaries, error guarantees, computational search methods, and illustrative applications. The section ends with exercises on Bernoulli distributions, entropy, and binomial normalization.

nodes.title: 2.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 2.16–2.61 develop Gaussian probability theory, matrix algebra, and related distributions. They cover Gaussian convolution and entropy; symmetry, eigenstructure, definiteness, inverses, parameter counting, and ellipsoid volumes; block-matrix and Woodbury identities; Gaussian marginal, conditional, posterior, predictive, summation, and sequential-estimation results; maximum-likelihood covariance estimation and Gaussian moments; gamma, generalized exponential-power, Gaussian-gamma, Wishart, and Student’s t distributions; periodic and von Mises distributions; exponential-family representations and information identities; scale normalization; histogram maximum likelihood; and the impropriety of the K-nearest-neighbour density model.

nodes.title: 3 Linear Models for Regression
3.1. Linear Basis Function Models
3.1.1 Maximum likelihood and least squares
nodes.summary: The text develops linear basis-function regression from its Gaussian-noise maximum-likelihood formulation. It describes common basis functions and modeling assumptions, derives the likelihood, least-squares objective, normal equations, design matrix, pseudoinverse, bias estimate, and noise-precision estimate, and explains their geometric meaning as projection in data space. It also discusses multimodal-noise extensions, numerical problems caused by collinear basis functions and their remedies through SVD or regularization, and introduces sequential learning for large data sets.

nodes.title: 3.1.2 Geometry of least squares
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometric interpretation of least squares: model outputs lie in the subspace spanned by basis-function vectors, and the optimal fit is the orthogonal projection of the target vector onto that subspace, with error given by the corresponding squared distance. It also relates inverse noise precision to residual variance, distinguishes rows and columns of the design matrix, discusses numerical problems caused by nearly dependent basis functions, and identifies SVD and regularization as remedies. Finally, it introduces sequential learning as a more scalable alternative to processing an entire large data set in a single batch.

nodes.title: 3.1.3 Sequential learning
nodes.summary: The text explains least squares geometrically as projecting the target vector onto the subspace spanned by basis-function vectors, with residual variance related to inverse noise precision. It discusses numerical instability in normal-equation solutions caused by collinear basis functions and the use of SVD or regularization to address it. It then introduces sequential learning through stochastic gradient descent and derives the LMS update, noting the importance of the learning rate. Finally, it presents regularized least squares, including quadratic weight decay, and explains how regularization controls overfitting by shrinking weights toward zero.

nodes.title: 3.1.4 Regularized least squares
nodes.summary: The text introduces sequential stochastic-gradient learning and the LMS update for least-squares regression, then develops regularized least squares. Quadratic weight decay yields a closed-form ridge-type solution, while q-norm penalties—especially the lasso—can produce sparse models by shrinking coefficients to zero. Regularization controls over-fitting and effective complexity but requires selecting the coefficient λ. The section then extends linear basis-function regression to multiple outputs using a shared basis-function matrix, an output-weight matrix, and an isotropic Gaussian likelihood.

nodes.title: 3.1.5 Multiple outputs
nodes.summary: The text concludes the regularization discussion by contrasting quadratic and lasso constraints, noting the lasso’s sparse solution and choosing the quadratic regularizer for the remainder. It extends linear regression to multiple outputs using a shared basis-function matrix and an isotropic Gaussian likelihood, derives the matrix maximum-likelihood solution and its per-output pseudoinverse form, and explains that regression decouples across targets, including under general Gaussian covariance. It then returns to one target and motivates the bias-variance decomposition: maximum likelihood can overfit complex models on small data, while overly simple models lack flexibility; regularization helps but λ cannot be selected by minimizing the training objective jointly with the weights. Bayesian parameter marginalization avoids this issue, and the chapter next develops Bayesian model complexity after introducing the more general frequentist bias-variance trade-off in the context of regression decision theory.

This section introduces linear basis-function regression, expressing predictions as functions linear in adjustable parameters but potentially nonlinear in the inputs through fixed polynomial, spline, Gaussian, sigmoidal, Fourier, or wavelet bases. It develops Gaussian maximum likelihood and least-squares estimation, including design-matrix, normal-equation, pseudoinverse, noise-precision, and geometric projection interpretations. It addresses multimodal noise, collinearity and numerical instability, and scalable sequential stochastic-gradient/LMS learning. Regularized least squares is presented through quadratic and q-norm penalties, including ridge and sparse lasso solutions, with discussion of overfitting and regularization selection. The framework is extended to multiple correlated or independent outputs using matrix notation and Gaussian likelihoods, concluding with the bias-variance trade-off and motivation for Bayesian treatment of model complexity.

nodes.title: 3.2. The Bias-Variance Decomposition
nodes.summary: The text first derives the multivariate linear-regression maximum-likelihood solution, showing that target variables decouple and share a single design-matrix pseudoinverse, including for general Gaussian noise covariance. It then introduces the frequentist bias-variance decomposition to explain model complexity: expected squared loss consists of squared bias, variance, and irreducible noise. Flexible models tend to have low bias and high variance, while rigid models show the opposite trade-off. A sinusoidal-data experiment demonstrates how regularization controls this balance, provides empirical bias and variance formulas, and identifies an intermediate regularization value with the best predictive performance. Because the decomposition relies on unavailable ensembles of training sets, the text motivates Bayesian linear regression as a practical alternative for avoiding overfitting and selecting model complexity, beginning with a Gaussian conjugate prior over the weights.

nodes.title: 3.3. Bayesian Linear Regression
3.3.1 Parameter distribution
nodes.summary: The text moves from the limitations of the frequentist bias-variance view and regularization trade-off to Bayesian linear regression as a way to prevent overfitting and select model complexity using training data. It derives Gaussian conjugate priors and Gaussian posteriors for the weights, explains MAP, maximum-likelihood and sequential-update special cases, and shows that an isotropic Gaussian prior reproduces quadratic regularization. A synthetic straight-line example illustrates how likelihoods and posteriors evolve as observations accumulate. It also discusses non-Gaussian exponential-power priors and their connection to alternative regularizers. Finally, it derives the Gaussian predictive distribution, whose variance consists of data noise plus parameter uncertainty, with uncertainty decreasing as more data are observed.

nodes.title: 3.3.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text extends Bayesian linear regression by discussing generalized weight priors and their connection to regularization, then derives the Gaussian predictive distribution and separates its noise and parameter-uncertainty contributions. It explains how additional data reduce predictive uncertainty, illustrates this with sinusoidal-data figures and posterior function samples, identifies overconfident extrapolation with localized basis functions, and notes Gaussian processes and Student's t prediction as alternatives or extensions. Finally, it rewrites the posterior mean as a kernel-weighted combination of training targets, introducing the data-dependent equivalent kernel and its preference for nearby observations.

nodes.title: 3.3.3 Equivalent kernel
nodes.summary: The text explains that Bayesian linear-regression predictions are linear combinations of training targets governed by an input-dependent equivalent kernel. The kernel emphasizes nearby points, determines correlations and joint predictive uncertainty, has weights summing to one but potentially of either sign, and can be represented as an inner product in a transformed feature space. Directly specifying such kernels motivates Gaussian processes. The text then introduces Bayesian model comparison, in which models are evaluated through posterior probabilities and marginal model evidence rather than parameter point estimates or cross-validation, reducing overfitting and permitting efficient selection of model complexity parameters.

This section develops Bayesian linear regression from its motivation in overcoming frequentist overfitting and model-complexity limitations through priors and posterior inference. It derives Gaussian weight posteriors, connects MAP and maximum-likelihood estimation, sequential updates, and regularization, and considers non-Gaussian priors. It then derives and illustrates predictive distributions that separate noise from parameter uncertainty, including uncertainty behavior with additional data, extrapolation issues, and alternatives such as Gaussian processes and Student’s t predictions. Predictions are recast through the data-dependent equivalent kernel, which emphasizes nearby observations and determines predictive correlations and uncertainty, motivating Gaussian processes. The section concludes with Bayesian model comparison using posterior model probabilities and marginal evidence for efficient complexity selection and reduced overfitting.

nodes.title: 3.4. Bayesian Model Comparison
nodes.summary: The text introduces Bayesian model comparison, contrasting it with cross-validation and explaining how marginalizing parameters prevents overfitting while enabling direct training-data-based comparison. It defines posterior model probabilities, evidence, Bayes factors, Bayesian model averaging, and model selection; derives the evidence as a parameter integral and gives a peaked-posterior approximation showing the trade-off between data fit and parameter-complexity penalties. Generative data-set distributions explain why evidence can favor intermediate-complexity models, and a KL-divergence argument shows that the correct model is favored on average when included among the candidates. The text also discusses sensitivity to priors, problems with improper priors, and the value of an independent test set. Finally, it introduces the evidence approximation for linear regression, in which α and β are selected by maximizing the marginal likelihood after integrating over w, replacing otherwise intractable full marginalization over parameters and hyperparameters.

nodes.title: 3.5. The Evidence Approximation
3.5.1 Evaluation of the evidence function
nodes.summary: The text develops the evidence framework for Bayesian linear regression: it explains estimating the hyperparameters alpha and beta by maximizing the marginal likelihood, contrasts this with Gamma-prior marginalization and the generally inadequate Laplace approximation, and notes equivalence between analytical re-estimation and EM. It derives the evidence by completing the square in the regularized quadratic error, identifies the Hessian and posterior mean, evaluates the Gaussian integral, and obtains the log-evidence expression. A polynomial-regression example shows how evidence balances data fit against model complexity and selects a cubic model. Finally, it begins maximizing the evidence with respect to alpha by diagonalizing beta Phi^T Phi and deriving the corresponding stationary-point equation.

nodes.title: 3.5.2 Maximizing the evidence function
nodes.summary: The text explains why Bayesian model evidence selects a cubic polynomial despite similar generalization errors for higher orders, balancing fit quality against complexity. It derives iterative evidence-maximization updates for the prior precision α and noise precision β using the eigenvalues of βΦᵀΦ and the posterior mode, emphasizing that training data alone suffice for complexity optimization. It then interprets γ = Σ_i λ_i/(α + λ_i) as the effective number of parameters: well-constrained directions retain their maximum-likelihood values, whereas weakly constrained directions are suppressed by the prior. Finally, it compares the Bayesian noise-variance estimate with the maximum-likelihood estimate, showing the replacement of N by N − γ.

nodes.title: 3.5.3 Effective number of parameters
nodes.summary: The text explains the eigenvalue-based interpretation of Bayesian regularization in linear regression. In rotated parameter coordinates, α shrinks weakly data-constrained directions toward zero while leaving strongly constrained directions near their maximum-likelihood values. The resulting quantity γ measures the effective number of parameters determined by the data and replaces the nominal parameter count in the Bayesian variance estimate, correcting maximum-likelihood bias analogously to the N − 1 correction for estimating a Gaussian mean. A sinusoidal-data example illustrates evidence-based selection of α, its relationship to log evidence and generalization error, and its effect on parameter magnitudes. In the large-data limit, γ equals M and simplified re-estimation formulas for α and β result. The section concludes by noting the benefits and impending limitations of models using fixed nonlinear basis functions.

This section introduces the evidence approximation for Bayesian linear regression, replacing analytically intractable full marginalization over weights and hyperparameters with empirical-Bayes maximization of the marginal likelihood. It derives the Gaussian evidence and log-evidence, explains how evidence balances fit against complexity and supports model selection, and develops iterative estimates for the prior and noise precisions. The effective parameter count gamma explains eigenvalue-based shrinkage and corrects the noise-variance estimate from N to N minus gamma. Polynomial and sinusoidal examples demonstrate these ideas, followed by large-data simplifications and a discussion of the sensitivity of evidence to priors, the need for test data, and limitations of fixed basis-function models.

nodes.title: 3.6. Limitations of Fixed Basis Functions
nodes.summary: The text discusses evidence-based selection of α, illustrated by figures showing that the intersection of γ and 2αE_W matches the log-evidence maximum and nearly the best test-set performance, and shows how model weights vary with effective model complexity. It then explains the strengths and limitations of fixed-basis linear regression: although such models offer closed-form fitting, tractable Bayesian analysis, and flexible nonlinear mappings, fixed bases suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Data lying near lower-dimensional manifolds, localized basis functions, adaptive neural-network bases, and dependence on a few relevant directions can alleviate this problem, motivating later study of more advanced models. The exercise proves the relationship between logistic sigmoid and tanh functions and derives the associated basis-function parameter transformation.

This section introduces linear regression for supervised learning and develops fixed-basis models that are linear in their parameters but can be nonlinear in their inputs. It covers least-squares and maximum-likelihood estimation, design-matrix and projection interpretations, numerical issues, stochastic learning, regularization, sparse and ridge solutions, multivariate outputs, and the bias-variance trade-off. Bayesian linear regression is then developed through priors, Gaussian posteriors, MAP estimation, sequential learning, predictive uncertainty, equivalent kernels, Gaussian-process connections, and Bayesian model comparison. Evidence, Bayes factors, model averaging, complexity penalties, prior sensitivity, and the evidence approximation are derived, including empirical-Bayes estimation of precision parameters and effective model dimensionality. The section concludes by discussing the curse of dimensionality and alternatives to fixed bases, while its exercises provide detailed derivations involving multivariate Gaussian regression, conjugate posteriors, Student's t predictions, kernel identities, regularization, and marginal likelihood and evidence calculations.

nodes.title: 4 Linear Models for Classification
4.1. Discriminant Functions
4.1.1 Two classes
nodes.summary: The text introduces linear discriminant functions for classification, contrasting their parameter nonlinearity with regression and noting the applicability of fixed basis-function transformations. It defines two-class linear discriminants, explains how the weight vector and bias determine the orientation and position of the hyperplane decision boundary, derives the signed-distance interpretation of the discriminant output, and presents augmented-vector notation. It then begins the extension to multiple classes, warning that combining binary classifiers—such as one-versus-the-rest classifiers—creates difficulties.

nodes.title: 4.1.2 Multiple classes
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometry of binary linear discriminants, including the orientation and offset of the decision hyperplane, the signed distance from a point to it, and an augmented-vector notation. It then examines multiclass classification, showing why one-versus-the-rest and one-versus-one combinations of binary classifiers can yield ambiguous regions. A single set of K linear discriminants avoids these issues: class boundaries are hyperplanes, and the resulting decision regions are singly connected and convex, as demonstrated using convex combinations. The binary and multiclass formulations are noted to be equivalent for two classes. Finally, the text introduces least squares, Fisher's discriminant, and the perceptron as learning methods, and begins the least-squares treatment for 1-of-K targets, noting its interpretation as an approximation to posterior probabilities and its limitations with linear models.

nodes.title: 4.1.3 Least squares for classification
nodes.summary: The text proves that multiclass linear-discriminant decision regions are convex and singly connected, notes the equivalence of two-class single- and dual-discriminant formulations, and introduces least squares, Fisher’s discriminant, and the perceptron as parameter-learning methods. It develops least-squares classification with 1-of-K targets, derives its matrix and pseudoinverse solution, and explains its linear prediction constraints. Although outputs sum to one, they are not valid probabilities because they can lie outside (0, 1). The text then details least squares’ sensitivity to outliers and poor performance in multiclass settings, contrasts it with logistic regression, explains the mismatch between Gaussian assumptions and binary targets, and transitions to Fisher’s linear discriminant.

nodes.title: 4.1.4 Fisher’s linear discriminant
nodes.summary: The text discusses the limitations of least-squares classification, including sensitivity to outliers and poor multiclass results caused by its inappropriate Gaussian assumption. It then introduces Fisher’s linear discriminant as a dimensionality-reduction approach that projects data onto a line while maximizing separation between class means relative to within-class variance. The resulting optimal direction is proportional to the inverse within-class covariance matrix times the difference of the class means. A threshold, optionally based on Gaussian models of the projected classes, converts the projection into a classifier. Finally, it contrasts Fisher’s separation-based objective with least squares’ target-fitting objective and introduces their relationship for two-class problems.

nodes.title: 4.1.5 Relation to least squares
nodes.summary: The text derives Fisher's linear discriminant by maximizing the ratio of between-class to within-class projected variance, obtaining the projection direction w proportional to S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1), with the isotropic-covariance case reducing to the difference of class means. It explains that this direction must be combined with a threshold to form a classifier, and discusses Gaussian modeling of the projected classes, maximum-likelihood parameter estimation, optimal threshold selection, and central-limit-theorem support for the Gaussian assumption. It then establishes that, for two classes, Fisher's criterion is a special case of least squares when targets are coded as N/N_1 and -N/N_2. The least-squares normal equations yield the same weight direction and the bias w_0 = -w^T m, giving classification by the sign of w^T(x - m).

nodes.title: 4.1.6 Fisher’s discriminant for multiple classes
nodes.summary: The text extends Fisher’s discriminant analysis from two to K classes by projecting inputs into multiple linear features and defining within-class, total, and between-class covariance matrices in both the original and projected spaces. It presents a trace-based criterion for maximizing between-class separation relative to within-class variation, identifies the optimal projection directions through generalized eigenvectors, and shows that at most K − 1 informative features can be obtained because the between-class covariance has rank at most K − 1. It then introduces the two-class perceptron, which applies a fixed nonlinear input transformation before a generalized linear classification function.

nodes.title: 4.1.7 The perceptron algorithm
nodes.summary: The text first develops projected-space linear discriminant analysis, defining within- and between-class covariance matrices, a trace-based optimization criterion, its eigenvector solution, and the rank limitation that permits at most K - 1 discriminant features. It then introduces Rosenblatt's perceptron with fixed nonlinear features, bipolar targets, a step activation, and a perceptron error function optimized by stochastic gradient updates. The learning rule adjusts weights only for misclassified samples, reduces the selected sample's error but not necessarily total error, and is guaranteed to converge in finite time only for linearly separable data; otherwise it may be slow or fail to converge, with the result dependent on initialization and data order. The passage also covers the perceptron's history, hardware implementation, applications and limitations, mentions the related adaline, and leads into probabilistic generative models of classification.

This section develops linear discriminant functions for binary and multiclass classification, explaining decision-hyperplane geometry, signed distances, augmented notation, and the problems with combining binary classifiers. It shows that a unified set of multiclass discriminants produces convex, singly connected regions. It then presents least-squares classification, including its matrix solution, target interpretation, and limitations such as nonprobabilistic outputs, outlier sensitivity, poor multiclass behavior, and unsuitable Gaussian assumptions. Fisher’s linear discriminant is introduced as a variance-ratio projection method, with thresholding and Gaussian modeling, and its two-class equivalence to specially coded least squares is derived. The treatment is extended to multiple classes through covariance matrices, generalized eigenvectors, and the K - 1 feature limit. Finally, the perceptron is described through its nonlinear features, learning rule, convergence properties, history, applications, limitations, and connection to adaline, leading toward probabilistic generative models.

nodes.title: 4.2. Probabilistic Generative Models
4.2.1 Continuous inputs
nodes.summary: The text develops probabilistic classification using logistic and softmax posteriors. It shows that Gaussian class-conditional densities with a shared covariance matrix lead to linear discriminant functions and linear decision boundaries, while class-specific covariances produce quadratic boundaries. It explains the role of prior probabilities as bias shifts, illustrates the multiclass softmax formulation, and introduces maximum-likelihood estimation for a labeled two-class Gaussian model, including its joint probabilities and likelihood function.

nodes.title: 4.2.2 Maximum likelihood solution
nodes.summary: The text explains how Gaussian generative classifiers produce linear or quadratic decision boundaries depending on covariance sharing, then derives maximum-likelihood estimates for class priors, means, and a shared covariance matrix from labeled data. It notes the extension to multiple classes and the lack of robustness to outliers. It next treats discrete features, showing that naive Bayes conditional independence reduces an exponentially large parameterization to independent Bernoulli parameters and produces linear class scores, with analogous results for multistate features and logistic regression. The section concludes by introducing the broader exponential-family connection to generalized linear posterior models.

nodes.title: 4.2.3 Discrete features
nodes.summary: The passage completes the shared-covariance Gaussian classifier derivation, identifying the maximum-likelihood covariance as a class-size-weighted average of within-class covariances, noting its extension to K classes and its lack of robustness to outliers. It then develops classification with discrete features: a full binary-feature model has exponentially many parameters, while the naive Bayes conditional-independence assumption reduces this to Bernoulli parameters per feature and class, producing linear discriminant functions and logistic-sigmoid posteriors for two classes. The same ideas extend to multistate discrete variables, leading into the exponential-family treatment of generalized linear classification models.

nodes.title: 4.2.4 Exponential family
nodes.summary: The text completes the shared-covariance Gaussian classifier discussion by defining the pooled covariance maximum-likelihood estimate, noting its extension to multiple classes and its lack of robustness to outliers. It then treats discrete features using the naive Bayes conditional-independence assumption, showing that Bernoulli or general discrete class models produce linear log scores and logistic or softmax posteriors. More generally, exponential-family class-conditional densities with a shared scale parameter also yield linear discriminants with sigmoid or softmax activation. Finally, it introduces probabilistic discriminative models, contrasting direct maximum-likelihood estimation of generalized linear-model parameters—efficiently performed by IRLS—with the indirect generative approach of fitting class densities and priors before applying Bayes' theorem.

This section develops probabilistic generative classification from Bayes’ theorem, deriving logistic and softmax posteriors from class likelihoods and priors. Gaussian models yield linear boundaries with shared covariance and quadratic boundaries with class-specific covariance, with maximum-likelihood estimates for priors, means, and covariance. Discrete-feature models are simplified by naive Bayes independence assumptions, producing logistic or softmax classifiers for binary and multistate features. The treatment is unified through exponential-family distributions and concludes by contrasting indirect generative estimation with direct discriminative generalized linear models trained using IRLS.

nodes.title: 4.3. Probabilistic Discriminative Models
4.3.1 Fixed basis functions
nodes.summary: The text contrasts generative and discriminative classification, then introduces fixed nonlinear basis functions, which create feature spaces where linear classifiers correspond to nonlinear decision boundaries in the original input space. It discusses bias basis functions, class overlap, the inability of transformations to remove overlap, and the limitations and practical importance of fixed bases. It then presents two-class logistic regression, defining posterior probabilities through a logistic sigmoid of a linear feature function, emphasizing its classification role and substantially smaller parameter count than Gaussian generative models, and notes that maximum-likelihood training relies on the sigmoid derivative σ(1−σ).

nodes.title: 4.3.2 Logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text introduces fixed nonlinear basis-function models, explaining their bias term, usefulness, limitations, and inability to remove class overlap. It then develops two-class logistic regression, in which the posterior probability is a sigmoid of a linear feature function, and contrasts its linear parameter growth with the quadratic complexity of Gaussian generative models. Using maximum likelihood, it derives the binary likelihood, cross-entropy error, sigmoid derivative, and simplified gradient, noting its similarity to linear regression and its use in sequential learning. Finally, it explains the severe overfitting and infinite-weight problem caused by linearly separable data, the nonuniqueness of separating solutions, and the remedy of priors or regularization.

nodes.title: 4.3.3 Iterative reweighted least squares
nodes.summary: The text develops Newton–Raphson optimization for logistic regression. It first shows that Newton–Raphson recovers the closed-form least-squares solution for quadratic linear-regression error in one step. For logistic regression, it derives the cross-entropy gradient and parameter-dependent Hessian, establishes a unique minimum through positive definiteness, and rewrites the update as iteratively solved weighted least-squares normal equations. This produces IRLS, whose weights equal the Bernoulli variances and whose adjusted targets arise from local linearization of the sigmoid. The text then introduces multiclass logistic regression, defining softmax class probabilities and their derivatives, formulating the 1-of-K likelihood and cross-entropy error, and deriving the gradient with respect to each class’s parameter vector.

nodes.title: 4.3.4 Multiclass logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text develops multiclass logistic regression by expressing class posteriors through a softmax of linear activations, deriving the softmax derivatives, likelihood, multiclass cross-entropy error, gradient, and Hessian. It highlights the common error-times-feature gradient structure, describes sequential learning and Newton-Raphson/IRLS batch optimization, and notes positive definiteness and uniqueness of the minimum. It then introduces probit regression as an alternative binary discriminative model for cases where logistic or softmax posteriors are unsuitable, motivating it through a noisy threshold model.

nodes.title: 4.3.5 Probit regression
nodes.summary: The text completes the multiclass logistic-regression optimization discussion by deriving the error-times-feature gradient, the block Hessian, and the Newton/IRLS approach, noting positive definiteness and a unique minimum. It then introduces probit regression through a stochastic threshold model, derives its cumulative-distribution activation and relation to the Gaussian and erf functions, compares it with logistic regression, and discusses sensitivity to outliers and modeling mislabeled targets. Finally, it explains canonical link functions as the general exponential-family reason that gradients take the prediction-error times feature-vector form, and gives the corresponding conditional-mean identity.

nodes.title: 4.3.6 Canonical link functions
nodes.summary: The passage discusses classifier outliers and label noise, emphasizing the greater outlier sensitivity of probit regression and presenting a probabilistic label-flip model. It then explains canonical link functions for generalized linear models: exponential-family target distributions, their conditional means, activation and link functions, and the derivation showing that canonical links reduce likelihood gradients to prediction error times the feature vector, with model-specific scale parameters. It concludes by introducing the greater integration difficulty of Bayesian logistic regression and motivating the Laplace approximation.

This section develops probabilistic discriminative classification from exponential-family class models to generalized linear models. It introduces fixed nonlinear feature bases, binary logistic regression, its likelihood-based training, gradients, overfitting issues, and IRLS optimization; extends these ideas to multiclass softmax regression with Newton/IRLS methods; and presents probit regression as an alternative based on a noisy threshold model. It also discusses class overlap, outliers, label noise, canonical links and their error-times-feature gradients, and the motivation for Laplace approximation in Bayesian logistic regression.

nodes.title: 4.4. The Laplace Approximation
4.4.1 Model comparison and BIC
nodes.summary: The text explains the scope and limitations of the Laplace approximation, including its local Gaussian nature, handling of multimodal and non-real variables, dependence on dataset size, and inability to capture global distributional structure. It derives a Laplace approximation to Bayesian model evidence, identifies the Hessian and Occam complexity penalty, and motivates the BIC approximation while noting its stronger penalty than AIC and potential unreliability for poorly determined parameters. It then introduces Bayesian logistic regression, whose exact posterior and predictive inference are intractable, and proposes Laplace approximation beginning with a general Gaussian prior over the weights.

The section reviews generalized linear-model links and gradients, then develops the Laplace approximation as a Gaussian approximation obtained from the mode and local negative Hessian of a density, first in one dimension and then in multiple dimensions. It explains the numerical steps and validity conditions, discusses limitations for multimodal or poorly determined distributions, and applies the method to Bayesian evidence and model comparison through the Occam penalty and BIC. It concludes by motivating and setting up Laplace-approximated Bayesian logistic regression with a Gaussian weight prior.

nodes.title: 4.5. Bayesian Logistic Regression
nodes.summary: The text completes the Laplace-approximation discussion by defining the posterior Hessian, explaining the Occam factor in Bayesian evidence, and deriving the BIC approximation while warning about rank-deficient Hessians. It then introduces Bayesian logistic regression, whose exact posterior and predictive distributions are intractable, and applies a Gaussian prior and Laplace approximation to obtain a Gaussian posterior centered at the MAP solution with covariance determined by the Hessian. Prediction is reduced to integrating a logistic sigmoid over the Gaussian distribution of the projected weight a=w^Tφ; approximating the sigmoid by a suitably scaled probit yields a closed-form approximate predictive probability. The resulting decision boundary matches the MAP boundary, though uncertainty remains important for nonstandard decision rules. The section ends with exercises on convex-hull separability and preservation of linear target constraints by least-squares predictions.

It then presents exercises on the relationship between convex-hull intersection and linear separability, and on preservation of linear constraints by least-squares predictions.

nodes.summary: The text derives a Gaussian-convolution approximation for the logistic sigmoid and applies it to Bayesian predictive classification, showing that weight marginalization leaves the equal-prior, minimum-error decision boundary unchanged while affecting more complex decisions. It then presents Exercises 4.1–4.10 covering convex-hull separability, preservation of linear target constraints under least squares, multiple constraints, class-separation and Fisher criteria, covariance-based least-squares classification, sigmoid identities and inversion, Gaussian generative posterior parameters, and maximum-likelihood estimates for multiclass priors and shared-covariance Gaussian means.

nodes.title: Exercises on Linear Models and Classification
nodes.summary: This page presents exercises on least-squares linear models, constrained class separation, Fisher’s discriminant criterion, covariance-based solutions, logistic sigmoid properties, Gaussian generative classification, and maximum-likelihood estimation of class priors and means.
