Topics include bias basis functions, preservation of linear constraints by least squares, Fisher discriminant optimization and covariance formulations, sigmoid identities and derivatives, Gaussian generative classifiers, maximum-likelihood estimation of class priors, means, and shared covariance, naive Bayes softmax linearity, logistic-regression likelihood behavior for separable data, Hessian positive definiteness and uniqueness of the optimum, and likelihood formulation for probabilistically mislabeled binary training data.

nodes.title: Classification Models, Logistic Regression, and Covariance Estimation
nodes.summary: The page covers maximum-likelihood estimation of class means and shared covariance, linear softmax scores in discrete naive Bayes, derivatives of the logistic sigmoid and logistic-regression error, behavior on linearly separable data, Hessian definiteness and uniqueness of the logistic-regression solution, and likelihood construction for probabilistically mislabeled binary training data.

nodes.title: 4.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 4.17–4.25 cover derivatives and gradients for softmax and cross-entropy models; gradient and Hessian derivation for probit regression; positive semidefiniteness of the multiclass logistic-regression Hessian; the relationship between probit and erf functions; Laplace-approximation model evidence and its reduction to BIC under a broad Gaussian prior and iid data; Gaussian-posterior marginalization in logistic regression; and matching the logistic sigmoid to a scaled probit function, yielding λ² = π/8.

nodes.title: 4.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 4.17–4.26 cover derivatives and gradients for softmax and cross-entropy functions; gradient and Hessian derivation for probit regression and IRLS; positive semidefiniteness of the multiclass logistic-regression Hessian; the relationship between probit and erf functions; derivation of the Laplace log model evidence and the BIC approximation; Gaussian marginalization of logistic regression; matching logistic and scaled-probit derivatives; and proof of the probit–Gaussian convolution identity.

This section presents linear models for binary and multiclass classification, beginning with target representations, linear decision surfaces, discriminant functions, least-squares methods, Fisher’s discriminant, and the perceptron. It then develops probabilistic generative classifiers based on Bayes’ theorem, Gaussian and discrete naive Bayes models, exponential-family distributions, and their resulting logistic or softmax posteriors. Probabilistic discriminative models are introduced through generalized linear models, logistic and softmax regression, IRLS/Newton optimization, probit regression, and issues such as overfitting, separability, overlap, outliers, and label noise. The section explains Laplace approximation, Bayesian evidence, Occam penalties, and BIC, and applies these ideas to Bayesian logistic regression and approximate predictive inference. Exercises reinforce geometric separability, least-squares and Fisher classification, covariance estimation, sigmoid and softmax calculus, generative and discriminative likelihoods, Hessian properties, probit models, Bayesian marginalization, and model evidence.

nodes.title: 5 Neural Networks
5.1. Feed-forward Network Functions
5.1.1 Weight-space symmetries
nodes.summary: The text illustrates the expressive power of two-layer neural networks through function approximation and binary classification examples, showing how multiple tanh hidden units combine to form nonlinear mappings and decision boundaries. It then explains weight-space symmetries: sign flips of hidden-unit parameters and permutations of hidden units produce multiple equivalent weight vectors, yielding an M!2^M symmetry factor for a two-layer network and corresponding products across deeper layers. These symmetries are broadly applicable across activation functions and can matter in Bayesian model comparison. Finally, it introduces network training as parameter estimation for nonlinear input-output mappings, beginning with sum-of-squares minimization over a paired training set.

This section introduces feed-forward neural networks as learned nonlinear extensions of linear models. It develops their layered computation from biased weighted inputs through nonlinear hidden units to task-dependent outputs, explains biases, forward propagation, multilayer-perceptron terminology, differentiability, and extensions such as extra layers and skip connections. It also discusses why linear hidden-unit networks collapse to linear mappings and their connection to principal component analysis, illustrates the expressive power of nonlinear two-layer networks, analyzes parameter symmetries from hidden-unit sign changes and permutations, and introduces network training as nonlinear parameter estimation via sum-of-squares minimization.

nodes.title: 5.2. Network Training
5.2.1 Parameter optimization
nodes.summary: The text introduces softmax outputs and their matching multiclass cross-entropy error, explains their normalization, invariance-induced degeneracy, and regularization, and summarizes the appropriate activation/error pairs for regression and classification. It then presents neural-network training as minimizing a nonlinear error surface: gradients identify directions of greatest increase, minima require zero gradients, and stationary points include minima, maxima, and saddle points. Neural networks have multiple equivalent and inequivalent minima due to nonlinearities and parameter symmetries, so iterative numerical optimization is used rather than analytical solutions. Finally, it introduces Taylor expansion as a local quadratic approximation for understanding optimization algorithms.

nodes.title: 5.2.2 Local quadratic approximation
nodes.summary: The text explains neural-network error minimization as the search for stationary points where the gradient vanishes, distinguishing global and local minima and noting the abundance of equivalent and inequivalent solutions in nonlinear error landscapes. Since analytical solutions are generally unavailable, iterative numerical updates are used. It then develops a local quadratic approximation using the gradient and Hessian, showing through eigenvalues and eigenvectors that minima require a positive-definite Hessian and produce elliptical constant-error contours. Finally, it introduces the computational value of gradient information, obtainable efficiently by backpropagation, and notes that a quadratic model with W parameters contains O(W²) independent information.

nodes.title: 5.2.3 Use of gradient information
nodes.summary: The text explains how the Hessian characterizes minima: quadratic error contours are eigenvector-aligned ellipses, and a stationary point is a minimum when the Hessian is positive definite, equivalently when all its eigenvalues are positive. It then shows why efficiently computed gradients make neural-network training computationally practical, reducing the approximate cost from O(W³) without gradients to O(W²) with them. Basic batch gradient descent repeatedly moves weights opposite the gradient using a learning rate, but is inefficient compared with conjugate-gradient and quasi-Newton methods. Multiple random starts and validation may be needed to find a good minimum. Finally, it introduces online or stochastic gradient descent, which uses one data point at a time for summed maximum-likelihood error functions and is suited to large data sets.

nodes.title: 5.2.4 Gradient descent optimization
nodes.summary: The text compares the computational costs of gradient-free and gradient-based minimization, showing why efficient gradient evaluation through backpropagation is central to neural-network training. It explains batch gradient descent, its update rule, limitations, and stronger alternatives such as conjugate-gradient and quasi-Newton methods, including the possible need for multiple random restarts and validation. It then describes online/stochastic and minibatch gradient descent, emphasizing their efficiency with redundant or large data and their ability to escape some local minima. Finally, it introduces error backpropagation as the efficient forward-and-backward evaluation of error derivatives and distinguishes this process from the separate weight-update optimization stage.

This section develops neural-network training as maximum-likelihood or error-function minimization. It derives sum-of-squares training for Gaussian regression, estimates noise precision, and explains the corresponding activation/error pairings for regression, binary classification, and multiclass classification using identity, sigmoid, and softmax outputs. It then examines the nonconvex error landscape, including parameter symmetries, multiple solutions, stationary points, and local quadratic geometry characterized by the Hessian. Finally, it explains why backpropagated gradients make optimization practical and compares batch, stochastic, and minibatch gradient descent with conjugate-gradient and quasi-Newton methods, including initialization, validation, and the distinction between derivative computation and weight-update optimization.

nodes.title: 5.3. Error Backpropagation
5.3.1 Evaluation of error-function derivatives
Error Backpropagation
nodes.summary: The text explains hidden-unit error calculation by the chain rule and derives the backpropagation rule δj = h′(aj)Σk wkjδk, emphasizing the direction and indexing of backward propagation. It presents the complete backpropagation algorithm, explains summation of gradients for batch training and extension to unit-specific activation functions, and then introduces a two-layer example with linear outputs, tanh hidden activations, a sum-of-squares error, the tanh derivative, and the corresponding forward-propagation equations.

This section develops the evaluation of error-function derivatives for general feed-forward neural networks. It begins with per-pattern and batch gradients, illustrates the local error-times-input structure using a linear sum-of-squares model, and then applies the chain rule to define backpropagated unit errors and derive the weight gradient ∂En/∂wji = δjzi. Output and hidden-unit error formulas are established, including δj = h′(aj)Σk wkjδk, followed by the full forward- and backward-propagation algorithm, batch accumulation, and support for unit-specific activations. A two-layer linear-output, tanh-hidden network with sum-of-squares error provides a concrete example.

nodes.title: 5.3.2 A simple example
nodes.summary: The text completes the batch-error gradient formulation, notes that backpropagation supports different activation functions for different units, and works through a two-layer tanh-hidden, linear-output network with sum-of-squares error. It gives the forward equations, output and hidden error signals, and gradients for both layers. It then explains backpropagation's O(W) computational efficiency and contrasts it with forward and central finite-difference derivatives, discussing their accuracy, roundoff limitations, doubled cost for central differences, and loss of O(W) scaling.

nodes.title: 5.3.3 Efficiency of backpropagation
nodes.summary: The text completes the backpropagation formulas for output and hidden-unit errors and for derivatives of first- and second-layer weights. It explains backpropagation’s O(W) computational efficiency, contrasts it with forward and central finite-difference differentiation—with O(W²) cost and different accuracy— and recommends numerical derivatives as implementation checks. It then introduces the Jacobian matrix of network outputs with respect to inputs, explaining its role in applying the chain rule and propagating sensitivities or errors through differentiable modular systems.

nodes.title: 5.3.4 The Jacobian matrix
nodes.summary: The text explains numerical differentiation as a costly but valuable validation tool for backpropagation, then develops backpropagation for computing the input-output Jacobian of differentiable neural-network modules. The Jacobian supports chain-rule error propagation through modular systems and local propagation of small input uncertainties, with recursive formulas, sigmoid and softmax output cases, and numerical finite-difference verification. It then introduces the Hessian of the error with respect to weights and biases, describing its roles in second-order training, retraining, pruning, and Bayesian Laplace approximations, and notes that it can be computed exactly through an extended backpropagation procedure.

This section distinguishes online, batch, and minibatch gradient methods before developing error backpropagation as an efficient O(W) procedure for computing feed-forward network error derivatives, separate from the choice of weight-update optimizer. It derives the chain-rule error signals, weight gradients, and complete forward/backward algorithms for general activations and batch training, illustrating them with a tanh-hidden, linear-output network. It compares backpropagation with finite-difference derivatives and their computational and numerical trade-offs, while recommending numerical checks. The section then extends backpropagation to compute network Jacobians for sensitivity, uncertainty, and modular chain-rule propagation, covers sigmoid and softmax cases and numerical verification, and introduces exact Hessian computation and its applications to second-order training, retraining, pruning, and Bayesian approximations.

nodes.title: 5.4. The Hessian Matrix
5.4.1 Diagonal approximation
nodes.summary: The text discusses efficient Hessian evaluation in neural networks, focusing on diagonal and outer-product approximations. A diagonal approximation reduces computation from O(W²) to O(W) by discarding off-diagonal terms, though it can be inaccurate because Hessians are often strongly nondiagonal; retaining all terms gives exact diagonals but removes the efficiency benefit. For sum-of-squares regression, neglecting residual-weighted second derivatives leads to the Levenberg–Marquardt outer-product Hessian, efficiently formed from backpropagated output gradients, with related weighted forms for logistic cross-entropy and softmax outputs. Several exercises are listed.

nodes.title: 5.4.2 Outer product approximation
nodes.summary: This section develops the Levenberg–Marquardt or outer product approximation to the Hessian for neural networks. For sum-of-squares regression, the exact Hessian consists of a first-derivative outer-product sum plus a residual-weighted second-derivative sum. The latter may be ignored when predictions are accurate or when zero-mean residuals are assumed uncorrelated with the second derivatives, producing an efficiently computable Hessian approximation based on backpropagated gradients. Its validity is mainly associated with trained networks. The corresponding cross-entropy approximation for sigmoid outputs weights each outer product by y_n(1−y_n), with a similar result for softmax multiclass networks; several related exercises are referenced.

nodes.title: 5.4.3 Inverse Hessian
nodes.summary: The text presents two methods for obtaining second-order information in neural networks. First, it derives a sequential, computationally efficient inverse-Hessian approximation from the outer-product Hessian using the Sherman–Morrison/Woodbury identity, starting from a small diagonal regularizer and processing data points one at a time. It notes extensions to multiple-output networks and the related use of quasi-Newton methods. Second, it describes estimating Hessian elements by central finite differences of the error function, with accuracy constrained by numerical precision and a second-order truncation error.

nodes.title: 5.4.4 Finite differences
nodes.summary: The text presents three approaches to Hessian computation in neural networks: a sequential inverse-Hessian update based on the outer-product approximation and the Sherman–Morrison/Woodbury identity, finite-difference approximations, and exact backpropagation-based evaluation. The inverse-Hessian method processes data points in one pass, uses αI initialization for regularization, extends readily to multiple outputs, and is related to quasi-Newton training methods. Finite differences using direct error evaluations cost O(W^3), while differencing backpropagated gradients costs O(W^2); central differences provide O(δ^2) accuracy. Exact Hessian evaluation applies to arbitrary differentiable feed-forward networks and also costs O(W^2). For a two-layer network, the exact method defines output-error derivatives and begins deriving Hessian blocks, including the block for pairs of second-layer weights.

nodes.title: 5.4.5 Exact evaluation of the Hessian
nodes.summary: The passage compares numerical and exact Hessian evaluation methods. Direct symmetric finite differences achieve O(δ²) accuracy but cost O(W³), while finite differences of backpropagated gradients reduce this to O(W²). An exact backpropagation-based Hessian method works for general differentiable feed-forward networks and error functions, with explicit three-block formulas given for a two-layer network, plus handling of biases and skip connections. It then introduces direct Hessian-vector products, which avoid O(W²) storage and computation and can be obtained in O(W) using Pearlmutter’s directional-derivative operator applied to forward- and backpropagation equations; the worked example is cut off in the excerpt.

nodes.title: 5.4.6 Fast multiplication by the Hessian
nodes.summary: The text completes formulas for Hessian entries in two-layer networks, including bias and skip-connection handling, then develops an efficient O(W) procedure for computing Hessian-vector products by differentiating forward and backward propagation with the operator R{·} = vᵀ∇. It gives the resulting propagation and gradient-product equations, explains implementation and recovery of the full Hessian, and begins a discussion of neural-network regularization, covering hidden-unit count, model complexity, local minima, validation-based selection, and quadratic regularization.

This section defines the Hessian of a neural-network error function and explains its importance for second-order training, retraining, pruning, and Bayesian inference. It compares diagonal and outer-product/Levenberg–Marquardt approximations, derives efficient inverse-Hessian updates, and examines finite-difference methods with their accuracy and computational costs. It then develops exact Hessian computation through extended backpropagation, including biases and skip connections, and presents O(W) Hessian-vector products using directional derivatives. The section concludes by introducing regularization and related issues of model complexity and optimization.

nodes.title: 5.5. Regularization in Neural Networks
5.5.1 Consistent Gaussian priors
nodes.summary: The text discusses neural-network complexity control through weight decay, consistent Gaussian priors, and early stopping. Standard L2 regularization corresponds to a zero-mean Gaussian weight prior but is not invariant to affine rescaling of inputs and outputs. A layer-specific quadratic regularizer excluding biases restores the required invariance when its coefficients are transformed appropriately, though the resulting unconstrained-bias prior is improper; separate bias priors, grouped weight priors, and automatic relevance determination are also described. Early stopping controls overfitting by halting iterative training when validation error reaches its minimum, reflecting a gradual increase in effective model complexity. Figures illustrate network fits with different hidden-unit counts and test-error variation caused by local minima and initialization.

nodes.title: 5.5.2 Early stopping
nodes.summary: The text discusses structured priors and regularization in neural networks, noting transformation-related rescaling, the problems of improper priors, separate bias hyperparameters, grouped weight priors, and automatic relevance determination. It explains how prior precisions affect sampled network functions. It then presents early stopping as an alternative complexity-control method: validation error identifies the stopping point, effective complexity grows during training, and for quadratic loss early stopping is quantitatively analogous to weight decay, with τ η related to 1/λ. Finally, it introduces invariance in pattern recognition, gives examples from images and speech, explains why learning invariance solely from transformed examples can be impractical, and begins the first of four approaches—training-set augmentation with transformed replicas.

nodes.title: 5.5.3 Invariances
nodes.summary: The text discusses early stopping as a generalization technique and its qualitative relationship to weight decay, then introduces invariance in neural networks. It explains why predictions should remain unchanged under transformations, the limitations of learning invariance solely from data, and four alternatives: data augmentation, output-penalizing regularization, invariant feature extraction, and invariant network or kernel structures. It describes the benefits and drawbacks of these approaches, illustrates synthetic image warping, and introduces tangent propagation, which uses local tangent vectors to regularize a model against continuous input transformations.

nodes.title: 5.5.4 Tangent propagation
nodes.summary: The text discusses transformation invariance as a form of neural-network regularization. It introduces tangent propagation, where continuous transformations trace input manifolds and their local tangent vectors are combined with the network Jacobian to penalize output sensitivity. The resulting regularizer, its weighting, finite-difference implementation, backpropagation, extension to multiple transformations, and relation to tangent distance are explained, with handwritten-digit rotation and synthetic warping illustrations. It then introduces training on transformed data and begins deriving its relationship to tangent propagation using an infinite-data sum-of-squares error formulation.

nodes.title: 5.5.5 Training with transformed data
nodes.summary: The text explains how tangent distance and training on transformed data promote invariance. A Taylor expansion of small random input transformations shows that the augmented-data error equals the original error plus a variance-weighted regularizer; to leading order this is tangent propagation, while additive noise produces Tikhonov regularization, which can be optimized by extended backpropagation and may improve generalization. It then introduces convolutional neural networks as an architectural way to encode image invariances, emphasizing their handling of translations, scaling, rotations, and elastic deformations through local feature extraction and hierarchical combination rather than fully connected processing.

nodes.title: 5.5.6 Convolutional networks
nodes.summary: The text explains how small input-transformation noise produces gradient-based regularization, reducing in the additive-noise case to Tikhonov regularization, and notes its connection to improved generalization and extended backpropagation. It then introduces convolutional neural networks as architectures that encode image invariances through local receptive fields, shared convolutional weights, and subsampling, describing feature maps, translation robustness, multilayer structures, training, and parameter savings. Finally, it introduces soft weight sharing, which learns groups of similar weights and their statistical properties instead of imposing exact equality.

nodes.title: 5.5.7 Soft weight sharing
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of convolutional networks by explaining feature maps, local receptive fields, subsampling, increasing transformation invariance, final classification layers, backpropagation with shared weights, and the resulting parameter savings. It then presents soft weight sharing, which regularizes weights toward groups modeled by a learnable Gaussian mixture. The mixture prior, regularized objective, joint optimization, posterior responsibilities, and gradients for weights, means, variances, and mixing coefficients are given, including exponential variance and softmax mixing parameterizations. Finally, it introduces mixture density networks for modeling multimodal conditional distributions, motivating them with inverse problems such as the two-solution robot-arm kinematics example and disease diagnosis, and starts a toy multimodal data example.

This section presents regularization methods for controlling neural-network complexity and improving generalization. It covers hidden-unit selection, quadratic weight decay, Gaussian and structured priors, bias treatment, grouped priors, automatic relevance determination, and early stopping. It then develops invariance-based regularization through transformed-data augmentation, output penalties, invariant features and architectures, tangent propagation, tangent distance, and the connection between transformation noise, tangent propagation, and Tikhonov regularization. Convolutional networks are described as an architectural means of encoding image invariances through local shared processing and subsampling. Finally, the section introduces soft weight sharing with learnable Gaussian-mixture priors and mixture density networks for multimodal conditional modeling.

nodes.title: 5.6. Mixture Density Networks
nodes.summary: The text introduces mixture density networks as a solution for supervised inverse problems with multimodal and heteroscedastic conditional distributions. Robot-arm kinematics and a toy regression example show why Gaussian least-squares regression can fail when several outputs correspond to one input. A neural network can instead predict the parameters of an input-dependent Gaussian mixture, using softmax weights, positive variance transformations, and direct mean outputs; likelihood training and responsibility-based derivatives permit ordinary backpropagation. The resulting model can represent changing unimodal or multimodal densities, from which means, variances, and approximate modes can be extracted, although means may be inappropriate for multimodal predictions. The text then begins Bayesian neural networks, contrasting maximum-likelihood and MAP estimation with parameter marginalization, and explains why exact Bayesian inference is unavailable for multilayer networks, motivating variational approximations.

nodes.title: 5.7. Bayesian Neural Networks
5.7.1 Posterior parameter distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops Bayesian regression with neural networks using a Laplace approximation to the weight posterior and a local linearization of the network around its MAP solution. It specifies Gaussian observation and weight-prior models, derives the regularized posterior and Hessian-based Gaussian approximation, and obtains a Gaussian predictive distribution whose variance combines observation noise with parameter uncertainty. It then applies the evidence framework to estimate the hyperparameters alpha and beta and compare models, deriving the approximate log evidence and introducing Hessian eigenvalues and an effective parameter count for optimizing alpha.

nodes.title: 5.7.2 Hyperparameter optimization
nodes.summary: Bayesian neural-network regression has a Gaussian predictive distribution whose mean is the MAP network output and whose variance combines intrinsic noise with input-dependent uncertainty from parameter estimation. The evidence framework with a Laplace approximation provides iterative re-estimation formulas for the hyperparameters α and β, using the MAP error, Hessian eigenvalues, and effective parameter count γ. These procedures are complicated by the nonlinear dependence of the Hessian on α, multimodal posteriors, initialization sensitivity, equivalent and inequivalent hidden-unit modes, and the numerical difficulty of evaluating Hessian determinants. Evidence-based model comparison can include optimized or marginalized hyperparameters and must account for hidden-unit symmetry multiplicities. The section concludes by beginning the treatment of Bayesian neural networks for classification.

nodes.title: 5.7.3 Bayesian neural networks for classification
nodes.summary: The text completes the Bayesian neural-network regression evidence procedure, defining the effective parameter count, re-estimating beta, discussing alternating hyperparameter/posterior updates, multimodal solutions, model evidence, Hessian-determinant difficulties, and symmetry factors. It then develops the Laplace treatment for binary classification: Bernoulli likelihood, Gaussian prior, MAP optimization, Hessian-based posterior, evidence optimization of alpha, and predictive inference. Because sigmoid marginalization is intractable, the network activation is linearized and its Gaussian uncertainty is integrated using an approximation, producing less confident predictions while preserving the decision boundary. Figures illustrate evidence-based reduction of overfitting and uncertainty-aware classification. The section concludes with exercises on sigmoid–tanh network equivalence and the likelihood interpretation of sum-of-squares training.

The section moves from the limitations of conditional means in multimodal mixture-density regression to Bayesian neural networks. It develops Laplace-approximated Bayesian regression and classification, deriving MAP-based Gaussian parameter posteriors and predictive distributions that account for both observation noise and parameter uncertainty. The evidence framework is used to optimize hyperparameters, estimate effective model complexity, and compare models, with discussion of multimodality, hidden-unit symmetries, initialization, and numerical challenges. Binary classification is handled with a Bernoulli model and an approximation to otherwise intractable sigmoid marginalization, producing calibrated uncertainty. The section also includes practical illustrations and exercises on activation-function equivalence and the probabilistic interpretation of least-squares training.

nodes.title: 5.2 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of the Laplace approximation for Bayesian neural networks, presenting an approximation for logistic-sigmoid predictions and explaining how parameter marginalization makes predictions less confident without changing the decision boundary. It then provides ten exercises covering sigmoid–tanh network equivalence, likelihood and error-function derivations for regression and classification, robustness to label noise, cross-entropy and output-unit derivatives, tanh derivatives, alternative binary target coding, and the eigenvalue criterion for Hessian positive definiteness.

nodes.title: Neural Network Exercises on Likelihood, Errors, Activations, and Hessians
nodes.summary: This page contains exercises on probabilistic neural-network training and mathematical properties: multivariate Gaussian regression likelihood with known or learned covariance, robust binary classification under label noise, the equivalence of likelihood and cross-entropy for multiclass models, derivatives for sigmoid and softmax cross-entropy outputs, the tanh derivative, reformulation of binary classification using {-1, 1} targets, and the eigenvalue criterion for Hessian positive definiteness.

nodes.title: Neural Network Error Functions, Hessians, and Jacobians
key_items: 5.17 ( ) Consider a squared loss function of the form
nodes.summary: This page presents exercises on quadratic error geometry, Hessian definiteness and parameter counting, Taylor-expansion cancellations, forward and backward Jacobian computation, outer-product Hessian approximations for single and multiple outputs, conditional-expectation-based Hessian derivation, skip-layer derivative equations, and the corresponding Hessian approximation for sigmoid outputs with cross-entropy loss.

nodes.title: 5.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 5.11–5.41 cover quadratic-error geometry and Hessian properties; forward and backward computation of neural-network Jacobians, Hessians, and outer-product approximations; extensions to multiple outputs, skip connections, softmax and logistic-cross-entropy models; gradient-descent dynamics, early stopping, and its connection to regularization; tangent propagation, noise-induced Tikhonov regularization, and tied-weight backpropagation; verification of intermediate formulas; softmax mixture coefficients and mixture-density-network derivatives and moments; robot-arm forward kinematics; and Bayesian neural-network predictive distributions, evidence, and multiclass extensions.

This section presents multilayer feed-forward neural networks as adaptive, compact nonlinear models for statistical pattern recognition. It develops their layered functions and expressive properties, trains them by likelihood and error minimization for regression and classification, and explains efficient gradient, Jacobian, and Hessian computation through backpropagation. It covers optimization methods, nonconvex geometry, Hessian approximations, second-order techniques, regularization and invariance, convolutional architectures, soft weight sharing, and mixture density networks for multimodal conditional distributions. It concludes with Bayesian neural networks and Laplace and evidence-based approximations for parameter uncertainty, predictive distributions, model complexity, and classification calibration, supported by extensive exercises on the associated derivations, algorithms, and applications.

nodes.title: 6 Kernel Methods
6.1. Dual Representations
nodes.summary: The text derives the dual form of regularized linear least-squares regression. The optimal weight vector is expressed as a combination of training feature vectors, allowing the objective, solution, and predictions to be written entirely through the Gram matrix and kernel function. The resulting prediction uses kernel similarities and training targets, while the main benefit of the dual form is implicit access to high- or infinite-dimensional feature spaces despite its potentially larger matrix inversion. Duality is noted as important for perceptrons, Gaussian processes, and support vector machines. The text then begins discussing kernel construction, explaining both feature-map-based kernels and directly constructed valid kernels, with the squared inner-product kernel as an example.

nodes.title: 6.2. Constructing Kernels
Techniques for Constructing New Kernels.
nodes.summary: The text presents systematic rules for constructing valid symmetric positive-semidefinite kernels and illustrates kernel engineering with polynomial, Gaussian, nonlinear-distance, symbolic-set, generative-model, sequence, Fisher, and sigmoidal kernels. It explains the feature-space and validity rationale for these constructions, including latent-variable and hidden-Markov-model kernels, Fisher-score whitening and practical approximations, and the limitations of sigmoidal kernels. It then introduces radial basis function networks, describing their distance-based basis functions, exact interpolation formulation, overfitting with noisy data, and origin in regularization theory through Green's functions.

This section explains how to construct valid kernels either from explicit feature mappings or directly, using the polynomial kernel to illustrate the induced nonlinear feature space. It gives the Gram-matrix positive-semidefiniteness criterion for validity and presents systematic closure rules for building kernels from simpler ones, covering polynomial, Gaussian, distance-based, symbolic, generative, sequence, Fisher, and sigmoidal constructions, including latent-variable and hidden-Markov-model settings, Fisher-score approximations, and sigmoidal limitations. It concludes by introducing radial basis function networks, their interpolation and overfitting behavior, and their connection to regularization theory and Green's functions.

nodes.title: 6.3. Radial Basis Function Networks
6.3.1 Nadaraya-Watson model
nodes.summary: The text discusses selecting centres for radial basis functions and introduces the Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression model by deriving it from Parzen estimation of the joint input-target density. The resulting predictor is a normalized, locality-based weighted average of training targets and also defines a complete conditional distribution. Gaussian examples and an illustrative sinusoidal-data figure are described, followed by extensions using more flexible Gaussian components and Gaussian mixture models, which can reduce prediction cost while increasing training cost. The discussion concludes by transitioning to Gaussian processes.

This section introduces radial basis function networks as linear models whose basis functions depend on distance from centres. It covers their origins in exact interpolation, regularization and Green’s functions, and noisy-input modeling, including normalized bases and the Nadaraya-Watson estimator. It explains the computational motivation for using fewer data-selected centres with least-squares weights, then develops the Nadaraya-Watson model through Parzen joint-density estimation as a normalized local target average and complete conditional distribution. Gaussian and mixture-based extensions, illustrative examples, their computational trade-offs, and the transition to Gaussian processes are also covered.

nodes.title: 6.4. Gaussian Processes
6.4.1 Linear regression revisited
nodes.summary: The text introduces Gaussian processes as Bayesian distributions over functions and motivates them by reformulating Bayesian linear regression in terms of function values. A Gaussian prior over linear-regression weights induces a Gaussian distribution over values at any finite set of inputs, with covariance represented by a Gram matrix whose entries are given by a kernel. It defines Gaussian processes through finite-dimensional Gaussian marginals, discusses zero means, kernel-based covariance, direct and basis-function kernel constructions, and gives Gaussian and exponential-kernel examples, including the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. It then extends the framework to regression by adding independent Gaussian observation noise, deriving the Gaussian likelihood for targets conditional on latent function values and the Gaussian marginal target distribution obtained by integrating those values out. Connections to kriging and other stochastic or time-series models, along with relevant references, are also noted.

nodes.title: 6.4.2 Gaussian processes for regression
nodes.summary: The text develops Gaussian process regression by adding independent Gaussian observation noise to a zero-mean Gaussian-process prior, deriving the resulting Gaussian marginal target distribution and its covariance. It presents a flexible quadratic-exponential kernel with constant and linear components, explains the joint Gaussian conditioning formulas for predictive means and variances, and interprets the predictive mean as a kernel or radial-basis expansion. It states the positive-semidefinite kernel requirement, compares Gaussian-process and finite-basis computational costs, and discusses scalability, approximation methods, and extensions such as co-kriging, manifold learning, and stochastic differential equations. It then explains learning covariance hyperparameters through marginal-likelihood optimization, gives the likelihood and gradient expressions, notes nonconvexity and Bayesian alternatives, and introduces the need for input-dependent noise models in heteroscedastic regression. Figures illustrate prior samples, noisy process observations, Gaussian conditioning, and predictive uncertainty.

nodes.title: 6.4.3 Learning the hyperparameters
nodes.summary: The text discusses applications of Gaussian process regression, learning covariance-function hyperparameters through likelihood optimization and gradient formulas, challenges posed by nonconvex likelihoods and Bayesian marginalization, and modeling input-dependent noise with a second Gaussian process. It then introduces automatic relevance determination, explaining how dimension-specific kernel precisions reveal the relative importance of inputs, with prior-function illustrations and a synthetic example.

nodes.title: 6.4.4 Automatic relevance determination
nodes.summary: The text introduces input-dependent variance modeling with a second Gaussian process for log variance, then explains automatic relevance determination, in which separate kernel precisions are optimized to infer the relevance of input variables. It presents the ARD kernel, illustrates how small precisions reduce sensitivity, describes a three-variable synthetic example where optimization identifies relevant, noisy, and irrelevant inputs, and gives an augmented ARD exponential-quadratic kernel. Finally, it begins Gaussian-process classification by transforming real-valued GP outputs with a logistic sigmoid to obtain probabilities between zero and one.

nodes.title: 6.4.5 Gaussian processes for classification
nodes.summary: The text first demonstrates ARD for Gaussian processes, showing how optimized input-specific hyperparameters identify relevant, noisy, and irrelevant predictors, and gives the corresponding ARD kernel. It then introduces Gaussian-process classification by applying a logistic sigmoid to latent GP functions, yielding Bernoulli class probabilities. The latent training and test values follow a zero-mean GP prior with a kernel covariance plus a small numerical diagonal term. Binary predictive probabilities require integrating the sigmoid likelihood over the latent posterior, an intractable operation addressed by sampling, Gaussian-based approximations, variational inference, expectation propagation, and the Laplace approximation. The text explains the main properties of these methods, including variational extensions to multiclass classification, and begins deriving the Laplace method’s posterior integral using Bayes’ theorem.

nodes.title: 6.4.6 Laplace approximation
nodes.summary: The text develops Gaussian-process classification, focusing on approximating the intractable logistic predictive integral. It reviews variational inference and expectation propagation, then derives the Laplace approximation: the logistic posterior mode is found by Newton–Raphson/IRLS, its positive-definite Hessian defines a Gaussian posterior, and Gaussian-process conditioning yields predictive latent mean and variance for approximating class probabilities. It also derives a Laplace marginal likelihood and its covariance-parameter gradient, including derivatives through the posterior mode, and notes optimization, regularization, multiclass extension, and a synthetic example. Finally, it explains how infinite-width Bayesian neural networks converge to Gaussian processes, while losing output sharing, and notes explicit nonstationary kernels for probit and Gaussian hidden units.

nodes.title: 6.4.7 Connection to neural networks
nodes.summary: The text explains the infinite-width connection between Bayesian neural networks and Gaussian processes, including the loss of output sharing, the resulting nonstationary kernels for specific activations, and the role of weight-prior hyperparameters. It also presents a Gaussian-process classification illustration and lists exercises on dual linear regression, kernelized perceptrons and nearest neighbours, positive-definite matrices, valid-kernel constructions, and a function-specific kernel.

This section develops Gaussian processes as Bayesian distributions over functions, beginning with the connection to Bayesian linear regression and kernelized covariance functions. It derives Gaussian-process regression with noisy observations, predictive distributions, kernel expansions, hyperparameter learning, computational considerations, approximation strategies, and extensions such as kriging and stochastic models. It covers heteroscedastic noise and automatic relevance determination for identifying informative inputs. The section then develops Gaussian-process classification with sigmoid likelihoods and approximate inference methods, especially the Laplace approximation and its optimization and marginal-likelihood calculations. Finally, it connects Gaussian processes to infinite-width Bayesian neural networks and records related kernel methods, applications, illustrations, references, and exercises.

This section introduces kernel methods, their dual representations, the kernel trick, and criteria and constructions for valid kernels. It develops radial basis function and Nadaraya–Watson models, including interpolation, regularization, noisy inputs, computational approximations, and density-based interpretations, then presents Gaussian-process regression and classification with prediction, covariance modeling, hyperparameter learning, noise extensions, approximations, and links to Bayesian linear models and neural networks. It concludes with extensive exercises on dual formulations, kernel validity and feature spaces, Fisher and subset kernels, positive-definite matrix properties, the representer theorem, kernel regression, predictive distributions, Gaussian-process equivalences, and Laplace-based classification inference.

nodes.title: 7 Sparse Kernel Machines
7.1. Maximum Margin Classifiers
Joseph-Louis Lagrange
nodes.summary: The text derives the kernelized dual form of the maximum-margin classifier, including its quadratic objective, constraints, computational considerations, and the role of positive-definite kernels. It gives the kernel-based prediction rule and explains the KKT conditions, support vectors, sparsity, and computation of the bias term. It also reformulates the hard-margin classifier using an infinite-penalty error function and quadratic regularization, illustrates nonlinear separation with a Gaussian kernel, and introduces the soft-margin extension for overlapping classes using nonnegative slack variables and linear penalties for margin violations.

nodes.title: 7.1.1 Overlapping class distributions
nodes.summary: The text explains soft-margin and kernel SVMs. Kernel mappings allow nonlinear separation, while support vectors determine the maximum-margin boundary and produce sparsity. For overlapping classes, slack variables permit margin violations and misclassification, leading to a C-regularized primal problem whose dual retains the separable objective but adds box constraints. It interprets support vectors and the bias term, introduces the nu-SVM and its error/support-vector interpretation, and discusses quadratic-programming training methods including chunking, decomposition, and SMO. It also explains why kernels do not remove the curse of dimensionality, illustrates polynomial feature mappings, and describes Platt sigmoid calibration for probabilistic outputs, noting its possible inaccuracy. Finally, it introduces the connection between nonseparable SVMs and regularized logistic-regression-style error minimization.

nodes.title: 7.1.2 Relation to logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text explains that polynomial kernels can represent constrained low-dimensional manifolds in higher-dimensional feature spaces; discusses the lack of native SVM probability outputs and Platt’s sigmoid calibration method, including its overfitting and calibration limitations; reformulates nonseparable SVMs using regularized hinge loss and compares hinge, logistic, misclassification, and squared losses; and reviews multiclass SVM strategies, including one-versus-the-rest, modified targets, and joint optimization, along with their consistency, scaling, class-balance, and computational-cost issues.

nodes.title: 7.1.3 Multiclass SVMs
nodes.summary: The passage compares classification error functions, explaining that the support vector loss's flat region yields sparse solutions, while logistic and hinge losses approximate misclassification error and squared loss can overemphasize confidently correct points. It then surveys multiclass SVM methods: one-versus-the-rest and its scaling and imbalance problems, joint multiclass optimization and its higher cost, one-versus-one voting, DAGSVM efficiency, and error-correcting output codes, noting that one-versus-the-rest remains most widely used. It also describes single-class SVMs for enclosing a specified high-density region using either a maximum-margin hyperplane or a minimum enclosing feature-space sphere, which are equivalent for translation-invariant kernels, and introduces sparse SVM regression.

nodes.title: 7.1.4 SVMs for regression
nodes.summary: The text discusses multiclass and single-class SVMs, SVM regression, and the foundations of computational learning theory. It compares one-versus-one, DAGSVM, error-correcting output codes, and the widely used one-versus-the-rest strategy for multiclass classification. Single-class methods instead enclose a chosen high-density region using either a maximum-margin hyperplane or a minimum enclosing feature-space sphere, which are equivalent for translation-invariant kernels. For regression, SVMs use ε-insensitive linear loss and slack variables to form a regularized constrained optimization problem. Its dual, kernel representation, box and equality constraints, and KKT conditions establish that only observations on or outside the ε-tube become support vectors, yielding sparse predictions; the bias is estimated from margin points. The ν-SVM formulation controls the fraction of points outside the tube and the number of support vectors, with parameters typically selected by cross-validation. Finally, the text introduces PAC/statistical learning theory, defining generalization through error and probability thresholds and identifying VC dimension as the key measure of function-class complexity used to derive sample-size bounds.

nodes.title: 7.1.5 Computational learning theory
nodes.summary: The text concludes the SVM discussion with an illustration of ν-SVM Gaussian-kernel regression, reviews PAC and PAC-Bayesian learning theory—including generalization criteria, VC dimension, worst-case bounds, and their conservatism—and introduces Bayesian Relevance Vector Machines as sparser alternatives to SVMs that provide probabilistic outputs, avoid several multiclass and parameter-selection limitations, and use a sparse-prior linear regression model with Gaussian target noise.

This section develops SVMs from maximum-margin linear classification through kernelization, duality, KKT conditions, support-vector sparsity, and quadratic-programming training. It covers hard- and soft-margin classifiers, slack penalties and ν-SVMs, nonlinear kernels, hinge-loss and logistic-regression connections, probability calibration, multiclass and single-class methods, and ε-insensitive sparse regression. It also introduces PAC and PAC-Bayesian learning theory and VC-dimension generalization bounds, and concludes by presenting Bayesian relevance vector machines as typically sparser, probabilistic alternatives to SVMs.

nodes.title: 7.2. Relevance Vector Machines
7.2.1 RVM for regression
nodes.summary: The text contrasts conservative PAC and PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds with practical machine-learning behavior, then introduces the Bayesian relevance vector machine as a sparse-kernel alternative to SVMs. It develops the RVM regression model, Gaussian likelihood, individual weight-precision priors, Gaussian posterior, evidence-based hyperparameter learning, re-estimation and EM procedures, and automatic relevance determination that prunes most basis functions and identifies relevance vectors. It derives the Gaussian predictive distribution and discusses its extrapolation-variance weakness, compares RVMs with Gaussian processes and SVMs using an example, and reviews RVM sparsity, prediction speed, accuracy, computational cost, nonconvex training disadvantage, and automatic parameter selection. The text ends by introducing a detailed analysis of the sparsity mechanism.

nodes.title: 7.2.2 Analysis of sparsity
Sequential Sparse Bayesian Learning Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how the relative quality and sparsity of a basis function determine the marginal-likelihood optimum for its hyperparameter: basis functions with q_i^2 <= s_i are pruned by setting alpha_i to infinity, whereas those with q_i^2 > s_i receive a finite closed-form update. It presents the resulting sequential sparse Bayesian learning algorithm for adding, updating, or removing basis functions, defines convenient Q_i and S_i quantities and their equivalent forms, and notes the O(M^3) cost based on the number of active vectors. It then introduces the extension of the RVM to binary classification using an ARD-weighted logistic sigmoid model.

This section explains why relevance vector machines are substantially sparser than SVMs, while comparing their accuracy, training behavior, computational cost, and automatic hyperparameter selection. It develops an intuitive geometric and mathematical account of sparsity using the marginal likelihood, showing how poorly aligned basis functions are pruned through the sparsity and quality measures s_i and q_i. These results produce a sequential sparse Bayesian learning method that explicitly adds, updates, or removes bases with cost tied to the active set, and the discussion concludes by extending the RVM framework to binary logistic classification.

nodes.title: 7.2.3 RVM for classification
nodes.summary: The text completes the fast sequential RVM training procedure by describing basis-function addition, removal, and hyperparameter updates, defining efficient quality and sparseness quantities, and establishing O(M^3) computation in terms of active bases. It then extends RVMs to binary classification through an ARD-prior logistic model and Laplace approximation, deriving the IRLS gradient, Hessian, posterior mean and covariance, marginal-likelihood hyperparameter updates, and the regression-like sparse learning formulation. Multiclass RVMs use softmax models and Laplace/IRLS optimization, offering probabilistic predictions and a principled alternative to pairwise SVMs at higher computational cost. The text compares RVM and SVM sparsity, training, and prediction costs, and concludes with exercises on Parzen and feature-space classification, maximum-margin properties, margin-dual relationships, logistic regression regularization, and derivation of the regression SVM dual.

This section develops relevance vector machines for regression and classification as sparse Bayesian alternatives to SVMs. It covers Gaussian-process-style regression modeling, ARD priors, evidence maximization, posterior prediction, pruning and the mathematical basis of sparsity, including efficient sequential basis selection. It then extends the framework to binary and multiclass logistic or softmax classification using Laplace and IRLS methods, compares RVMs with SVMs and Gaussian processes in accuracy, sparsity, training, prediction, and computational cost, and concludes with related theoretical and derivational exercises.

This chapter presents sparse kernel machines as computationally efficient kernel methods and develops support vector machines and relevance vector machines in depth. It covers SVM geometry, convex primal and dual optimization, KKT-based sparsity, hard and soft margins, ν-SVMs, nonlinear kernels, classification, regression, novelty detection, loss-function and probabilistic connections, multiclass methods, learning-theoretic bounds, and ε-insensitive regression. It then develops Bayesian RVMs for regression and binary or multiclass classification through ARD priors, evidence maximization, posterior prediction, pruning, sequential selection, Laplace and IRLS approximations, and comparisons with SVMs and Gaussian processes. The section concludes with derivational and conceptual exercises covering SVM geometry and duality, logistic regression, kernel classification, and detailed RVM posterior, evidence, prediction, sparsity, and hyperparameter-update calculations.

nodes.title: 8 Graphical Models
8.1. Bayesian Networks
8.1.1 Example: Polynomial regression
nodes.summary: The text explains how directed acyclic graphs represent joint probability distributions through products of node-specific conditional distributions given their parents, emphasizing normalization and the absence of directed cycles. It applies this framework to Bayesian polynomial regression, introducing graphical representations, plates for repeated observations, explicit deterministic parameters, observed-node shading, latent variables, posterior inference, and predictive distributions obtained by integrating out model parameters. It concludes by describing ancestral sampling, which generates joint or marginal samples by sampling DAG nodes in parent-to-child order.

nodes.title: 8.1.2 Generative models
nodes.summary: The text explains that Bayesian predictive distributions are found by integrating out model parameters, then introduces ancestral sampling for directed graphical models, in which variables are sampled in topological order and unwanted variables can be discarded to obtain marginals. It describes generative models as graphical representations of how observations arise, often using latent variables such as object identity, position, and orientation to model images. Such latent variables may be physically meaningful or merely computational constructs. Generative models can produce synthetic data through ancestral sampling, whereas polynomial regression is not generative unless a distribution over inputs is added. The section concludes by beginning a discussion of discrete variables and the role of exponential-family distributions as components of complex models.

nodes.title: 8.1.3 Discrete variables
nodes.summary: The text explains how graphical models represent observations through latent variables and simpler conditional distributions, emphasizing generative models, causal interpretation, object-recognition inference, the non-generative nature of ordinary polynomial regression, and ancestral sampling for synthetic data. It then develops Bayesian networks for discrete variables: multinomial parameter counts, exponential complexity of fully general joint distributions, reductions from independence and sparse graphs, linear complexity in chains, parameter tying, and Dirichlet priors. Finally, it introduces parameterized conditional distributions, showing how logistic-sigmoid regression for a binary child replaces an exponentially large conditional table with a linear number of parameters.

nodes.title: 8.1.4 Linear-Gaussian models
nodes.summary: The text develops linear-Gaussian graphical models, showing that Gaussian conditional distributions whose means are linear functions of parent variables produce a multivariate Gaussian joint distribution. It gives noise-based representations and recursive formulas for the joint mean and covariance, discusses independent, fully connected, and partially connected graphs and their parameter counts, and extends the construction to multivariate nodes. It also connects the framework to Gaussian conjugate priors and hierarchical Bayesian models. The section then introduces conditional independence, defining it through an invariant conditional distribution and demonstrating its equivalent factorization of the conditional joint distribution.

This section introduces Bayesian networks as directed graphical models for factorizing joint probability distributions, contrasting them with undirected graphs and factor graphs. It explains graph-based conditional distributions, parent-child structure, variable ordering, DAG factorization, and the meaning of missing links as independence assumptions. Applications include polynomial regression, latent-variable and generative models, posterior and predictive inference, and ancestral sampling. It then treats discrete networks, emphasizing parameter complexity, sparsity, parameter tying, Dirichlet priors, and logistic parameterizations, followed by linear-Gaussian networks, their noise, moment, covariance, parameter-count, conjugate-prior, and hierarchical-model formulations. The section concludes by formalizing conditional independence and its factorization properties.

nodes.title: 8.2. Conditional Independence
8.2.1 Three example graphs
nodes.summary: The text introduces conditional independence and its notation, explains why it is useful in probabilistic graphical models, and presents d-separation as a graphical alternative to algebraic testing. Three three-node DAGs illustrate the effects of common causes, serial connections, and colliders: conditioning blocks common-cause and serial paths but opens collider paths, including through observed descendants. A binary battery–fuel–gauge example demonstrates explaining away numerically, showing how observing a gauge reading and then the battery changes the inferred probability of an empty tank. The section concludes with the general d-separation criterion for node sets, defining when paths are blocked and therefore when a conditional independence is implied by a directed acyclic graph.

nodes.title: 8.2.2 D-separation
nodes.summary: The text explains explaining away through a fuel-gauge and battery example, then develops d-separation for directed acyclic graphs, including its path-blocking rules, examples, parameter nodes, and implications for conditional independence. It applies these ideas to i.i.d. Gaussian observations, Bayesian regression, and the naive Bayes classifier, discussing conditional versus marginal dependence, Gaussian diagonal covariances, practical benefits, and limitations. It presents the d-separation theorem as equivalent to directed factorization and frames graphical models as filters over families of distributions, including fully connected and disconnected extremes. It then derives the Markov blanket as the parents, children, and co-parents of a node, before introducing undirected graphical models or Markov random fields and their simpler graph-separation semantics.

The section introduces conditional independence and its factorization, situating it within multivariate linear-Gaussian and hierarchical Bayesian graphical models. It develops d-separation through common-cause, serial, and collider examples, including explaining away in a battery–fuel–gauge model, and gives the general criterion for graphically implied independencies. The concepts are applied to Gaussian observations, Bayesian regression, and naive Bayes, with discussion of conditional versus marginal dependence, covariance structure, benefits, and limitations. The section also presents the d-separation theorem, views graphical models as filters over distribution families, derives the Markov blanket, and introduces undirected graphical models and their graph-separation semantics.

nodes.title: 8.3. Markov Random Fields
8.3.1 Conditional independence properties
nodes.summary: The text contrasts directed-graph Markov blankets with Markov random fields. It explains that a directed node’s blanket includes parents, children, and children’s co-parents because explaining away prevents parents and children alone from isolating the node. It then introduces MRFs as undirected graphical models that encode factorizations and conditional independences. In these graphs, A is conditionally independent of B given C when C separates every A–B path, equivalently when removing C leaves no A–B path; unlike d-separation, this involves no explaining away. An undirected node’s Markov blanket is simply its neighbors. The section concludes by beginning the discussion of factorizing the joint distribution into functions over local variable sets.

nodes.title: 8.3.2 Factorization properties
nodes.summary: The text explains conditional independence, Markov blankets, and factorization in undirected graphical models. Independence is determined by graph separation: all paths between A and B must pass through C, or equivalently disappear after removing C. A node’s Markov blanket is its neighbors. Joint distributions factorize over maximal cliques using nonnegative potential functions and an explicit partition function, unlike directed models whose normalized conditional factors require no such constant. The partition function can be computationally expensive, though it cancels for local conditionals and can be deferred for small marginals. For strictly positive potentials, the Hammersley-Clifford theorem establishes equivalence between graph-separation independences and clique factorization. Potentials may be represented as Boltzmann exponentials of energy functions, expressing preferences among local configurations. The section then introduces binary image denoising, modeling noisy pixel flips and leveraging correlations between clean and observed pixels and between neighboring clean pixels.

nodes.title: 8.3.3 Illustration: Image de-noising
nodes.summary: The text establishes the equivalence, for strictly positive distributions, between conditional independencies encoded by separation in an undirected graph and factorization over its maximal cliques via the Hammersley–Clifford theorem. It introduces exponential clique potentials and additive energy functions, explaining their interpretive flexibility. It then develops a Markov-random-field model for binary image denoising, combining observed-pixel agreement, neighboring-pixel smoothness, and optional sign bias in an Ising-model energy. The ICM coordinate-ascent procedure is described, including initialization, local updates, convergence to local rather than necessarily global optima, parameter settings, and comparison with max-product and globally optimal graph-cut methods. Finally, the text begins explaining conversion between directed and undirected models using an equivalent directed and undirected chain factorization.

nodes.title: 8.3.4 Relation to directed graphs
nodes.summary: The text concludes a discussion of image denoising, contrasting local ICM optimization with max-product and globally optimal graph-cut methods. It then explains how directed factorizations can be converted to undirected ones through clique potentials and moralization, including the need to connect co-parents, the resulting loss of some independencies, and the relevance to junction-tree inference. It defines D maps, I maps, and perfect maps, shows that directed and undirected graphs express different conditional-independence patterns through three- and four-variable examples, and introduces chain graphs as a broader but still non-universal framework. Finally, it introduces inference as computing posteriors for unobserved nodes given observed nodes by exploiting graphical structure.

The section presents Markov random fields as undirected models whose separation properties determine conditional independence and whose node blankets are their neighbors. It develops clique-based factorization with partition functions, the Hammersley–Clifford theorem, and potential or energy representations. These ideas are applied to binary image denoising through an Ising-style model and ICM optimization, contrasted with max-product and graph-cut inference. The section then relates directed and undirected models through moralization and clique potentials, discusses D maps, I maps, perfect maps, and chain graphs, and concludes by introducing structure-exploiting posterior inference.

nodes.title: 8.4. Inference in Graphical Models
8.4.1 Inference on a chain
nodes.summary: The text introduces graphical-model inference through a graphical interpretation of Bayes’ theorem and then develops exact inference on an undirected chain. By exploiting factorization, conditional independence, and distributivity, node marginals can be computed by forward and backward local messages in O(NK²) rather than exponential time. It gives recursive message equations, explains normalization, relates the method to Markov chains and Chapman–Kolmogorov equations, and shows how to efficiently obtain all node marginals, incorporate observations by clamping, and compute neighboring-node or clique marginals. These local distributions support EM parameter learning, and the discussion concludes by moving from chains to general trees.

nodes.title: 8.4.2 Trees
nodes.summary: The text explains efficient two-direction message passing for obtaining every chain marginal, handling observed variables by clamping, and computing neighboring-node and clique joint distributions for applications such as EM parameter learning. It then generalizes exact message-passing inference from chains to trees, defining undirected trees, directed trees, and polytrees and discussing moralization. Finally, it introduces factor graphs as an explicit variable-factor representation of factorizations of joint distributions, forming the basis for the sum-product algorithm.

nodes.title: 8.4.3 Factor graphs
nodes.summary: The text explains why local message passing enables exact inference on chains, trees, and polytrees, defines these graph structures, and describes how moralization affects them. It introduces factor graphs as bipartite representations that explicitly separate variables from factors, formalizes joint distributions as products of factors, and shows how directed and undirected graphs—including examples with equivalent but differently detailed factorizations—convert into factor graphs. Factor graphs preserve tree structure even for directed polytrees and can eliminate apparent local cycles by combining factors. The section then sets up the sum-product algorithm for exact marginal inference on tree-structured models, notes its later max-sum extension, and explains its applicability to both discrete and linear-Gaussian variables.

nodes.title: 8.4.4 The sum-product algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how factor graphs preserve tree structure and provide a unified representation for directed and undirected graphical models, then derives the sum-product algorithm for exact marginal inference. It defines factor-to-variable and variable-to-factor messages, explains leaf initialization, recursive and bidirectional propagation, efficient computation of variable and factor marginals, normalization for undirected models, and illustrates the method with a four-variable example. It also covers conditioning on observed variables, extension from discrete sums to continuous integrals, and introduces the max-sum algorithm for finding globally most probable joint assignments, emphasizing why marginal maximization is insufficient.

nodes.title: 8.4.5 The max-sum algorithm
nodes.summary: The text introduces max-sum inference as the logarithmic, maximization-based counterpart of sum-product. It explains why maximizing marginals does not generally maximize the joint distribution, derives max-product and max-sum message passing for chains and trees, gives message initialization and root maximization, and emphasizes the need for stored backpointers and backward tracing to obtain a globally consistent maximizing assignment. It discusses the trellis interpretation, ties, the Viterbi algorithm, incorporation of observations, and the contrast with the non-global ICM algorithm, while noting that continuous-variable sum-product uses integration.

nodes.title: 8.4.6 Exact inference in general graphs
nodes.summary: The text outlines exact inference in loopy graphs using the junction tree algorithm: moralization, triangulation, maximal-clique join-tree construction, maximum-weight spanning-tree selection, condensation, the running intersection property, and junction-tree message passing for marginals and conditionals. It explains that computational cost is governed exponentially by the largest clique and formalized by treewidth. It then introduces loopy belief propagation as an approximate extension of sum-product inference to cyclic graphs, discussing possible convergence or failure, initialization with unit messages, message-update rules, flooding and serial schedules, and the notion of pending messages.

nodes.title: 8.4.7 Loopy belief propagation
nodes.summary: The text explains how treewidth controls the complexity of junction-tree inference, then introduces loopy belief propagation as an approximate sum-product method for cyclic graphs, including initialization, message schedules, pending messages, convergence behavior, marginal computation, and applications to error-correcting codes. It next discusses Bayesian learning of graph structures from data, including posterior scoring, model evidence, latent-variable marginalization, and heuristic search over exponentially many structures. The section concludes with exercises on normalization of directed-graph distributions and the relationship between node ordering and acyclicity.

nodes.title: 8.4.8 Learning the graph structure
nodes.summary: The text explains termination, convergence, and marginal computation for belief propagation on trees and loopy graphs, noting its variable performance and success in error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces learning graph structure from data, describing Bayesian posterior scoring through model evidence and the computational challenges caused by latent-variable marginalization and the exponential number of candidate graphs. Finally, it presents exercises on proving normalization of directed-graph joint distributions and the equivalence between an acyclic ordering condition and the absence of directed cycles.

The section surveys inference in graphical models, beginning with the representational limits of directed, undirected, and chain graphs, then developing exact message-passing inference from chains and trees to factor graphs and the sum-product and max-sum algorithms. It covers observations, marginal and clique computations, continuous variables, global optimization, Viterbi decoding, and ICM. For general graphs it explains junction-tree inference and treewidth, followed by approximate loopy belief propagation and its convergence and coding applications. It concludes with Bayesian graph-structure learning, model evidence, latent variables, search complexity, and related exercises.

nodes.title: 8.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text explains termination, convergence, marginal computation, and practical performance of belief propagation on trees and loopy graphs, including its use in error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces Bayesian learning of graph structures, emphasizing posterior scoring, difficult evidence computation, and exponentially large structure spaces requiring heuristics. Two exercises concern normalization of directed-graph joint distributions and the relationship between node ordering and the absence of directed cycles.

nodes.title: 8.2 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of loopy belief propagation, contrasting exact termination and marginals on trees with possible nontermination and approximate results on loopy graphs, and noting its effectiveness in error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces Bayesian learning of graph structures, including posterior scoring by prior times model evidence, computational difficulties from latent-variable marginalization, and the exponential structure space. The remainder lists Exercises 8.1–8.9 covering normalization and acyclicity of directed graphical models, dependence and conditional independence in a tabulated binary distribution, factorization and graph construction, a relevance-vector-machine graph, interpretation of the noisy-OR model, Gaussian recursion-based moments, conditional-independence implications, and the Markov-blanket property via d-separation.

nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on graphical models, conditional independence, d-separation, Bayesian-network factorization, noisy-OR models, relevance-vector-machine graphical representations, recursive Gaussian moments, Markov blankets, explaining-away through observed descendants, noisy evidence in a fuel-system example, counting undirected graphs, local energy changes for ICM, maximum-probability latent configurations, and pairwise distributions in graphical models. It includes a joint distribution table for three binary variables and references several figures and equations used in the exercises.
