nodes.summary: The text introduces a graphical-model example showing that a head-to-head path blocks dependence between a and b when unobserved but can become active when a descendant d is observed. It then presents exercises on explaining this phenomenon and its fuel-gauge interpretation with noisy observations, counting undirected graphs, analyzing local energy changes for iterated conditional modes, identifying the maximum-probability configuration when interaction and bias coefficients vanish, and deriving the joint distribution of neighboring nodes in a graph.

nodes.title: 8.15 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents Figure 8.54 and Exercises 8.10–8.24 on graphical-model independence, noisy observations, graph enumeration, local energy optimization, tree and factor-graph representations, d-separation, and sum-product message passing. It covers how observing descendants changes dependencies, inference with unreliable evidence, counting undirected graphs, locality of ICM energy updates, maximum-probability configurations, pairwise tree distributions, efficient message passing and message-order proofs, equivalence of directed and undirected trees, and computation of variable, connected-subset, and factor marginals from messages.

nodes.title: 8.18 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 8.16–8.29 cover inference and message scheduling in directed and factor-tree graphical models. They examine conditional independence and d-separation, equivalence between directed and undirected trees, derivation and verification of sum-product marginal formulas, efficient message-passing schedules proved by induction, computation of variable, factor, joint, and connected-subset marginals, clamping methods for pairwise distributions, and a counterexample showing marginal modes need not jointly maximize probability. The final exercises establish that cyclic factor graphs retain pending messages indefinitely, whereas sum-product terminates after finitely many messages on trees.

This section develops graphical models as visual frameworks for representing and reasoning about probability distributions and conditional independence. It covers Bayesian networks, conditional independence and d-separation, Markov random fields, directed-undirected relationships, and exact and approximate inference through factorization, message passing, junction trees, belief propagation, optimization, and sampling. Applications include regression, latent and generative models, naive Bayes, image denoising, decoding, and hierarchical Gaussian models. It also introduces Bayesian graph-structure learning and concludes with extensive exercises on factorization, independence, graph structure, d-separation, energy optimization, tree and factor-graph inference, message scheduling, marginal computation, and related graphical-model properties.

nodes.title: 9 Mixture Models and EM
9.1. K -means Clustering
9.1.1 Image segmentation and compression
nodes.summary: The text generalizes K-means to K-medoids using arbitrary dissimilarities, explains its assignment and prototype-update costs, and contrasts hard assignments with the soft assignments of probabilistic mixture models. It illustrates K-means for RGB image segmentation and lossy vector-quantization compression, including storage formulas, numerical compression examples, quality trade-offs, and the limitation of ignoring spatial correlations. It then introduces Gaussian mixtures as latent-variable models in which a 1-of-K variable selects among Gaussian components according to mixing coefficients, providing the basis for EM.

This section introduces K-means clustering as an alternating optimization of hard point assignments and cluster means under a squared-distance distortion objective, explains its convergence and local-minimum limitation, and illustrates it with the Old Faithful data. It extends the ideas to K-medoids and arbitrary dissimilarities, contrasts hard clustering with soft mixture-model assignments, and shows applications to RGB image segmentation and lossy vector-quantization compression, including storage and quality trade-offs and the neglect of spatial structure. It concludes by motivating Gaussian mixtures as latent-variable models underlying EM.

nodes.title: 9.2. Mixtures of Gaussians
9.2.1 Maximum likelihood
nodes.summary: The text explains posterior component responsibilities in Gaussian mixture models, their prior interpretation, and how they support ancestral sampling and responsibility-based visualizations. It formulates an i.i.d. mixture data set, its latent-variable representation, graphical model, and log-likelihood. It then discusses maximum-likelihood difficulties, especially variance-collapse singularities, overfitting, practical remedies, and label-switching non-identifiability. Because the likelihood has no closed-form maximizer due to a sum inside the logarithm, EM is introduced as a broadly applicable alternative. The initial EM derivation shows that differentiating with respect to component means produces the posterior responsibilities and the responsibility-weighted mean update, with effective component count N_k.

nodes.title: 9.2.2 EM for Gaussian mixtures
EM for Gaussian Mixtures
nodes.summary: The text explains EM for Gaussian mixtures through an illustrative two-cluster example, showing responsibility-based soft assignments, weighted parameter updates, and convergence over successive cycles. It contrasts EM with K-means, recommends K-means initialization, and warns about likelihood singularities and local maxima. It then specifies the complete Gaussian-mixture EM algorithm—including responsibility, mean, covariance, mixing-coefficient, likelihood, and convergence calculations—and introduces an alternative latent-variable view in which the observed-data log likelihood contains a sum, or integral for continuous latents, over the joint distribution inside the logarithm.

This section motivates and derives the EM algorithm for Gaussian mixtures. It shows that responsibilities provide soft cluster assignments and lead to weighted updates for component means, covariances, and mixing coefficients, which are iterated through E and M steps until convergence. A two-component Old Faithful example illustrates the process and its relation to K-means, while noting initialization issues, local maxima, and likelihood singularities. The discussion also frames EM as a general latent-variable method and prepares for its broader and variational formulations.

The section first illustrates K-means-based image compression and its compression-quality trade-off, then develops Gaussian mixtures through discrete 1-of-K latent variables, showing how the joint model marginalizes to the mixture density. It derives posterior responsibilities and formulates mixture-data likelihood, explains maximum-likelihood pathologies and non-identifiability, and motivates EM because direct optimization is not closed form. EM is derived through responsibility-based weighted updates for means, covariances, and mixing coefficients, illustrated on Old Faithful data, and related to K-means, initialization and local-optimum issues, singularities, and broader latent-variable and variational methods.

nodes.title: 9.3. An Alternative View of EM
The General EM Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text introduces the latent-variable interpretation and general procedure of the EM algorithm. Observed data are treated as incomplete because latent variables are unknown; EM alternates computing their posterior distribution in the E step with maximizing the expected complete-data log likelihood in the M step. It gives the definition of Q, the update and convergence procedure, notes the monotonic likelihood increase, and explains the MAP extension using a parameter prior. It also describes EM for missing-data problems under missing-at-random assumptions and begins applying the framework to Gaussian mixture models, where latent component labels remove the difficulty caused by sums inside logarithms.

nodes.title: 9.3.1 Gaussian mixtures revisited
nodes.summary: The section presents EM as alternating posterior evaluation for latent variables and maximization of the expected complete-data log likelihood, including its MAP extension and use with missing-at-random data. It revisits Gaussian mixtures, showing that complete labels yield simple closed-form estimates, while their posterior expectations produce responsibilities and the usual Gaussian-mixture EM updates. It then contrasts EM's soft assignments with K-means' hard assignments and begins deriving K-means as a limiting case of EM with shared isotropic covariance.

nodes.title: 9.3.2 Relation to K -means
nodes.summary: The text derives the Gaussian-mixture EM algorithm from the posterior over latent assignments, showing that responsibilities are posterior indicator expectations and that their weighted log likelihood is the expected complete-data log likelihood optimized through the E and M steps. It then shows that K-means is the zero-variance, hard-assignment limit of EM for spherical Gaussian mixtures, with the same mean updates and an objective equivalent to K-means distortion, while noting the elliptical K-means generalization. Finally, it introduces Bernoulli mixture models, or latent class analysis, as a discrete-variable application and a foundation for hidden Markov models.

nodes.title: 9.3.3 Mixtures of Bernoulli distributions
nodes.summary: The text first shows that EM for an isotropic Gaussian mixture with fixed variance converges to K-means as the variance tends to zero: responsibilities become hard nearest-mean assignments, mean updates match K-means, mixing coefficients become assignment fractions, and the likelihood objective becomes the K-means distortion. It then develops mixtures of multivariate Bernoulli distributions, deriving their moments, latent-variable formulation, complete-data likelihood, EM responsibilities, weighted mean updates, and mixing-coefficient updates. Bernoulli mixtures can model correlations, have bounded likelihoods without Gaussian-style infinite singularities, and successfully cluster binarized handwritten digits. The discussion also covers beta and Dirichlet priors and multinomial extensions. Finally, it begins an EM treatment of Bayesian linear-regression evidence approximation by treating the regression weights as latent variables and outlining the E and M steps.

nodes.title: 9.3.4 EM for Bayesian linear regression
nodes.summary: The text discusses Bernoulli mixture models for binarized digit data, including visualization, comparison with a single Bernoulli model, extensions to multinomial variables, and the use of priors. It then applies EM to Bayesian linear regression and relevance vector machines by treating weights as latent variables, deriving hyperparameter re-estimation equations and showing their equivalence to direct evidence maximization. Finally, it introduces the general EM framework for latent-variable maximum likelihood, defining the observed-data likelihood and its decomposition into an expected complete-data log-likelihood term plus a KL divergence, with sums replaced by integrals for continuous latent variables.

This section gives an alternative, latent-variable view of EM, beginning with the iterative Gaussian-mixture updates and then explaining the general E-step/M-step framework, convergence, MAP extensions, and missing-data interpretation. It revisits Gaussian mixtures and shows that K-means is their zero-variance hard-assignment limit. It extends EM to Bernoulli and multinomial mixture models, including priors and digit-clustering applications, and applies the method to Bayesian linear regression and relevance vector machines. The section concludes by framing EM through the decomposition of observed-data likelihood into expected complete-data likelihood and a KL-divergence term.

nodes.title: 9.4. The EM Algorithm in General
nodes.summary: The text transitions from mixture-model re-estimation equations to a general proof and treatment of EM. It derives the log-likelihood decomposition into a variational lower bound and a KL divergence, explains the E and M steps and their monotonic likelihood improvement, relates the M step to expected complete-data log likelihoods, and discusses exponential-family simplifications, graphical interpretation, and factorization for iid data. It extends EM to MAP estimation, GEM, ECM, partial E steps, and incremental online updates, including Gaussian-mixture sufficient-statistic formulas and convergence properties. It concludes with exercises on finite K-means convergence and the Robbins-Monro derivation of stochastic K-means.

nodes.title: 9.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text describes incremental EM for independently observed latent-variable data, including responsibility updates, efficient sufficient-statistic updates for exponential-family mixtures, Gaussian-mixture mean and count formulas, fixed per-step computational cost, and convergence and likelihood properties. It then presents exercises on finite convergence of K-means and deriving stochastic K-means via Robbins–Monro estimation.

nodes.title: Gaussian Mixture Models and EM Exercises
nodes.summary: The page presents exercises on Gaussian mixture models and the EM algorithm: deriving the mixture marginal, extending EM to MAP estimation, proving posterior factorization through d-separation, deriving updates under shared covariance constraints, interpreting complete-data likelihood maximization, verifying mean, covariance, and mixing-coefficient updates using fixed responsibilities, and showing that conditional distributions of partitioned mixture variables remain mixtures.

nodes.title: 9.10 ( ) Consider a density model given by a mixture distribution
nodes.summary: Exercises 9.3–9.17 develop Gaussian and Bernoulli mixture models and their EM algorithms. They cover marginalization and conditional mixture distributions, MAP-EM modifications, posterior factorization via d-separation, EM updates under shared covariances, complete- and expected-data likelihood maximization, the connection between Gaussian-mixture EM and K-means, general mixture moments, and Bernoulli-mixture mean and mixing-coefficient updates. They also analyze a degenerate one-step-convergence case for identical Bernoulli components and establish that Bernoulli-mixture likelihoods are bounded and free of infinite singularities.

nodes.title: Exercises on Gaussian and Bernoulli Mixture Models
key_items: 9.12 ( ) www Consider a mixture distribution of the form

It examines a degenerate one-iteration convergence case, derives the Bernoulli mixture by marginalizing latent variables, obtains M-step updates for component means and mixing coefficients, and proves that Bernoulli-mixture likelihoods have no singularities because they are bounded above.

nodes.title: 9.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on mixture models and EM, covering the limiting connection between Gaussian-mixture EM and K-means; moments of mixture distributions; Bernoulli-mixture marginalization, parameter updates, degeneracy, bounded likelihoods, and Bayesian priors; EM for mixtures of multinomial variables; Bayesian linear regression and RVM hyperparameter re-estimation; variational lower bounds, KL divergence, and gradient equivalence; and incremental EM updates for Gaussian-mixture means, covariances, and mixing coefficients.

This section develops mixture models and the EM algorithm from latent-variable marginalization, beginning with K-means clustering and its variants and applications. It then formulates Gaussian mixtures, derives responsibilities and maximum-likelihood EM updates, and examines identifiability, singularities, initialization, convergence, and the connection to K-means. EM is presented in general through latent-variable, missing-data, variational, KL-divergence, exponential-family, and graphical-model perspectives, with MAP, generalized, ECM, partial, and online forms. The treatment extends to Bernoulli and multinomial mixtures, Bayesian regression, and relevance vector machines, and concludes with extensive exercises on mixture distributions, EM derivations and constraints, convergence, stochastic and incremental methods, mixture moments and conditionals, priors, and boundedness of Bernoulli-mixture likelihoods.

nodes.title: 10 Approximate Inference
10.1. Variational Inference
10.1.1 Factorized distributions
nodes.summary: The text explains variational inference for intractable posteriors, emphasizing tractable yet flexible approximating families and illustrating parametric Gaussian approximation. It develops mean-field variational inference by factorizing the distribution into unrestricted component factors, derives the optimal factor as the normalized exponential of the expected joint log density over all other factors, and describes cyclic coordinate updates and their convergence. It begins analyzing the accuracy of such factorized approximations through a correlated two-variable Gaussian example, and includes a sidebar biography of Leonhard Euler and his major achievements.

nodes.title: 10.1.2 Properties of factorized approximations
nodes.summary: The text derives the general coordinate-wise optimum for factorized variational inference, explains its iterative coordinate-ascent solution and convergence, and analyzes the resulting approximation through a correlated-Gaussian example. It shows that KL(q‖p) produces coupled Gaussian factors with correct means but overly narrow variances, while minimizing KL(p‖q) yields the true marginals and broader, support-covering approximations. It compares the behavior of both divergences for correlated and multimodal distributions, introduces their unification through alpha divergences and the Hellinger distance, and then sets up a factorized variational treatment of a Gaussian model with unknown mean and precision under conjugate Gaussian-Gamma priors.

nodes.title: 10.1.3 Example: The univariate Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text discusses alpha-divergences, their KL limiting cases, nonnegativity, and the contrasting zero-forcing and zero-avoiding behavior obtained when optimizing over q, with the Hellinger distance as the symmetric alpha=0 case. It then develops a factorized variational approximation for the posterior of the mean and precision of a univariate Gaussian under Gaussian-Gamma conjugate priors. The optimal factors are derived as Gaussian and Gamma distributions whose parameters depend on moments of the other factor; these are solved iteratively by coordinate updates, illustrated through posterior contour plots, and shown to approach the optimal factorized approximation. Finally, the text considers broad noninformative priors, introduces the relevant Gamma expectation and residual-moment equations, and begins deriving an explicit solution.

This section introduces variational inference as a deterministic approach to otherwise intractable Bayesian inference, contrasting it with sampling and local Gaussian approximations. It reviews functionals and variational optimization, then derives the evidence lower bound and its KL-divergence interpretation for approximating posteriors over latent variables and parameters. Mean-field factorization is developed through coordinate-wise optimal factors and iterative updates, followed by analyses of its Gaussian behavior, variance underestimation, multimodal effects, and comparison with reverse KL. Alpha divergences and the Hellinger distance provide a unified view of these approximation criteria. The methods are applied to a Gaussian model with unknown mean and precision under Gaussian-Gamma priors, including iterative factor derivations, convergence illustrations, and the start of the noninformative-prior solution, alongside a sidebar on Euler.

This section motivates approximate inference by explaining the difficulty of computing posterior distributions and expectations in complex probabilistic models. It develops variational inference through variational optimization, the evidence lower bound, KL divergence, and mean-field coordinate updates; analyzes its Gaussian, multimodal, and variance properties in relation to reverse KL, alpha divergences, and Hellinger distance; and applies the method to a Gaussian model with unknown mean and precision under informative and noninformative priors, with convergence illustrations and an Euler sidebar.

The section develops a broad foundation in probabilistic modeling, statistical learning, and inference. It begins with Gaussian distributions, their geometry, matrix representations, conditional and marginal identities, Bayes’ theorem, maximum-likelihood and sequential estimation, Bayesian conjugacy, Student’s t-distributions, periodic variables, Gaussian mixtures, and the exponential family. It then introduces nonparametric density estimation through histograms, kernels, and nearest neighbours, with exercises covering probability distributions, moments, entropy, KL divergence, maximum entropy, matrix algebra, Gaussian identities, and related distributions. The material progresses to linear regression and classification, Bayesian modeling and evidence, neural networks, kernel methods and Gaussian processes, sparse kernel machines including SVMs and RVMs, graphical models, mixture models and EM, and finally variational and other approximate-inference methods. Across these topics it treats likelihood and Bayesian estimation, regularization, uncertainty, optimization, model comparison, sparsity, latent variables, conditional independence, computational approximations, and theoretical properties, while the accompanying exercises reinforce the principal derivations and algorithms.

nodes.title: Appendix B
10.1.4 Model comparison
nodes.summary: The text completes a variational derivation for a Gaussian mean and precision, showing that the resulting precision estimate corresponds to the unbiased sample variance rather than the biased maximum-likelihood estimate. It then develops variational model comparison using q(Z,m)=q(Z|m)q(m), derives the evidence lower bound and the model posterior approximation q(m) ∝ p(m)e^{L_m}, and explains separate optimization of the latent-variable distributions for each model. Finally, it begins a variational treatment of Bayesian Gaussian mixtures, specifying the latent assignment variables, mixture and data likelihoods, use of precision matrices, and a symmetric Dirichlet conjugate prior over mixing coefficients.

nodes.title: 10.2. Illustration: Variational Mixture of Gaussians
10.2.1 Variational distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops variational inference for a Bayesian mixture of Gaussians. It specifies the conjugate Dirichlet and Gaussian-Wishart priors, explains the graphical model and latent-variable/parameter distinction, derives the joint distribution and a minimal variational factorization, and obtains categorical responsibility updates for assignments. Responsibility-weighted sufficient statistics then yield Dirichlet and Gaussian-Wishart posterior updates for mixture weights, means, and precisions, with expectations expressed using Wishart and Dirichlet identities. The resulting algorithm alternates variational E- and M-like steps and closely parallels EM. An Old Faithful example illustrates automatic suppression of unused components and the effect of alpha0. The Bayesian method has EM-like computational cost while avoiding singularities and overfitting and allowing the effective number of components to be inferred. Finally, the variational lower bound is decomposed and presented as a convergence and correctness diagnostic, with several of its evaluated terms given explicitly.

nodes.title: 10.2.2 Variational lower bound
nodes.summary: The text explains that priors and variational inference resolve Gaussian-mixture singularities, avoid overfitting with large component counts, and can determine the component number automatically. It presents the variational lower bound, its explicit likelihood, prior, posterior-entropy, and Wishart-related terms, and explains its use for convergence monitoring, implementation checks, and deriving update equations. It concludes by defining the predictive density for a new observation as an integral over the latent assignment and posterior mixture parameters.

nodes.title: 10.2.3 Predictive density
nodes.summary: The text presents the separate expected-log-joint and entropy contributions to the variational lower bound for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, explains their notation and use in deriving variational re-estimation equations, and then derives the approximate predictive density for a new observation. Replacing the intractable posterior with the factorized variational posterior gives a mixture of Student's t distributions that approaches a Gaussian mixture for large data sets. Finally, it explains that the lower bound can help determine the number of components and introduces the Bayesian complication of K! equivalent parameter settings caused by component label switching.

nodes.title: 10.2.4 Determining the number of components
nodes.summary: The text derives the variational predictive distribution for a Gaussian mixture model as a mixture of Student’s t-distributions, approaching a Gaussian mixture for large data sets. It explains how to select the number of components using the variational lower bound while correcting for K! label-switching symmetries, contrasts this Bayesian approach with maximum likelihood, and presents an alternative method that optimizes mixing coefficients to automatically prune unnecessary components. It then discusses induced factorizations in the optimal variational posterior, their implications for efficient computation, and their detection through conditional independence and d-separation.

nodes.title: 10.2.5 Induced factorizations
nodes.summary: The text explains how automatic relevance determination removes unnecessary Gaussian-mixture components, then discusses induced factorizations in variational inference. It shows how optimal posterior factors can arise beyond the assumed factorization, derives a conditional-independence criterion for detecting them via d-separation, and applies it to the Gaussian mixture model. It then introduces variational Bayesian linear regression, contrasting it with evidence-based hyperparameter point estimates, specifying the Gaussian likelihood and prior, the conjugate gamma hyperprior on α, the resulting joint model, and the goal of approximating the posterior over w and α while treating β as known.

This section develops variational Bayesian inference for Gaussian mixtures, beginning with the latent-variable likelihood and conjugate Dirichlet and Gaussian-Wishart priors, then deriving the factorized posterior, responsibility and parameter updates, sufficient statistics, and EM-like iterative algorithm. It illustrates Bayesian benefits on data, including automatic component pruning, protection against singularities and overfitting, and inference of the effective number of components. The variational lower bound is decomposed into likelihood, prior, entropy, and Wishart terms for derivation, convergence assessment, and model selection. Predictive inference yields a mixture of Student's t distributions, while component-number selection must account for label-switching symmetries. The section also discusses alternative relevance-based pruning, induced posterior factorizations and their d-separation interpretation, and extends the framework to variational Bayesian linear regression with conjugate priors and hyperpriors.

nodes.title: 10.3. Variational Linear Regression
10.3.1 Variational distribution
nodes.summary: The text first illustrates how d-separation determines allowable variational factorization in a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model. It then develops mean-field variational inference for Bayesian linear regression with known noise precision: a Gamma variational factor for the weight precision α and a Gaussian factor for the weights w are derived, along with their parameters and moments. An alternating update procedure is described, and the method is shown to coincide with the evidence/EM solution under an infinitely broad prior on α. Finally, integrating the predictive likelihood over the Gaussian variational posterior gives a Gaussian predictive distribution for new inputs.

nodes.title: 10.3.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the Gaussian variational posterior for linear-regression weights and the Gamma moments for alpha, describes their alternating iterative estimation, and shows that with an infinitely broad alpha prior the variational method coincides with evidence maximization except for replacing alpha by its expectation. It then derives the Gaussian predictive distribution with input-dependent uncertainty, formulates and evaluates the variational lower bound term by term, and explains how the bound can approximate posterior model probabilities and favor the correct polynomial complexity over the overfitting tendency of maximum likelihood.

nodes.title: 10.3.3 Lower bound
nodes.summary: The passage completes variational linear regression by giving the predictive variance and explicit terms for the variational evidence lower bound. It explains how the bound supports model selection, correctly favoring a degree-three polynomial in a synthetic example, unlike maximum likelihood, which overfits. It then introduces exponential-family modeling, distinguishes observed variables, extensive latent variables, and fixed-dimensional parameters, presents the exponential-family form of an i.i.d. observed-and-latent-data distribution and its conjugate prior, and begins the corresponding variational analysis.

This section develops variational linear regression through allowable factorization, Gaussian-Gamma variational posteriors, alternating updates, and their connection to evidence maximization. It derives predictive means and input-dependent variances, evaluates the variational evidence lower bound, and shows how it supports reliable model selection over maximum likelihood. The section concludes by introducing exponential-family and conjugate-prior formulations with observed and latent variables as a basis for further variational analysis.

nodes.title: 10.4. Exponential Family Distributions
nodes.summary: The text first illustrates model-order selection through a lower-bound plot whose maximum recovers the true polynomial order. It then develops variational inference for exponential-family complete-data models with conjugate priors, distinguishing extensive latent variables from fixed-dimensional parameters. The optimal factorized posteriors retain exponential-family forms, are coupled through expected sufficient statistics and natural parameters, and are solved by alternating variational E and M updates. Finally, it generalizes these ideas to directed graphical models, showing that factor updates depend locally on each node's Markov blanket and can be implemented as scalable conjugate-exponential message passing, with efficient lower-bound evaluation.

nodes.title: 10.5. Local Variational Methods
nodes.summary: The text develops local variational methods, which simplify probabilistic models by bounding functions locally rather than approximating an entire posterior. It explains how convex and concave functions are bounded by tangent lines and formulates these bounds through convex conjugacy, illustrating the construction with exp(-x). It then treats the logistic sigmoid: transforming its logarithm yields an entropy-based exponential upper bound, while the Jaakkola-Jordan construction gives a Gaussian-shaped quadratic lower bound. These bounds enable analytic approximation of sigmoid-Gaussian integrals, with variational parameters optimized for the tightest generally nonexact result. The limitations for the multiclass softmax are noted. Finally, the text introduces variational Bayesian logistic regression, contrasting its rigorous evidence-bound optimization and flexible Gaussian posterior with Laplace approximation, and begins deriving the factorized logistic likelihood and its variational treatment under a Gaussian prior.

nodes.title: 10.6. Variational Logistic Regression
10.6.1 Variational posterior distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using the Jaakkola–Jordan local quadratic bound on the sigmoid. Each observation receives a variational parameter, and combining the resulting likelihood bound with a Gaussian prior produces an unnormalized quadratic expression whose normalized form is a Gaussian posterior with explicitly defined mean and precision. This approach improves on Laplace approximation accuracy and optimizes a rigorous evidence lower bound, though the bound is directly applicable only to binary classification. The parameters are optimized either through EM, beginning with initial values, or by analytically integrating out the weights and directly maximizing the lower bound; batch and sequential use, as well as later inference of prior hyperparameters, are noted.

nodes.title: 10.6.2 Optimizing the variational parameters
nodes.summary: The text derives a Gaussian variational posterior for Bayesian logistic regression from a quadratic likelihood bound, specifies its mean and covariance, and explains why it can improve on Laplace inference and support sequential learning, while noting its binary-class limitation. It then develops optimization of the local variational parameters ξ_n through either EM or direct analytic maximization, obtaining identical re-estimation equations and a closed-form marginal-likelihood lower bound. Sequential posterior updating and predictive inference are described, with a figure illustrating uncertainty and large-margin-like behavior. Finally, the text introduces inference of the prior hyperparameter α using combined global and local variational approximations.

nodes.title: 10.6.3 Inference of hyperparameters
nodes.summary: The text illustrates variational Bayesian logistic regression and its uncertainty behavior, including sequential updating and large-margin-like decision boundaries. It then extends the method to infer the prior precision hyperparameter α using a gamma hyperprior and a factorized variational distribution, deriving Gaussian and gamma updates for q(w) and q(α), local parameter re-estimation equations, and an iterative coordinate-update procedure. Finally, it introduces expectation propagation as a reverse-KL deterministic approximation whose defining optimization property is matching the approximating distribution's exponential-family moments to those of the target distribution.

The section develops variational Bayesian logistic regression by applying the Jaakkola–Jordan local quadratic sigmoid bound, yielding a Gaussian approximate posterior and an optimizable evidence lower bound. It presents EM and direct optimization of local variational parameters, sequential and predictive inference, uncertainty and large-margin-like behavior, and extension to learning the prior precision through gamma-hyperprior variational updates. It concludes by introducing expectation propagation as a reverse-KL, moment-matching approximation.

nodes.title: 10.7. Expectation Propagation
Expectation Propagation
nodes.summary: The text explains how EP obtains factor-update normalization constants through zeroth-moment matching, then presents the complete EP algorithm for posterior and evidence approximation. It compares EP with assumed density filtering and variational Bayes, discussing batch versus online use, order dependence, convergence guarantees, energy functions, and differing KL objectives. It then introduces the Gaussian-mixture clutter problem, showing why exact inference is exponentially difficult and defining the spherical Gaussian EP approximation used to solve it.

nodes.title: 10.7.1 Example: The clutter problem
nodes.summary: The text illustrates expectation propagation using a Gaussian-signal inference problem with Gaussian background clutter. It defines the mixture likelihood and Gaussian prior, explains why exact inference is exponentially difficult, and develops a spherical-Gaussian EP approximation with factor-specific exponential-quadratic terms. It details initialization and the iterative cavity, tilted-distribution, moment-matching, and factor-refinement calculations, including the interpretation of the non-clutter probability and the approximate evidence. It discusses convergence, visual examples, unusual factor variance parameters, and comparisons with variational Bayes and Laplace methods, then introduces EP for graphical models whose factors depend only on subsets of variables and are represented using factor graphs.

nodes.title: 10.7.2 Expectation propagation on graphs
nodes.summary: The text concludes the EP treatment by giving an evidence approximation, convergence criterion, clutter-problem illustrations, and a comparison with variational Bayes and Laplace methods, while noting that EP factor variances can be infinite or negative provided the total posterior variance is valid. It then develops EP on factor graphs, showing through an explicit example and a general derivation that fully factorized EP updates are equivalent to sum-product or loopy belief propagation, with sequential updates reproducing standard message-passing schedules and yielding exact inference on trees. It discusses possible improvements from partial factorization and grouped updates, relates EP and variational message passing through alpha-divergence methods, lists other related algorithms, and presents exercises on KL decompositions, moment matching, variational-factor optimization, and Gaussian approximation.

The section finishes the variational Bayes update cycle and then develops expectation propagation as a reverse-KL, moment-matching method for approximating factored posteriors and model evidence. It presents the cavity, tilted-distribution, site-update, normalization, convergence, and scheduling principles; applies them in detail to the Gaussian clutter problem; compares EP with variational Bayes, assumed density filtering, and Laplace methods; and extends EP to factor graphs, where fully factorized updates recover belief propagation and exact tree inference. It also covers grouped or partial updates, alpha-divergence connections, related algorithms, and exercises on the underlying approximation techniques.

nodes.title: 10.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text connects the sum-product algorithm with expectation propagation, explains factor-to-variable message computation, and discusses accuracy improvements through partially disconnected approximations and grouped factor updates. It notes that variational message passing and expectation propagation optimize different KL divergences and places them, along with several other message-passing methods, within Minka’s alpha-divergence framework. It then lists exercises on KL-divergence decomposition, solving for factor means, deriving variational updates via Lagrange multipliers, and fitting a Gaussian approximation to a fixed distribution, with the final exercise statement incomplete in the excerpt.

nodes.title: 10.3 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text explains the factor-to-variable sum-product update, its interpretation within expectation propagation, and possible accuracy improvements through partially connected approximations or grouped factors. It relates variational message passing, belief propagation, and expectation propagation through alpha-divergence minimization and lists further message-passing methods. The exercises cover variational lower-bound and KL decompositions, moment matching, factorized variational optimization, Gaussian projection, the EM connection, alpha-divergence limits, variational inference for Gaussian mean and precision, asymptotic behavior, expected-precision calculations, model-posterior decompositions, normalized model probabilities, and latent-variable updates for Bayesian Gaussian mixtures.

nodes.title: Variational Inference Exercises and Approximate Posterior Derivations
nodes.summary: The page presents exercises on variational inference, including moment matching under KL minimization, the equivalence of variational optimization and EM, limiting forms of alpha divergences, Gaussian mean and precision factor updates, their large-sample behavior and expected-precision relation, decomposition of model posterior approximation, constrained optimization of model probabilities, and derivation of the optimal latent-variable distribution for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture.

nodes.title: Variational Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Model Exercises
key_items: 10.14 ( ) Using the distribution (10.59), verify the result (10.64).
nodes.summary: A set of exercises develops and verifies variational Bayesian results for Gaussian mixture models, including posterior distributions, expected mixing coefficients, lower-bound terms, direct derivation of re-estimation equations, and the predictive distribution. It also examines the large-data limit, showing convergence toward maximum-likelihood EM behavior and a Gaussian-mixture predictive distribution, and establishes the K! parameter-setting symmetry from component permutations.

nodes.title: 10.19 ( ) Derive the result (10.81) for the predictive distribution in the variational treatment of the Bayesian mixture of Gaussians model.
nodes.summary: Exercises 10.13–10.28 develop and verify variational Bayesian inference for Gaussian mixtures and linear regression, including posterior factors, expectations, lower bounds, re-estimation equations, prediction, large-sample convergence to EM, label-switching symmetry, model-selection effects, hyperpriors, and exponential-family formulations. Exercises 10.29–10.35 establish concavity and variational bounds for logarithmic and logistic functions and apply them to sequential and standard variational Bayesian logistic regression, deriving updates and lower bounds. Exercises 10.36–10.39 analyze assumed-density filtering and expectation propagation, including evidence accumulation, invariance of exact exponential-family factors, and detailed cavity, normalization, moment, and site-update calculations for the clutter problem.

nodes.title: 11 Sampling Methods
11.1. Basic Sampling Algorithms
11.1.1 Standard distributions
nodes.summary: The text introduces basic sampling algorithms, beginning with pseudo-random uniform-number generation and the transformation method for converting uniform samples into samples from desired distributions via inverse integration. It covers exponential and Cauchy examples, the multivariate Jacobian formulation, and the Box–Muller construction of standard and multivariate Gaussian samples, including scaling, shifting, and Cholesky decomposition. Because inverse transformations are practical only for limited distributions, the text then motivates rejection and importance sampling and begins rejection sampling by defining an unnormalized target distribution and a convenient proposal distribution.

nodes.title: 11.1.2 Rejection sampling
nodes.summary: The text completes the Gaussian transformation discussion, deriving independent standard normal variables and extending the method to multivariate Gaussians through Cholesky decomposition. It explains why transformation sampling is limited and introduces rejection sampling as an alternative: samples from a proposal distribution are accepted under an envelope above the unnormalized target, with efficiency determined by the envelope area. A gamma-distribution example uses an optimized Cauchy proposal. It then introduces adaptive rejection sampling, in which tangent lines to a log-concave target construct and progressively refine the sampling envelope.

nodes.title: 11.1.3 Adaptive rejection sampling
nodes.summary: The text discusses rejection sampling with a scaled Cauchy proposal for gamma distributions, optimal proposal parameters, and adaptive rejection sampling for log-concave targets using tangent-based piecewise exponential envelopes that are refined after rejection. It notes derivative-free and Metropolis–Hastings extensions. Rejection sampling suffers an exponential decline in acceptance rate with dimensionality, making it generally unsuitable for high-dimensional problems. It then introduces importance sampling, which evaluates expectations by sampling from an easier proposal distribution and weighting samples by the target-to-proposal density ratio, avoiding inefficient uniform-grid integration.

nodes.title: 11.1.4 Importance sampling
nodes.summary: The text introduces importance sampling as a way to estimate expectations when direct sampling from p(z) is difficult, using samples from an accessible proposal q(z) and correcting them with importance weights. It explains why uniform grids are inefficient, derives both ordinary and self-normalized estimators for distributions known with or without normalization constants, and emphasizes the method's dependence on proposal quality, including weight degeneracy, reduced effective sample size, and potentially undetectable large errors. It then describes uniform and likelihood-weighted sampling for discrete graphical models, along with self-importance sampling, and briefly transitions to sampling-importance-resampling and the difficulty of choosing rejection-sampling constants in high-dimensional settings.

nodes.title: 11.1.5 Sampling-importance-resampling
nodes.summary: The text discusses limitations and failure modes of importance sampling, especially weight degeneracy, missed high-mass regions, and the need for a proposal distribution that covers the target. It describes uniform sampling, likelihood-weighted ancestral sampling, and adaptive self-importance sampling for graphical models. It then presents sampling-importance-resampling, including its two-stage procedure, convergence justification, dependence on the proposal distribution, and use of weighted original samples for moment estimation. Finally, it explains Monte Carlo EM, its MAP extension through a prior term, and stochastic EM for mixture models using single-sample hard assignments.

nodes.title: 11.1.6 Sampling and the EM algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains weighted Monte Carlo evaluation of expectations, then shows how sampling approximates the E step in Monte Carlo EM, including its MAP extension and the stochastic EM variant for mixture models. It next presents Bayesian data augmentation, alternating imputation and posterior steps to sample hidden variables and parameters when joint posterior sampling is difficult. Finally, it motivates the transition to Markov chain Monte Carlo as a broadly applicable alternative to rejection and importance sampling in high-dimensional settings.

This section presents fundamental sampling methods, beginning with uniform generation and transformation-based sampling for exponential, Cauchy, and Gaussian distributions. It then develops rejection sampling, including gamma proposals and adaptive rejection sampling for log-concave targets, and explains its high-dimensional limitations. Importance sampling is introduced as a weighted alternative, with ordinary and self-normalized estimators, graphical-model applications, proposal-quality issues, and sampling-importance-resampling. The section concludes with Monte Carlo, MAP, and stochastic EM, Bayesian data augmentation, and the motivation for Markov chain Monte Carlo.

nodes.title: 11.2. Markov Chain Monte Carlo
11.2.1 Markov chains
nodes.summary: The text illustrates Metropolis sampling and explains why ordinary random walks are inefficient: their typical exploration distance grows only as the square root of the number of steps. It then develops Markov-chain foundations, including the Markov property, transition and marginal distributions, homogeneity, invariant distributions, detailed balance and reversibility, ergodicity and equilibrium, and the construction of transition kernels from mixtures or successive base transitions. Finally, it introduces and verifies the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm for asymmetric proposals, notes that normalization is unnecessary and symmetric proposals recover Metropolis, and begins discussing how Gaussian proposal variance affects efficiency.

nodes.title: 11.2.2 The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how to construct composite Markov transitions by mixing or sequentially applying base transitions, including their invariance and detailed-balance properties and the use of symmetric ordering to restore detailed balance. It then presents the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm for asymmetric proposals, gives its acceptance rule and detailed-balance proof, and discusses how proposal scale and anisotropic correlations affect acceptance, random-walk behavior, and convergence. Finally, it introduces Gibbs sampling as an MCMC method that updates variables from their full conditional distributions.

This section presents Bayesian data augmentation and then develops Markov chain Monte Carlo as a general method for sampling from difficult, especially high-dimensional, posterior distributions. It explains Metropolis sampling and correlated-chain behavior, establishes the relevant theory of Markov chains and invariant distributions, extends the method to asymmetric proposals through Metropolis-Hastings, examines proposal-scale and correlation effects on efficiency and convergence, and introduces Gibbs sampling as conditional-distribution-based MCMC.

nodes.title: 11.3. Gibbs Sampling
nodes.summary: The text explains why Metropolis-Hastings mixes slowly for highly anisotropic correlated distributions, then presents Gibbs sampling as a conditional-update MCMC method and special case of Metropolis-Hastings with automatic acceptance. It gives the cyclic update algorithm, explains invariance, ergodicity, initialization, and sample correlation, analyzes Gaussian mixing, and introduces over-relaxation. It discusses implementation through graphical-model Markov blankets, conjugate and log-concave conditionals, adaptive rejection sampling, ICM as a greedy alternative, and blocking to reduce dependence. Finally, it introduces slice sampling as an adaptive auxiliary-variable method and includes a biography of Josiah Willard Gibbs.

nodes.title: 11.4. Slice Sampling
nodes.summary: The text explains refinements of Gibbs sampling, including conditional sampling based on Markov blankets, adaptive rejection sampling for log-concave conditionals, ICM as a mode-based greedy approximation, and blocking to reduce sample dependence. It then presents slice sampling, which adaptively samples from an unnormalized distribution by introducing an auxiliary height variable, alternating between height and slice-position draws, and using an expanding-and-shrinking interval when direct slice sampling is impractical; the method also extends componentwise to multivariate distributions. Finally, it introduces hybrid Monte Carlo as a gradient-based approach for continuous distributions that makes large, low-rejection moves, beginning with Hamiltonian dynamical systems and momentum variables.

nodes.title: 11.5. The Hybrid Monte Carlo Algorithm
11.5.1 Dynamical systems
nodes.summary: The text briefly completes the discussion of multivariate slice sampling, then introduces Hybrid Monte Carlo as a gradient-based method for avoiding Metropolis random walks. It develops Hamiltonian dynamics from position and momentum variables, defines potential energy, kinetic energy, and the Hamiltonian, derives Hamilton’s equations, and explains conservation of energy and phase-space volume through Liouville’s theorem. These properties establish invariance of the joint position-momentum distribution and permit large systematic state changes, while momentum resampling supplies ergodicity. The text then presents the volume-preserving leapfrog integrator, discusses discretization errors and their later correction in HMC, and emphasizes the efficiency of using gradients. It also includes a biographical sidebar on William Rowan Hamilton.

nodes.title: 11.5.2 Hybrid Monte Carlo
nodes.summary: The text explains Hybrid Monte Carlo as leapfrog Hamiltonian dynamics corrected by a Metropolis test, including its acceptance probability, time-reversal and volume-preservation properties, detailed-balance proof, and ergodicity considerations. It analyzes HMC on multivariate Gaussians, showing the step-size and trajectory-length requirements and its favorable scaling compared with random-walk Metropolis. It then introduces partition functions as normalization constants and Bayesian model evidence, explains why their ratios matter for model comparison, and derives an importance-sampling estimator for ratios of partition functions.

This section develops Hybrid Monte Carlo from Hamiltonian dynamics, explaining its energy- and volume-preserving properties, momentum refreshment, leapfrog integration, discretization errors, and use of gradients to make efficient large moves. It then formulates HMC with a Metropolis correction and establishes its acceptance, reversibility, detailed-balance, and ergodicity properties, including performance requirements and favorable Gaussian scaling relative to random-walk Metropolis. Finally, it introduces partition functions and Bayesian evidence, motivates ratios of normalizing constants for model comparison, and derives an importance-sampling estimator for those ratios, with a biographical sidebar on William Rowan Hamilton.

nodes.title: 11.6. Estimating the Partition Function
nodes.summary: The text compares the scaling of HMC leapfrog exploration with isotropic random-walk Metropolis, showing HMC requires order σ_max/σ_min steps versus the random walk's order (σ_max/σ_min)^2. It then explains estimating partition functions and their ratios through importance sampling, including Markov-chain-based proposals, the need for distributional overlap, and chaining through interpolating intermediate energy functions, potentially with one continuously equilibrated Markov chain. The section concludes with ten exercises covering estimator properties, inverse-transform and Gaussian sampling, Cauchy transformations, change-of-variables proofs, rejection and adaptive rejection sampling, piecewise exponential sampling, and a random-walk second-moment result.

nodes.title: Sampling Methods Exercises
nodes.summary: The page contains exercises on sampling methods, covering Monte Carlo estimator moments, inverse transformation and Cauchy sampling, variable transformations, multivariate Gaussian generation via Cholesky decomposition, rejection and adaptive rejection sampling, piecewise exponential sampling, and the second-moment behavior of a simple random walk.

nodes.title: 11.6 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sampling methods, covering Monte Carlo estimator moments, inverse-transform sampling, transformations for Cauchy and Gaussian variables, sampling on the unit circle, Cholesky-based multivariate Gaussian generation, rejection and adaptive rejection sampling, random-walk moments, Gibbs sampling and detailed balance, ergodicity, conditional distributions in a Gaussian-gamma model, over-relaxation, Hamiltonian dynamics, and Gaussian conditional distributions. It also includes figures illustrating a disconnected two-variable distribution relevant to Gibbs-sampling ergodicity and a Bayesian graph for Gaussian observations with uncertain mean and precision.

nodes.title: Exercises on Gibbs Sampling and Hamiltonian Methods
key_items: 11.16 ( ) By making use of (11.56), (11.57), and (11.63), show that the conditional distribution p(r|z) is a Gaussian.
nodes.summary: This page presents exercises on Gibbs sampling, including detailed balance, ergodicity, conditional distributions for a Gaussian model, and verification of over-relaxation moments. It also covers equivalences between Hamiltonian and earlier sampling equations and asks for a proof that p(r|z) is Gaussian, with figures illustrating a non-ergodic sampling example and a Gaussian hierarchical model.

nodes.title: 11.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text closes a hybrid Monte Carlo section with a detailed-balance verification exercise, then introduces continuous latent-variable models for data concentrated near low-dimensional, potentially nonlinear manifolds. Digit-image and oil-flow examples illustrate latent dimensions, manifold segments, and noise-based generative modelling. It motivates linear-Gaussian latent models, probabilistic PCA, factor analysis, EM and Bayesian extensions, and broader nonlinear or non-Gaussian models. It then develops standard PCA, presenting its maximum-variance and minimum-error definitions. The variance formulation derives principal components as covariance-matrix eigenvectors, explains selection of the leading M components, and gives computational costs and alternatives. The minimum-error formulation begins by expressing observations in a complete orthonormal basis and restricting them to an M-dimensional approximation.

This section presents Monte Carlo methods for approximating expectations and performing inference when exact computation is infeasible. It covers direct, transformed, rejection, adaptive, and importance sampling; sampling in graphical models; stochastic estimation, MAP, EM, and data augmentation; and the theory and practice of MCMC, including Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs, slice sampling, and hybrid Monte Carlo. It analyzes convergence, ergodicity, autocorrelation, proposal efficiency, blocking, over-relaxation, Hamiltonian dynamics, and partition-function or evidence estimation. Exercises and biographical notes reinforce these methods, while the closing material connects sampling and latent-variable modelling to probabilistic PCA, factor analysis, manifold models, and standard PCA.

Appendix B continues variational inference from Gaussian mean-and-precision updates through model comparison, Bayesian Gaussian mixtures, linear regression, exponential-family and graphical-model methods, local bounds, logistic regression, and expectation propagation. It explains posterior and predictive derivations, evidence lower bounds, model selection, pruning, symmetries, message passing, and approximation relationships, and includes extensive exercises on these techniques. It then introduces the next chapter's Monte Carlo and MCMC framework, including major sampling algorithms, convergence and efficiency issues, evidence estimation, and applications to latent-variable and PCA-related models.

nodes.title: Appendix C
12.1.2 Minimum-error formulation
nodes.summary: The text explains PCA both as variance-maximizing projection and as minimum-reconstruction-error dimensionality reduction. PCA computes the data mean and covariance matrix and selects the eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues; efficient partial eigensolvers can reduce computational cost. In the minimum-error formulation, data are expressed in an orthonormal basis, approximated in an M-dimensional subspace, and optimized under squared-distance distortion. The optimal reconstruction is an orthogonal projection, with discarded variance equal to the sum of the omitted covariance eigenvalues, so the retained subspace consists of the largest-eigenvalue directions. The discussion covers the two-dimensional intuition, degenerate eigenvalues, the M=D rotation case, and the related CCA method for multiple variables, then introduces PCA-based compression of digit data.

nodes.title: 12.1.3 Applications of peA
nodes.summary: The text completes the PCA derivation, showing that the optimal M-dimensional principal subspace is formed by covariance eigenvectors with the M largest eigenvalues, while reconstruction distortion is the sum of the discarded eigenvalues. It discusses equal-eigenvalue cases and the no-reduction M=D case, briefly introduces CCA, and presents PCA applications in digit-image compression, preprocessing, standardization, whitening, visualization, and comparison with Fisher’s discriminant. It concludes by explaining why conventional PCA is problematic for high-dimensional data with fewer samples than dimensions, due to zero eigenvalues and costly covariance eigendecomposition.

nodes.title: 12.1.4 peA for high-dimensional data
nodes.summary: The text contrasts unsupervised PCA with label-aware Fisher discriminant analysis, illustrates PCA projections of oil-flow data, and explains an efficient approach to PCA when dimensionality exceeds the number of observations by solving the smaller dual eigenvalue problem and reconstructing normalized original-space eigenvectors. It then introduces probabilistic PCA as a maximum-likelihood latent-variable formulation that constrains Gaussian parameters while retaining the ability to capture major data correlations.

nodes.title: 12.2. Probabilistic peA
12.2.1 Maximum likelihood peA
nodes.summary: The text develops maximum-likelihood probabilistic PCA. It derives the likelihood, identifies the sample mean, and gives the exact solutions in terms of the leading covariance eigenvectors, their eigenvalues, an arbitrary latent-space rotation, and noise variance equal to the average discarded variance. It explains the resulting variance representation, rotational non-identifiability, the full-dimensional Gaussian special case, and the relationship between probabilistic and conventional PCA through posterior latent projections. It also discusses parameter-count advantages over full and diagonal covariance models, deriving the covariance degrees of freedom, and introduces EM estimation for PPCA as a computationally useful method that also extends to factor analysis and missing-data settings.

nodes.title: 12.2.2 EM algorithm for peA
nodes.summary: The text explains PPCA as a low-dimensional covariance model that captures important correlations with only linear parameter growth, derives its effective degrees of freedom after accounting for latent-space rotations, and identifies its full-covariance and isotropic special cases. It then derives and describes an EM algorithm for PPCA, including posterior sufficient statistics, parameter updates, computational advantages over covariance-based PCA, online implementation, and principled treatment of missing data. The zero-noise limit gives an EM procedure for standard PCA, interpreted as alternating projection and principal-subspace re-estimation or as a spring-and-rod energy minimization. Finally, it introduces Bayesian PCA and discusses choosing the latent dimension using application needs or gaps in the eigenvalue spectrum, with an example of missing-data visualization and references to related exercises, equations, and figures.

nodes.title: 12.2.3 Bayesian peA
nodes.summary: The text explains EM for probabilistic PCA through a spring-and-rod analogy, including its projection and subspace-update steps, and illustrates robustness to missing data. It then develops Bayesian PCA for automatically selecting latent dimensionality: likelihood-based cross-validation and variational model comparison are discussed, followed by an ARD prior on loading-matrix columns whose optimized precision hyperparameters prune irrelevant dimensions. Laplace-approximated updates are combined with EM, with discussion of limiting covariance cases, computational trade-offs, graphical and comparative figures, and Gibbs-sampling multimodality. Fully Bayesian extensions and related dimensionality-selection work are noted, before introducing factor analysis as a closely related linear-Gaussian model.

nodes.title: 12.2.4 Factor analysis
nodes.summary: The text develops Bayesian PCA, explaining its Laplace-approximation re-estimation and EM updates, the role of hyperparameters in automatically suppressing unnecessary dimensions, computational trade-offs, Gibbs-sampling behavior, and extensions to fully Bayesian treatments. It then introduces factor analysis as a related linear-Gaussian latent-variable model with diagonal, coordinate-specific noise, explains its covariance interpretation, rotational non-identifiability, relation to PCA, EM estimation equations, computational advantages, Bayesian extension, and behavior under data rescaling. Finally, it begins kernel PCA, showing how PCA can be reformulated in terms of scalar products and generalized through a nonlinear feature mapping and kernel substitution.

The section first presents an efficient dual-space computation for conventional PCA, then develops probabilistic PCA as a generative linear-Gaussian latent-variable model and derives its maximum-likelihood solution, covariance structure, identifiability, special cases, and links to ordinary PCA. It explains PPCA's modeling and computational benefits, including reduced parameterization, EM estimation, online learning, missing-data handling, generative and classification uses, and the zero-noise connection to standard PCA. Bayesian PCA is then developed for automatic latent-dimension selection using model comparison, ARD, Laplace and EM methods, with discussion of computational and sampling issues. The section proceeds to factor analysis, comparing its diagonal noise model, estimation, Bayesian treatment, and relation to PCA, and concludes by introducing kernel PCA through nonlinear feature mappings and kernelized scalar products.

nodes.title: 12.3. Kernel peA
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of factor analysis by noting efficient M-step computation, Bayesian extensions, and its different transformation behavior from PCA and probabilistic PCA. It then develops kernel PCA by expressing PCA in terms of inner products, applying a nonlinear feature map, and reducing the feature-space eigenproblem to an N × N kernel-matrix eigenproblem. It gives the coefficient normalization and kernel-based projection formulas, explains the possible number of components, derives kernel-based centering, notes recovery of ordinary PCA with a linear kernel, and illustrates the method with a Gaussian-kernel synthetic example. Finally, it discusses kernel PCA's computational cost and its inability in general to perform exact truncated-space reconstruction, motivating approximate pre-image techniques.

nodes.title: 12.4. Nonlinear Latent Variable Models
12.4.1 Independent component analysis
nodes.summary: The text introduces nonlinear and non-Gaussian extensions of linear-Gaussian latent variable models, noting that nonlinear transformations of Gaussian reference densities can produce general distributions. It then explains ICA, where observed variables are linear mixtures of statistically independent, non-Gaussian latent variables, using blind separation of two mixed speech signals as an example. The noiseless square model treats samples as i.i.d., estimates the mixing matrix by likelihood maximization, and requires non-Gaussian latent distributions because Gaussian models are rotationally indeterminate and decorrelation does not imply independence. A heavy-tailed 1/cosh distribution is cited as a common prior. Probabilistic ICA motivates independent factor analysis, which supports unequal latent and observed dimensions, noise, and Gaussian-mixture latent distributions, fitted with EM and variational reconstruction. The text ends by beginning the discussion of autoassociative neural networks.

nodes.title: 12.4.2 Autoassociative neural networks
nodes.summary: The text discusses probabilistic ICA, explaining why Gaussian latent variables cannot identify independent components because of rotational invariance, why uncorrelated PCA components need not be independent, and why heavy-tailed non-Gaussian priors are used. It then introduces autoassociative neural networks: shallow networks reproduce linear PCA even with nonlinear hidden units, while deeper networks can learn nonlinear dimensionality reductions at the cost of difficult nonconvex optimization and preset latent dimensionality. Finally, it surveys nonlinear-manifold modeling through local or mixture-of-PCA models, Bayesian and hierarchical mixtures, and principal curves that generalize PCA to nonlinear embedded structures.

nodes.title: 12.4.3 Modelling nonlinear manifolds
nodes.summary: The text surveys nonlinear latent-variable and manifold models. It contrasts nonlinear neural-network PCA with conventional PCA, emphasizing its flexibility but also nonlinear optimization, local-minimum, and dimensionality-selection issues. It then covers piecewise-linear mixtures, probabilistic PCA mixtures and factor analysers, principal curves and surfaces, MDS, LLE, and Isomap for nonlinear dimensionality reduction. It discusses latent trait models for discrete observations, density networks using Monte Carlo marginalization, and GTM as an efficient probabilistic nonlinear manifold model trained by EM, including its relationship to SOM, extensions, and geometric visualization tools. The section concludes with exercises on PCA eigenvalue proofs, probabilistic PCA transformations, Gaussian properties, graphical models, marginal and posterior derivations, maximum-likelihood estimation, projection limits, shrinkage, and reconstruction.

This section surveys nonlinear latent-variable and manifold models, beginning with ICA and probabilistic independent-factor models for separating non-Gaussian independent sources and explaining identifiability, likelihood estimation, noise, and mixture priors. It then introduces autoassociative neural networks for nonlinear dimensionality reduction, along with their optimization and dimensionality-selection challenges, and reviews mixture, Bayesian, principal-curve, principal-surface, MDS, LLE, and Isomap approaches to nonlinear manifolds. It also covers latent-trait models, density networks, and GTM, including EM training, links to self-organizing maps, extensions, and visualization, and concludes with exercises on PCA, probabilistic PCA, Gaussian and graphical-model calculations, inference, estimation, projection, shrinkage, and reconstruction.

nodes.summary: The page presents exercises on probabilistic PCA, covering eigenvector normalization, reparameterization of Gaussian latent variables, affine transformations of Gaussians, graphical-model independence, derivation of marginal and posterior distributions, maximum-likelihood estimation and uniqueness of the mean, limiting recovery of conventional PCA projections, noise-induced shrinkage toward the origin, and least-squares optimal reconstruction.
