nodes.summary: This text presents exercises on probabilistic PCA and factor analysis. It covers eigenvector normalization; reparameterization of latent Gaussian distributions; affine transformations of Gaussians; graphical-model independence structure; derivation of marginal and posterior Gaussian distributions; maximum-likelihood estimation and uniqueness of the mean; connections between probabilistic and conventional PCA through limiting noise, shrinkage, and reconstruction; covariance parameter counting; EM derivations for probabilistic PCA, including missing data; least-squares derivations of PCA updates; and factor-analysis parameter counting, rotational invariance, mean estimation, and EM E-step formulas.

nodes.title: 12.19 (**) IIiI!I Show that the factor analysis model described in Section 12.2.4 is invariant under rotations of the latent space coordinates.
nodes.summary: The exercises cover parameter counting and EM derivations for probabilistic PCA and factor analysis, including missing-data PCA, linear reconstruction, latent-space rotational invariance, mean estimation, and expected complete-data likelihoods. They also address graphical models for PCA mixtures, EM for the Student's t-distribution, transformation and covariance properties of linear-Gaussian latent-variable models, eigenvector formulations of PCA, the recovery of linear PCA from kernel PCA, nonlinear transformations of probability densities, and the distinction between independence and zero correlation.

nodes.title: 13 Sequential Data
13.1. Markov Models
nodes.summary: The text introduces Markov and state space models for sequential data. It contrasts i.i.d. modeling with first- and higher-order Markov chains, explains their factorization, conditional-independence properties, stationarity, and parameter-growth limitations, and discusses autoregressive and neural-network alternatives. It then shows how latent Markov states create state space models capable of representing dependencies across the full observation history, gives their graphical and joint-distribution structure, and identifies hidden Markov models and linear dynamical systems as the principal examples. The opening of the HMM section interprets HMMs as temporally linked mixture models, lists major applications, and defines the transition-probability matrix for discrete latent states.

nodes.title: 13.2. Hidden Markov Models
13.2.1 Maximum likelihood for the HMM
nodes.summary: The text explains HMM time-warping invariance using handwritten digits and speech as examples, emphasizing accommodation of local compression and stretching but sensitivity to sequence order. It then develops maximum-likelihood HMM estimation: likelihood evaluation requires marginalizing over exponentially many latent state paths, so EM is used. The E step computes single-state and adjacent-state posterior probabilities, gamma and xi, and forms the expected complete-data log likelihood; the M step updates initial and transition probabilities and fits emission parameters by weighted maximum likelihood, with explicit Gaussian and multinomial formulas and analogous Bernoulli treatment. It discusses initialization, preservation of zero probabilities, and left-to-right models, and introduces the forward-backward/Baum-Welch algorithm as the efficient message-passing method for computing the required posterior quantities.

nodes.title: 13.2.2 The forward-backward algorithm
nodes.summary: The text completes the HMM EM framework by presenting emission-parameter updates for Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli observations and discussing initialization. It then develops the forward-backward/Baum-Welch algorithm from HMM conditional independencies and d-separation, defining α and β messages, deriving their O(K²N) recursions and boundary conditions, and using them to compute state posteriors γ, transition posteriors ξ, and the data likelihood without enumerating exponentially many state paths. It outlines the complete EM training procedure, initialization examples, convergence and sequence-length considerations, precomputation of emission probabilities, and special issues for left-to-right and multiple-sequence models. The text also derives online predictive distributions using the forward summary, discusses regularized and variational Bayesian extensions, and shows that the same recursions arise from applying the sum-product algorithm to a simplified factor-graph representation of the HMM.

nodes.title: 13.2.3 The sum-product algorithm for the HMM
nodes.summary: The text explains how HMM inference and learning extend beyond maximum likelihood, including regularized and variational Bayesian approaches, and shows that the forward-backward algorithm is an instance of sum-product message passing on a factor graph. It derives the alpha and beta recursions and the resulting hidden-state marginals, then addresses numerical underflow by normalizing the forward and backward quantities and introducing predictive scaling factors.

nodes.title: 13.2.4 Scaling factors
nodes.summary: The text connects HMM forward-backward inference with sum-product message passing, showing that alpha and beta messages yield the state and pairwise marginals. It introduces scaling factors to prevent numerical underflow, defines normalized alpha and beta variables, derives their recursions, explains likelihood and marginal computation from the scaling factors, and contrasts the standard alpha-beta procedure with an alpha-gamma alternative. It then introduces the Viterbi algorithm as max-sum message passing for finding the globally most probable hidden-state sequence, distinguishing it from independently maximizing state marginals and noting its efficient linear-time path search and use of log probabilities.

nodes.title: 13.2.5 The Viterbi algorithm
nodes.summary: The text contrasts α–γ and α–β forward-backward recursions, then explains the Viterbi max-sum algorithm for finding the globally most probable HMM state sequence. It presents its log-domain message recursion, initialization, probabilistic interpretation, dynamic-programming efficiency, and backtracking procedure, emphasizing why it differs from independently maximizing state marginals. It finally introduces HMM extensions, especially discriminative rather than maximum-likelihood training for sequence classification, with the corresponding cross-entropy objective expressed through class-specific model likelihoods and priors.

nodes.title: 13.2.6 Extensions of the hidden Markov model
nodes.summary: The passage explains the dynamic-programming intuition behind Viterbi decoding and surveys major HMM extensions. It covers discriminative training for sequence classification, explicit state-duration models, autoregressive HMMs for longer-range observation dependencies, input-output HMMs for supervised sequential data, and factorial HMMs with multiple latent chains. It explains the conditional-independence properties and EM/forward-backward implications of these models, the exponential cost of exact factorial inference, and sampling or variational alternatives. It concludes by motivating linear dynamical systems through noisy measurement of time-varying quantities, emphasizing the trade-off between averaging enough observations to suppress noise and using recent data to track changes.

This section introduces hidden Markov models as temporally dependent mixture or discrete-state state-space models, defining their initial, transition, and emission distributions, joint probability, graphical representations, homogeneous assumptions, applications, and relationship to mixture models and linear dynamical systems. It develops maximum-likelihood EM learning and the forward-backward/Baum-Welch algorithm for efficiently computing state and transition posteriors and likelihoods, interprets these recursions through sum-product message passing, and addresses initialization, scaling for numerical stability, prediction, Bayesian and regularized extensions, and multiple or constrained sequences. It then presents Viterbi max-sum decoding and discriminative sequence-classification training, before surveying duration, autoregressive, input-output, and factorial HMM extensions and motivating linear dynamical systems.

nodes.title: 13.3. Linear Dynamical Systems
13.3.1 Inference in LDS
nodes.summary: The text develops inference for linear dynamical systems using Gaussian sum-product message passing. It derives the forward Kalman filtering recursions for predicted and updated state means, covariances, Kalman gains, normalization constants, initial conditions, and likelihood evaluation; explains filtering as prediction followed by observation-based correction; discusses limiting noise regimes and two-dimensional tracking; and then derives backward Kalman smoothing recursions that incorporate future observations. It concludes with the pairwise Gaussian posterior marginals and cross-covariances needed by the EM algorithm, while referencing the relevant exercises and figures.

nodes.title: 13.3.2 Learning in LDS
nodes.summary: The text derives EM-based maximum-likelihood learning for linear dynamical systems: posterior state moments are obtained in the E step, and closed-form updates for the initial mean and covariance, transition matrix and covariance, and emission matrix and covariance are obtained by maximizing the expected complete-data log likelihood. It notes that MAP and approximate Bayesian learning are straightforward extensions. It then discusses LDS extensions, including Gaussian-mixture initial states, the exponential complexity caused by mixture emissions, approximate or sampling-based inference for non-linear/non-Gaussian models such as the extended Kalman filter, and switching state-space and switching hidden Markov models with their tractability and variational-inference properties.

nodes.title: 13.3.3 Extensions of LDS
nodes.summary: The text discusses maximum-likelihood, MAP, and approximate Bayesian parameter learning for linear dynamical systems, then explains extensions and their computational consequences. Gaussian-mixture initial states remain tractable, whereas mixture emissions cause exponential posterior growth. More general non-linear-Gaussian models require deterministic approximations, sampling, or methods such as the extended Kalman filter. It also presents switching state space models, combining continuous linear-Gaussian chains with a discrete switching chain, and notes that variational inference makes their otherwise intractable inference efficient; the discrete-only analogue is the switching hidden Markov model.

nodes.title: 13.3.4 Particle filters
nodes.summary: This section explains particle filtering as a sequential Monte Carlo method for nonlinear or non-Gaussian dynamical systems. It derives the weighted-sample approximation of the filtering posterior, shows how the predictive distribution becomes a mixture of transition distributions, and gives the recursive sampling-and-reweighting procedure based on conditional independence and d-separation. It also notes alternative names for the method and introduces an exercise on verifying graphical-model conditional independences.

This section introduces linear dynamical systems as linear-Gaussian state-space models for tracking time-varying latent quantities observed with noise. It explains their relation to HMMs and continuous latent-variable models, specifies their transition, emission, and initial distributions, and shows why Gaussian closure enables efficient sum-product inference. It develops Kalman filtering and Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing, including likelihoods and posterior moments, then uses those results in EM updates for maximum-likelihood parameter learning, with MAP and Bayesian extensions. The section also surveys mixture, nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and switching-model extensions, their tractability and approximate inference methods, and particle filtering as a sequential Monte Carlo alternative.

nodes.title: 13.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text derives the particle filter's predictive distribution as a weighted mixture of state-transition distributions using Bayes' theorem and d-separation-based conditional independences. It explains the two-stage sequential Monte Carlo procedure of propagating weighted particles and reweighting them with the next observation, lists alternative names for particle filtering, and describes its schematic illustration. The exercises address verifying first- and second-order Markov properties by d-separation and probability rules, showing that observed state-space data lack finite-order Markov independences, and learning parametric emission parameters by maximum likelihood.

nodes.title: 13.4 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents a schematic particle-filter operation and a set of exercises on Markov and higher-order Markov conditional independences, d-separation, hidden Markov model likelihood learning and EM updates, Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli emissions, persistence of zero parameters, factor-graph derivation of pairwise latent posteriors, and EM training with multiple independent sequences.

nodes.title: 13.8 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on deriving and verifying HMM EM-algorithm updates, including constrained updates for initial and transition probabilities, preservation of zero parameters, Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli emission updates, verification of conditional independences through d-separation and probability rules, derivation of pairwise latent-state posteriors using factor graphs and sum-product messages, and extension of forward-backward training and parameter re-estimation to multiple independent sequences.

nodes.title: 13.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 13.5–13.16 develop and verify the EM updates for HMM initial, transition, Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli emission parameters; establish preservation of zero parameters; verify HMM conditional independences through d-separation and probability rules; derive posterior marginals and alpha/beta messages using factor graphs; extend EM estimation to multiple independent sequences; express marginals using rescaled variables; and derive the forward recursion underlying the Viterbi algorithm.

nodes.title: 13.13 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text gives multi-sequence Baum–Welch re-estimation formulas, including the responsibility-weighted Gaussian mean update, and presents Exercises 13.13–13.25 on factor-graph interpretations of HMM messages, rescaled forward-backward quantities, Viterbi recursion, input-output HMMs, Gaussian latent-sequence maximization, Kalman filter and smoother identities, affine-offset augmentation, and the reduction of Kalman filtering to Gaussian mean maximum likelihood. The final exercise is only partially included.

nodes.title: 13.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text lists exercises on sequential data covering initialization of a recursion, factor-graph representations and forward-backward inference for input-output hidden Markov models, Gaussian posterior and most-probable latent sequences in linear dynamical systems, derivations of Kalman filtering and smoothing equations using Gaussian and matrix identities, incorporation of constant offsets through state and matrix augmentation, and the reduction of Kalman filtering for independent observations to Gaussian mean maximum likelihood. The final exercise is truncated after introducing the independent-observation mean-estimation problem.

nodes.title: 13.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sequential-data models, covering factor-graph and forward-backward formulations for input-output hidden Markov models; Gaussian properties of latent-sequence inference; derivations and verification of Kalman filtering, smoothing, pairwise covariance, and gain equations; affine extensions of linear dynamical systems; connections between Kalman filtering, independent Gaussian maximum likelihood, and probabilistic PCA; limiting cases of noiseless observations and constant states; and verification of EM M-step updates for initial, transition, and emission parameters. It also includes a request to establish an initial condition for a recursion involving the quantities defined in equation (13.70).

This section develops probabilistic models for dependent sequential data, contrasting them with i.i.d. data and motivating stationary Markov assumptions for prediction. It covers Markov and state-space models, with detailed treatment of hidden Markov models, their EM and forward-backward/Baum-Welch learning, Viterbi decoding, extensions, and particle filtering. It then develops linear dynamical systems, including Kalman filtering, smoothing, likelihood evaluation, EM learning, Bayesian extensions, and nonlinear or non-Gaussian alternatives. The section concludes with exercises covering conditional independence, factor graphs, HMM inference and parameter updates, multiple sequences, Viterbi methods, input-output models, particle filtering, and derivations and applications of Kalman and smoothing algorithms.

nodes.title: 14 Combining Models
14.1. Bayesian Model Averaging
nodes.summary: The text introduces model combination, where input-dependent selection assigns different models to different regions, contrasting hard-split decision trees with soft probabilistic mixtures of experts and relating them to mixture density networks. It distinguishes this from Bayesian model averaging: mixture models can assign different observations to different components, whereas Bayesian averaging assumes one alternative model generates the entire data set and updates uncertainty over that model as data accumulate. These ideas also apply to predictive and conditional distributions. The section then introduces committees, which average predictions from several models and can be motivated through the bias–variance trade-off.

nodes.title: 14.2. Committees
nodes.summary: The text distinguishes model combination from Bayesian model averaging: combination allows different observations to arise from different latent components, whereas Bayesian averaging assumes one model generated the whole data set and updates uncertainty over models through p(h|X). It then introduces committees, especially prediction averaging and bootstrap aggregation (bagging), explaining their bias-variance motivation and showing that uncorrelated, zero-mean errors yield a 1/M reduction in expected error, while correlated errors limit practical gains. Finally, it introduces boosting and AdaBoost, which sequentially train weighted weak classifiers, emphasize previously misclassified points, and combine the resulting classifiers by weighted voting; the framework is defined for binary targets and can be extended to regression.

nodes.title: 14.3. Boosting
14.3.1 Minimizing exponential error
nodes.summary: The text explains AdaBoost’s final weighted-vote prediction, the adaptive reweighting of misclassified examples, and the greater influence assigned to accurate base classifiers. It describes the decision-stump illustration and then derives AdaBoost as sequential minimization of an exponential loss: fixing earlier learners, the loss becomes a weighted error for the new learner, yields the coefficient based on weighted error, and produces the standard data-weight update. It also notes that the common scaling factor does not affect classification and begins an analysis of exponential loss, showing that its unrestricted population minimizer is one-half the log posterior-odds.

nodes.title: 14.3.2 Error functions for boosting
nodes.summary: The text completes the AdaBoost derivation by showing how exponential-error minimization yields the classifier coefficient, standard data-weight update, and sign-based final prediction. It explains that exponential-loss minimization targets the log odds, compares exponential loss with cross-entropy, hinge, and misclassification losses, and discusses its simplicity, lack of probabilistic interpretation and multiclass generalization, and sensitivity to outliers. The same additive-model viewpoint motivates multiclass and regression boosting, including residual fitting under squared error and more robust absolute-error alternatives. The text then introduces tree-based models, which partition input space into axis-aligned regions and use binary decision trees to select a simple model, focusing on CART and mentioning ID3 and C4.5.

The section motivates boosting by contrasting it with ordinary model averaging, whose benefits are limited by correlated errors. It presents AdaBoost as a sequential committee method that reweights training examples toward previous mistakes, assigns larger voting weights to more accurate weak learners, and combines their binary predictions by weighted majority vote. The algorithm and its exponential-loss derivation are developed, including weighted error, learner coefficients, data-weight updates, and the log-odds interpretation. The section compares exponential loss with other classification losses, discusses its strengths and limitations, and explains extensions of the additive boosting framework to multiclass classification and regression, including residual fitting and robust absolute-error methods. It concludes by introducing tree-based base models and decision-tree approaches such as CART, ID3, and C4.5.

nodes.title: 14.4. Tree-based Models
nodes.summary: The text contrasts robust absolute-error loss with squared error, then introduces CART tree-based models as interpretable systems that recursively partition input space with hard, axis-aligned binary splits and assign simple models to leaves. It explains tree representation, regression predictions, greedy tree growth, complexity-based pruning, and classification criteria such as cross-entropy and the Gini index. It also discusses interpretability alongside instability, inefficient axis-aligned boundaries, and discontinuous piecewise-constant regression predictions. Finally, it motivates conditional mixture models and hierarchical mixtures of experts, which use soft probabilistic splits and probabilistic conditional leaf models to overcome these restrictions.

nodes.title: 14.5. Conditional Mixture Models
14.5.1 Mixtures of linear regression models
nodes.summary: The text develops conditional mixture models, focusing first on mixtures of linear regressions and their EM estimation. It defines the conditional Gaussian mixture, latent component indicators, responsibilities, expected complete-data likelihood, and M-step updates for mixing coefficients, regression weights via weighted least squares, and shared noise precision. A two-line example illustrates convergence, responsibilities, improved multimodal fit, and the limitation of input-independent mixing weights, motivating mixture-of-experts extensions. It then introduces mixtures of logistic regression models, giving their conditional distribution and parameters.

nodes.title: 14.5.2 Mixtures of logistic models
nodes.summary: The text presents mixtures of logistic regression models and introduces mixtures of experts. It explains the likelihood formulation, latent component indicators, EM responsibilities, expected complete-data likelihood, mixing-coefficient update, and independent weighted logistic-regression M-step solved by IRLS, including the relevant gradient and Hessian. It notes extension to softmax mixtures and illustrates mixture behavior and its advantage over a single linear model through figures. Finally, it defines mixture-of-experts models, where input-dependent gating functions select among specialized component experts.

nodes.title: 14.5.3 Mixtures of experts
nodes.summary: The text completes the EM treatment of mixtures of logistic regression models: mixing weights are updated from responsibilities, while each component’s logistic parameters are independently fitted by weighted IRLS using the given gradient and Hessian. It illustrates the benefit over a single logistic classifier and notes extension to softmax mixtures. It then introduces mixtures of experts, in which input-dependent softmax gating functions select expert distributions, discusses EM/IRLS fitting, hierarchical mixtures of experts as probabilistic decision trees, their Bayesian treatment, and their relationship to mixture density networks. The section concludes with exercises on Bayesian model averaging, committee error derivations, Jensen-based error inequalities for convex losses, and the conditions under which weighted committee predictions remain within the range of member predictions.

This section motivates conditional mixture models by examining the instability and structural limitations of hard, axis-aligned decision trees. It develops EM-based mixtures of linear and logistic regression models, covering latent assignments, responsibilities, likelihoods, and weighted regression or IRLS updates, with examples showing their ability to model multimodal or nonlinear behavior. It then introduces mixtures of experts with input-dependent gating, including softmax and hierarchical forms that act as probabilistic decision trees, and discusses Bayesian treatments and connections to mixture density networks. The section concludes with exercises on Bayesian averaging, committee predictions, error analysis, convex-loss inequalities, and prediction-range conditions.

nodes.title: Combining Models and Committee Model Exercises
nodes.summary: The page discusses mixture density networks and exercises on combining models. It covers marginalizing latent variables and model indices in predictive distributions, contrasts Bayesian model averaging with within-model latent variables, derives committee error relationships, applies Jensen's inequality to sum-of-squares and general convex losses, and establishes that bounded weighted committee predictions require nonnegative coefficients summing to one.

nodes.title: Exercises on Boosting, Trees, and Mixture Regression Models
nodes.summary: The page presents exercises on AdaBoost and exponential-loss minimization, including parameter updates, variational solutions, and the lack of a corresponding normalized probabilistic model. It covers boosting with least-squares residual fitting, the mean as the optimal constant squared-error prediction, and comparisons of tree impurity and misclassification measures. The remaining exercises address extensions, likelihood verification, EM re-estimation, and conditional-mean prediction in mixtures of linear regression models, including limitations for multimodal targets.

nodes.title: 14.15 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The exercises derive and analyze boosting, error minimization, and model-combination methods. They cover the AdaBoost coefficient update, variational minimization of exponential loss, the lack of a normalized probabilistic interpretation for AdaBoost's exponential error, and residual fitting for squared-error boosting. They compare tree impurity and classification measures, extend mixtures of linear regressions to vector targets, verify and derive their likelihood and EM updates, and establish the conditional-mean prediction for such mixtures. They then extend mixture logistic regression to multiclass softmax mixtures with EM and investigate hierarchical mixtures, proving their equivalence to flat mixtures with arbitrary x-dependent weights but demonstrating that this equivalence generally fails when the weights are restricted to linear logistic or softmax models.

nodes.title: 14.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents two exercises on combining models: deriving EM for a mixture of softmax classifiers in a multiclass setting, and analyzing hierarchical conditional mixtures. Hierarchical mixtures collapse to ordinary mixtures when their coefficients are fixed or arbitrary functions of the input, but not generally when both levels use linear logistic or softmax gating functions; a two-level, three-component counterexample demonstrates this limitation.

This section surveys methods for combining predictive models, beginning with Bayesian model averaging, committees, prediction averaging, and bagging, and then develops boosting, especially AdaBoost, through sequential reweighting and exponential-loss optimization. It covers extensions to multiclass classification and regression, including residual and robust-loss methods. It then presents tree-based models such as CART, their construction, criteria, pruning, interpretability, and limitations, motivating conditional mixture models and mixtures of experts with soft input-dependent gating. These models include mixtures of linear and logistic regressions, EM estimation, hierarchical and softmax mixtures, Bayesian interpretations, and connections to mixture density networks. Exercises reinforce model-combination error analysis, convex-loss inequalities, boosting derivations, tree criteria, vector and multiclass mixture extensions, likelihood and EM calculations, conditional prediction, and the expressive limitations of hierarchical gating.

The section covers dimensionality reduction and latent-variable modeling, beginning with conventional PCA and its variance, reconstruction-error, computational, and application perspectives. It develops probabilistic and Bayesian PCA, factor analysis, and kernel PCA, followed by a broad survey of nonlinear latent-variable and manifold methods, with exercises on their mathematical derivations, inference, estimation, reconstruction, and graphical-model properties. It then turns to dependent sequential data, presenting Markov, hidden Markov, state-space, Kalman, smoothing, particle-filtering, and related learning methods. Finally, it surveys predictive model combination through averaging, bagging, boosting, decision trees, conditional mixtures, and mixtures of experts, including their estimation procedures, extensions, interpretations, limitations, and exercises.

structure.summary: The section surveys the foundations and advanced methods of probabilistic machine learning and pattern recognition. It covers learning and generalization, curve fitting, regularization, probability distributions, Bayesian and frequentist inference, decision and information theory, density estimation, Gaussian and exponential-family models, regression and classification, neural and kernel methods, graphical and mixture models, and approximate inference. It continues with variational inference, expectation propagation, Monte Carlo and MCMC methods, evidence estimation, dimensionality reduction and latent-variable models, sequential models and filtering, and ensemble and mixture-of-experts methods. Exercises, applications, historical material, and theoretical derivations accompany the topics, and the section concludes with appendices on calculus of variations and Lagrange multipliers, references, and an index.

structure.title: Appendix A. Data Sets

nodes.title: Handwritten Digits
nodes.summary: The appendix introduces the book's illustrative data sets and directs readers to the book website for files and format details. It describes MNIST handwritten digits, including their origin, composition, preprocessing, visualization, and representative classification error rates. It then explains the synthetic Oil Flow data set, its pipeline-measurement motivation, dual-energy gamma attenuation method, estimation of the three fluid fractions, and the complication of stratified flow at low velocity.

nodes.title: Oil Flow
nodes.summary: The text introduces an MNIST example figure, then describes the synthetic Oil Flow data set: its dual-energy gamma-densitometry motivation, three flow geometries, six-beam 12-dimensional measurements, Poisson noise and generation procedure, data organization, applications, and manifold structure. It concludes with the 272-observation Old Faithful data set, consisting of eruption duration and subsequent waiting time, whose relationship is visibly predictive despite considerable variation.

nodes.title: Old Faithful
nodes.summary: The text describes manifold structure in oil-and-water flow observations under homogeneous, annular, and laminar configurations, including noise, nonlinearities, discontinuities, segmentation, and intersections. It then introduces the 272-observation Old Faithful data set of eruption durations and subsequent waiting times, noting their predictive relationship. Finally, it presents two recurring synthetic data sets: a noisy sinusoidal regression problem and a two-class Gaussian classification problem for which posterior probabilities and the optimal misclassification decision boundary are known.

nodes.title: Synthetic Data
nodes.summary: The text introduces figures for the Old Faithful data set and two synthetic data sets used throughout the book: a noisy sinusoidal regression set and a two-class Gaussian-based classification set. It specifies how both sets are generated and explains that the known distributions allow the true conditional or posterior probabilities and the optimal classification boundary to be visualized in Figures A.6 and A.7.

structure.summary: Appendix A presents the book’s illustrative data sets and points readers to the website for files and formats. It covers MNIST handwritten digits, the synthetic Oil Flow measurements and their physical motivation, generation, organization, applications, and complex manifold structure, and the predictive Old Faithful eruption and waiting-time observations. It also introduces recurring noisy sinusoidal regression and two-class Gaussian classification data sets, whose known distributions permit visualization of true probabilities and the optimal decision boundary.

structure.title: Appendix B. Probability Distributions

nodes.title: Bernoulli
nodes.summary: The appendix introduces key statistics for common exponential-family distributions and then details the Bernoulli distribution: its binary support, parameterization, probability mass function, expectation, variance, mode, entropy, relationship to the binomial distribution, and beta conjugate prior.

nodes.title: Beta
nodes.summary: The text presents the beta and binomial probability distributions. It defines the beta distribution on [0,1], gives its parameter constraints, density, mean, variance, and mode, and explains its Bernoulli conjugacy, prior-count interpretation, boundary behavior, uniform special case, and relationship to the Dirichlet distribution. It then defines the binomial distribution for counting successes in N Bernoulli trials, provides its probability mass function, moments, mode, and binomial-coefficient and factorial definitions, and notes its Bernoulli special case, Gaussian approximation for large N, and beta conjugate prior.

nodes.title: Binomial
nodes.summary: The text presents the beta, binomial, and Dirichlet probability distributions, giving their definitions, parameter constraints, densities, means, variances, modes, and relevant normalization functions. It explains beta–Bernoulli and Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy, interprets distribution parameters as effective observation counts, describes endpoint or boundary singularities, identifies the beta as the two-category Dirichlet, and notes that the binomial becomes Bernoulli for N = 1 and approximately Gaussian for large N. It also defines binomial coefficients and factorials, and gives Dirichlet covariance, expected log values, entropy, gamma-function normalization, and the digamma function.

nodes.title: Gamma
nodes.summary: This section introduces the Gamma and Gaussian probability distributions. It gives the Gamma density, parameter constraints, moments, mode, expected log value, entropy, conjugacy to Gaussian precision, and its relationship to the exponential distribution. It then defines the scalar Gaussian density and its mean, variance, mode, and entropy; explains precision and standard deviation; identifies the relevant Gaussian, Gamma, and Gaussian-Gamma conjugate priors; and begins the multivariate Gaussian description using a mean vector and symmetric covariance matrix.

nodes.title: Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text presents the Gamma, Gaussian, Gaussian-gamma, Gaussian-Wishart, and multinomial distributions, giving their parameter constraints, densities, moments, modes, entropies, and key conjugacy relationships. It explains precision and covariance parameterizations; describes important Gaussian properties including closure under sums, transformations, marginalization, and conditioning, the central limit theorem, and maximum-entropy behavior; provides Gaussian marginal and conditional formulas for linear and partitioned models; defines the joint conjugate priors for unknown Gaussian means and precisions; and concludes with the probability, moments, covariance, and entropy of a one-hot multinomial distribution.

nodes.title: Gaussian Priors and Multinomial Distribution
nodes.summary: The page covers Gaussian marginal distributions, the Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart conjugate priors for unknown Gaussian means and precisions, their scalar relationship, and the multinomial distribution with its defining constraints, probability expression, moments, covariance, and entropy.

nodes.title: Multinomial
nodes.summary: The text presents Gaussian marginalization and conjugate priors for Gaussian parameters, including the Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart distributions and their scalar relationship. It then defines one-hot multinomial variables and the multinomial count distribution, giving their constraints, moments, entropy, combinatorial coefficient, and Dirichlet conjugate prior. It clarifies the terminology linking normal and Gaussian distributions, and introduces Student's t-distribution as the result of integrating out a Gamma-distributed Gaussian precision, including its historical naming.

nodes.title: Normal
nodes.summary: The text presents the multinomial distribution, including its parameter constraints, probability formula, moments, covariance, combinatorial coefficient, and Dirichlet conjugate prior. It then clarifies terminology for normal/Gaussian-related distributions and introduces Student’s t-distribution, its historical naming, and its derivation as a Gaussian model with gamma-distributed precision integrated out.

nodes.title: Student’s t
nodes.summary: The text presents the multinomial distribution, including its probability formula, parameter constraints, combinatorial interpretation, moments, and Dirichlet conjugate prior; clarifies terminology for normal/Gaussian-related distributions; develops univariate and multivariate Student’s t-distributions, their Bayesian origins, parameters, moments, special Cauchy case, Gaussian limit, and robustness; and defines the uniform distribution with its density, moments, entropy, and affine transformation property.

nodes.title: Uniform
nodes.summary: The text presents univariate and multivariate Student’s t-distributions, including their parameterization, moments, mode, degrees-of-freedom interpretation, Cauchy special case, Mahalanobis-distance form, Gaussian limiting case, and robustness to outliers. It then defines the continuous uniform distribution on [a, b], gives its density, mean, variance, and entropy, and describes the affine transformation from a standard uniform variable.

nodes.title: Von Mises
nodes.summary: The text presents the von Mises circular Gaussian distribution, giving its density, periodicity, interpretation of its location and concentration parameters, origin-dependence caveat, and Gaussian approximation for high concentration. It then defines the Wishart distribution as the multivariate Gaussian precision-matrix conjugate prior, including its density and normalization, mean, expected log determinant, entropy, parameter and positive-definiteness requirements, and its reduction to a one-dimensional gamma distribution.

nodes.title: Wishart
nodes.summary: The text introduces the von Mises circular analogue of a Gaussian, giving its density, periodicity, parameter interpretations, origin-dependence caveat, and Gaussian approximation for high concentration. It then defines the Wishart distribution as the multivariate Gaussian precision-matrix conjugate prior, providing its density and normalization, mean, expected log determinant, entropy, parameter requirements, matrix conditions, and its one-dimensional reduction to a gamma distribution.

structure.summary: This appendix surveys common probability distributions and their statistics, parameterizations, densities or mass functions, moments, modes, entropies, normalization functions, boundary conditions, special cases, approximations, transformations, and conjugate-prior relationships. It covers Bernoulli, beta, binomial, Dirichlet, gamma, Gaussian, Gaussian-gamma, Gaussian-Wishart, multinomial, Student’s t, uniform, von Mises, and Wishart distributions, together with Gaussian marginalization and conditioning, exponential-family interpretations, effective-count meanings, and the relevant links among these distributions.

structure.title: Appendix C. Properties of Matrices

nodes.title: Basic Matrix Identities
nodes.summary: The appendix reviews basic matrix notation and identities for transposes, inverses, efficient inverse transformations, and the Woodbury formula, then defines linear independence and matrix rank. It introduces trace and determinant, including trace commutation and cyclic properties and the signed permutation-sum definition of the determinant, while noting assumptions about valid dimensions and existing inverses and providing references for further study.

nodes.title: Traces and Determinants
nodes.summary: The text develops matrix properties, including efficient inverse identities, the Woodbury formula, linear independence and rank, trace and determinant definitions and identities, and basic vector and matrix derivative notation, culminating in the derivative of x^T a with respect to x.

nodes.title: Matrix Derivatives
nodes.summary: The text presents determinant properties, including permutation-based definition, the 2 × 2 formula, product and inverse rules, Sylvester’s theorem, and the matrix determinant lemma. It then defines vector and matrix derivatives and lists fundamental differentiation rules for products, inverses, log-determinants, and traces, including derivatives with respect to a matrix. Finally, it introduces the eigenvector equation Au_i = λ_i u_i for square matrices.

nodes.title: Eigenvector Equation
nodes.summary: The text presents fundamental matrix-calculus identities for products, inverses, determinants, and traces, then develops eigenvalue and eigenvector theory for square and especially symmetric matrices. It covers characteristic equations, rank, real eigenvalues, orthonormal eigenvectors, orthogonal transformations, spectral diagonalization, inverse, determinant, and trace formulas. It concludes by defining positive definite and positive semidefinite matrices through quadratic forms and eigenvalue signs, emphasizing that positive definiteness is unrelated to all matrix entries being positive.

structure.summary: This appendix presents foundational matrix notation and identities, including transpose and inverse operations, efficient inverse formulas, the Woodbury identity, rank and linear independence, and the properties and definitions of traces and determinants. It develops vector and matrix calculus rules for products, inverses, determinants, log-determinants, traces, and related scalar expressions. It then introduces eigenvalues and eigenvectors, with emphasis on symmetric matrices, covering characteristic equations, orthonormal spectral decompositions, and eigenvalue-based formulas for inverses, determinants, and traces. Finally, it defines positive definite and positive semidefinite matrices through quadratic forms and eigenvalue signs, clarifying that positive definiteness is unrelated to entrywise positivity.

structure.title: Appendix D. Calculus of Variations
structure.summary: The text introduces functionals as operators on functions and explains calculus of variations as the search for functions that optimize them, with examples including curve length and entropy. It defines functional derivatives through arbitrary small function perturbations, shows that stationarity implies a zero functional derivative, and derives the Euler–Lagrange equation for integral functionals depending on a function and its first derivative under fixed boundary conditions. An example yields a second-order differential equation. The text also covers the simpler case where the integrand has no derivative dependence, normalization constraints in probability optimization via Lagrange multipliers, and extensions to multidimensional variables.

structure.title: Appendix E. Lagrange Multipliers
structure.summary: The appendix explains Lagrange multipliers as a symmetric method for finding constrained stationary points. It derives the equality-constraint method geometrically from the normal gradients of the objective and constraint surfaces, defines the Lagrangian, and shows that stationarity with respect to variables and multipliers enforces both gradient alignment and the constraint. A quadratic two-variable example is solved explicitly. It then treats inequality constraints, distinguishing inactive and active cases and deriving the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, including complementary slackness and multiplier-sign requirements. The sign convention for minimization is given, followed by the formulation for multiple equality and inequality constraints and a note that the approach extends to constrained functional derivatives.

The references comprise books, journal articles, conference papers, reports, theses, encyclopedia entries, and reprints by authors ranging from Platt, Vapnik, Schölkopf, Rasmussen, Bishop, Tipping, Williams, and Rumelhart to Shannon, Viterbi, Quinlan, Sutton, and others.

It includes books and a wide range of scholarly publications and other reference materials.
